channel.title: From First Principles
channel.description: Data science innovation from first principles.

item.title: Bayesian Universal Modeling
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
In the conditionally sufficient statistics post, a streaming service prompted households to turn on a new playback setting and measured how it changed hours watched and rebuffers per play. One universal model handled everything that made that experiment hard: households with several profiles, a prompt that profiles could ignore, a ramp from 5% to 50% of new accounts, and a ratio metric. It reported each effect with a standard error, and it could do so from a compressed dataset of 8 rows.

The product manager reads the report and asks a different question: what is the probability that the setting cuts rebuffers per play by at least 10% for the profiles that use it? A standard error does not answer that. A posterior distribution does, and in the posterior distribution post we argued that a posterior is what decision makers want. The bootstrap post showed how to get one for a least squares fit without writing a likelihood, with the Bayesian bootstrap.

This post combines the two. We first show that the Bayesian bootstrap gives a posterior for every design the universal model covers, and then that it can be computed in one pass over the data, or from the compressed dataset itself.

The data in this post is synthetic and the scenario is educational. It does not describe a production system.

The Universal Model

The experiment

We use the same simulated experiment as the previous post. Each account enters on and is prompted, , with probability , which ramps from 5% to 50%. Each profile of the account has covariates measured before the experiment: hours per day , tenure , whether it is a kids profile, and its main device, coded as the indicators mobile and web. A prompted profile turns the setting on, , if it is a complier. We measure its hours per day , its plays and its rebuffers .

The code is the code of the previous post, folded. It simulates the 20,000 accounts, prepares the profile rows, and fits the universal model with its cluster robust standard errors. The only change is that the coefficient matrix is called beta, because in this post is the number of posterior draws.

Code 
simulate_accounts <- function(n_accounts = 20000, propensity = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50), force_Z = NULL,
                              full_compliance = FALSE, one_profile = FALSE) {
  accounts <- tibble(
    account = seq_len(n_accounts),
    day = sample.int(length(propensity), n_accounts, replace = TRUE, prob = rev(seq_along(propensity))),
    n_profiles = if (one_profile) 1L else pmin(1L + rpois(n_accounts, 1.2), 5L),
    quality = rnorm(n_accounts, 0, 0.5),                       # shared by the account's profiles
    engagement = rnorm(n_accounts, 0, 0.5)                     # account part of engagement
  ) |>
    mutate(Z = rbinom(n(), 1, propensity[day]), Z = if (is.null(force_Z)) Z else force_Z)
  accounts[rep(accounts$account, accounts$n_profiles), ] |>
    mutate(
      profile = sequence(accounts$n_profiles),
      kids = rbinom(n(), 1, if_else(profile == 1, 0.05, 0.3)),
      device = sample(c("tv", "mobile", "web"), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.35, 0.15)),
      engagement_p = engagement + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.8),          # the profile's engagement, not observed
      x1 = rlnorm(n(), 0.7 - 0.12 * day - 0.6 * kids + 0.3 * engagement_p, 0.6),
      x2 = rgamma(n(), 2, 1) * (1.2 - 0.15 * day),
      complier = rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-0.3 + 0.5 * log(x1) + 0.6 * engagement_p - 0.8 * kids)),
      T = if (full_compliance) Z else Z * complier,
      y = 0.5 + 0.8 * x1 + 0.1 * x2 + 0.5 * engagement_p + quality +
        T * (0.3 + 0.15 * x1 - 0.2 * kids) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5 + 0.3 * x1),
      D = 1 + rpois(n(), exp(1 + 0.4 * log(x1) + 0.3 * engagement_p + 0.2 * (device == "tv")) * (1 + 0.15 * T)),
      N = rpois(n(), D * 0.08 * exp(-0.4 * T * (1 + 0.5 * (device == "mobile")) + 0.4 * quality - 0.2 * engagement_p))
    )
}

propensity <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50)
x_cols <- c("x1", "x2", "kids", "mobile", "web")
x_ref <- c(x1 = 2, x2 = 2, kids = 0, mobile = 0, web = 0)
y_cols <- c("y", "N", "D", "TN", "TD")
d <- length(x_cols) + 1                              # intercept and k covariates
o <- length(y_cols)                                  # number of outcome columns

prepare <- function(profiles, ramp = TRUE) {
  e_hat <- profiles |>
    distinct(account, day, Z) |>
    group_by(day) |>
    summarise(e_hat = mean(Z))
  profiles |>
    left_join(e_hat, by = "day") |>
    mutate(w = if (ramp) if_else(Z == 1, 1 / e_hat, 1 / (1 - e_hat)) else 1,     # inverse propensity weight
           mobile = as.numeric(device == "mobile"), web = as.numeric(device == "web"),
           TN = T * N, TD = T * D)
}

centered <- function(df) {
  r <- cbind(1, sweep(as.matrix(df[x_cols]), 2, x_ref))
  colnames(r) <- c("1", paste0(x_cols, "_c"))
  r
}

design <- function(df) {
  r <- centered(df)
  list(M_1 = cbind(r, `colnames<-`(df$Z * r, paste0("Z*", colnames(r)))),     # first stage: instruments
       M_2 = cbind(r, `colnames<-`(df$T * r, paste0("T*", colnames(r)))))     # second stage: regressors
}

fit_rows <- function(df) {
  m <- design(df)
  Y <- as.matrix(df[y_cols])
  M1_W_M2 <- crossprod(m$M_1 * df$w, m$M_2)
  beta <- solve(M1_W_M2, crossprod(m$M_1 * df$w, Y))
  eps <- Y - m$M_2 %*% beta
  inner <- do.call(cbind, map(seq_len(o), \(l) rowsum(m$M_1 * (df$w * eps[, l]), df$account)))
  M1_W_M2_inv <- kronecker(diag(o), solve(M1_W_M2))
  list(beta = beta, V = M1_W_M2_inv %*% crossprod(inner) %*% t(M1_W_M2_inv))
}

complier_mean <- function(df) {
  if (all(df$T == df$Z)) return(colSums(df$w * df[x_cols]) / sum(df$w))
  arm <- df |>
    group_by(Z) |>
    summarise(across(all_of(x_cols), \(v) sum(w * T * v) / sum(w)), T = sum(w * T) / sum(w))
  unlist(arm[arm$Z == 1, x_cols] - arm[arm$Z == 0, x_cols]) / (arm$T[arm$Z == 1] - arm$T[arm$Z == 0])
}

gradient <- function(f, theta, kappa = 1e-20) {
  map_dbl(seq_along(theta), \(i) Im(f(theta + 1i * kappa * (seq_along(theta) == i))) / kappa)
}

effect_functions <- function(x_C, x_ref, cols) {
  delta <- c(rep(0, length(x_ref) + 1), 1, x_C - x_ref)
  line <- \(beta, col) sum(delta * beta[, col])
  effect_list <- list(tau_LATE = \(beta) line(beta, "y"))
  if ("TN" %in% cols) effect_list$tau_R <- \(beta) line(beta, "TN") / line(beta, "TD") -
    (line(beta, "TN") - line(beta, "N")) / (line(beta, "TD") - line(beta, "D"))
  effect_list
}

effects <- function(fit, x_C, x_ref) {
  effect_list <- effect_functions(x_C, x_ref, colnames(fit$beta))
  theta <- as.vector(fit$beta)
  map_dfr(names(effect_list), \(nm) {
    f <- \(th) effect_list[[nm]](matrix(th, nrow(fit$beta), dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(fit$beta))))
    grad <- gradient(f, theta)
    tibble(effect = nm, estimate = Re(f(theta)), se = sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% fit$V %*% grad)))
  })
}

set.seed(2026)
profiles <- simulate_accounts()
df <- prepare(profiles)
fit <- fit_rows(df)
x_C <- complier_mean(df)
css <- effects(fit, x_C, x_ref)
css
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  effect   estimate      se
  <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl>
1 tau_LATE   0.664  0.0572 
2 tau_R     -0.0255 0.00410

The model

The universal model is two stage least squares with weights and cluster robust standard errors. With the covariates centered at a fixed reference point, standing for , its two stages are

with covariates. Each account carries the inverse propensity weight if prompted and if not, where is the share of that day’s accounts that were prompted. One fit holds five outcome columns: hours , rebuffers , plays , and and , which equal and for profiles with the setting on and 0 otherwise.

Stacking the instruments into , the regressors into , and the weights into , the coefficients are

a matrix with one column per outcome, .

The model rests on three assumptions about the design.

(A1) Accounts are independent of each other. Profiles of the same account may be correlated in any way.

(A2) Within a cohort, the prompt is randomized with probability , independently of everything else.

(A3) The prompt affects a profile’s outcomes only through , and no profile turns the setting on only when it is not prompted.

The effects

The treatment line is fit to the compliers, so the effect for the compliers, the LATE, is the treatment line read at the compliers’ mean covariates , estimated as a ratio of two intent to treat effects:

Write for the treatment line of the outcome read at , and similarly for the other outcomes. Then is the compliers’ mean rebuffers with the setting on, , and is their mean rebuffers with it off, . The effect on rebuffers per play is

The product manager’s question is about the relative change in rebuffers per play,

a third function of the same coefficients. The previous post computed standard errors with the delta method, which needs the gradient of each effect and the joint covariance of all the coefficients. Because we simulated the data, we know the true effects. We simulate the same accounts twice, once with every account prompted and once with none, and compare the compliers in the two worlds.

Code 
truth_pair <- function(seed, n_accounts = 1e6) {
  set.seed(seed)
  p1 <- simulate_accounts(n_accounts, force_Z = 1)
  set.seed(seed)
  p0 <- simulate_accounts(n_accounts, force_Z = 0)
  C <- p1$complier == 1                                      # the same profiles comply in both worlds
  rate_1 <- sum(p1$N[C]) / sum(p1$D[C])
  rate_0 <- sum(p0$N[C]) / sum(p0$D[C])
  c(tau_LATE = mean(p1$y[C] - p0$y[C]), tau_R = rate_1 - rate_0, rho_R = rate_1 / rate_0 - 1)
}
truth <- colMeans(do.call(rbind, map(1:2, truth_pair)))
invisible(gc())
truth
   tau_LATE       tau_R       rho_R 
 0.61334648 -0.02724864 -0.37012026

The compressed dataset

The previous post compressed the profile rows in two steps. Each account becomes an account summary , the vector of the sums over its profiles

where is the row of all outcome columns. Accounts with the same prompt and cohort share and , so each stratum becomes one compressed row with three fields: the number of accounts , the first moments , which give , and the second moments , which give the cluster robust covariance. The compressed dataset has 8 compressed rows.

Why a Posterior

The previous post’s report reads: the LATE on hours is 0.664 with a standard error of 0.057, and the effect on rebuffers per play is -0.0255 with a standard error of 0.0041. These describe a sampling distribution. The standard error says how much the estimate would move if we reran the experiment on new accounts, while the effect stays fixed. As the posterior distribution post explained, that does not support the statement “there is a 95% probability that the effect is in this interval”, and it does not answer the product manager. A posterior, , does both: it treats the effect as uncertain and the data as fixed, so the probability that is the share of the posterior below .

A conjugate Bayesian model for this experiment would be hard to write. It would need a likelihood for hours, rebuffers and plays jointly, correlated within accounts, with a first stage for compliance, and it would be wrong in ways that make the posterior too narrow, as we saw for the Gaussian likelihood in the bootstrap post. That post showed the alternative. The Bayesian bootstrap puts the prior and the likelihood on the population instead of on the model, and the model is used only to define which summary of the population we want. The universal model is a summary of the population like any other, so the same idea should work. The rest of this post checks whether it does, and how to compute it at scale.

A Posterior for the Universal Model

The unit that gets a weight is the account

The Bayesian bootstrap treats the population as a mix of the units we observed, in unknown shares, and draws the shares from their posterior. The unit has to be the unit of independence. Here that is the account, by (A1): profiles of the same account are correlated, so a population is a mix of whole accounts, each with all its profiles. We add the two assumptions of the bootstrap post at the level of accounts.

(A4) The population contains only the kinds of accounts we observed. Writing for the population made only of copies of account , with its cohort, prompt, profiles and outcomes, the population is for unknown shares that add up to 1.

(A5) The prior on the shares , where is the number of accounts, is a Dirichlet distribution with zero pseudo-counts.

As the bootstrap post derived, the posterior of is then Dirichlet, and a draw is

is the account’s bootstrap weight. It is a weight but not a probability weight; is the probability weight. Every profile of an account shares the account’s bootstrap weight.

The effects as functions of the population

To compute an effect on a drawn population, we write each step of the universal model as a function of . With , an average over is a -weighted average over our accounts.

  1. The propensity. The share of a cohort’s accounts that were prompted is and the inverse propensity weights follow from it. Each draw of the population has its own share of prompted accounts, so the propensity is recomputed in every draw.
  2. The coefficients. The universal model solves on our sample. On the population the sum over accounts becomes a -weighted sum, so the solution is which is the universal model fit with the combined weight on every profile of account .
  3. The compliers’ mean. is the ratio of intent to treat effects, with each expectation a weighted average with weights .
  4. The effects. , and are the same functions of and as before.

Every step is unchanged when all the are multiplied by the same constant: the propensity is a ratio, and the constant cancels between the inverse and the second sum of , and in the ratio . So we can use the bootstrap weights directly, without normalizing them. With all the steps reproduce the estimates of the previous post exactly.

At the true population, is the LATE: the previous post derived that the treatment line is fit to the compliers’ effects under (A1)–(A3), and that derivation holds for any population that satisfies them. The posterior of is therefore a posterior for the LATE.

One draw, step by step

draw_rows computes the three effects on the profile rows for one vector of bootstrap weights, one per account. It recomputes the propensity, refits the model with the combined weights, and recomputes the compliers’ mean. rows_data prepares the matrices once, because they do not change across draws.

Code 
rows_data <- function(df) {
  accounts <- df |>
    distinct(account, day, Z) |>
    arrange(account)
  stopifnot(all(accounts$account == seq_len(nrow(accounts))))   # accounts numbered 1, 2, ...
  c(design(df), list(Y = as.matrix(df[y_cols]), r = centered(df), account = df$account, Z = df$Z, T = df$T,
                     accounts = accounts))
}

effect_values <- function(beta, x_C_c) {        # x_C_c: the compliers' mean in centered units
  delta <- c(rep(0, d), 1, x_C_c)
  l <- colSums(delta * beta)                     # each outcome's treatment line at the compliers' mean
  rate_1 <- l[["TN"]] / l[["TD"]]
  rate_0 <- (l[["TN"]] - l[["N"]]) / (l[["TD"]] - l[["D"]])
  c(tau_LATE = l[["y"]], tau_R = rate_1 - rate_0, rho_R = rate_1 / rate_0 - 1)
}

draw_rows <- function(rows, xi, ramp = TRUE, encouraged = TRUE) {
  acc <- rows$accounts
  # 1. The propensity: the xi-weighted share of each cohort's accounts that were prompted
  e_day <- rowsum(xi * acc$Z, acc$day)[, 1] / rowsum(xi, acc$day)[, 1]
  w <- if (ramp) if_else(acc$Z == 1, 1 / e_day[acc$day], 1 / (1 - e_day[acc$day])) else 1
  # 2. The coefficients, with the combined weight xi_a w_a on every profile of account a
  w_ap <- (xi * w)[rows$account]
  beta <- solve(crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$M_2), crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$Y))
  colnames(beta) <- y_cols
  # 3. The compliers' mean: ratio of the weighted intent to treat effects on T (1, x) and T
  x_C_c <- if (encouraged) {
    arm <- \(z) colSums(rows$r * (w_ap * rows$T * (rows$Z == z))) / sum(w_ap * (rows$Z == z))
    diff <- arm(1) - arm(0)
    diff[-1] / diff[1]
  } else colSums(rows$r * w_ap)[-1] / sum(w_ap)
  # 4. The effects
  effect_values(beta, x_C_c)
}

rows <- rows_data(df)
draw_rows(rows, rep(1, nrow(rows$accounts)))
   tau_LATE       tau_R       rho_R 
 0.66391019 -0.02547824 -0.33778566

With every bootstrap weight equal to 1, the draw reproduces the estimates of the previous post, 0.6639 for the LATE and -0.02548 for the ratio. Now we draw one vector of bootstrap weights. Here are the profile rows of two accounts, a prompted one and an unprompted one, with their weights:

Code 
set.seed(1)
xi <- rexp(nrow(rows$accounts))
example_accounts <- c(
  df |>
    group_by(account) |>
    filter(first(Z) == 1, n() >= 3, any(T == 1), any(T == 0)) |>
    pull(account) |>
    first(),
  df |>
    group_by(account) |>
    filter(first(Z) == 0, n() >= 2) |>
    pull(account) |>
    first())
df |>
  filter(account %in% example_accounts) |>
  mutate(xi = xi[account]) |>
  select(account, profile, day, Z, T, x1, y, w, xi)
# A tibble: 7 × 9
  account profile   day     Z     T    x1      y     w    xi
    <int>   <int> <int> <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1       1       1     2     0     0 1.89  0.0541  1.12 0.755
2       1       2     2     0     0 0.867 0.377   1.12 0.755
3      15       1     1     1     1 1.67  3.02   19.5  1.05 
4      15       2     1     1     0 2.21  1.96   19.5  1.05 
5      15       3     1     1     0 0.704 0.426  19.5  1.05 
6      15       4     1     1     0 0.481 0.173  19.5  1.05 
7      15       5     1     1     0 5.61  4.87   19.5  1.05

Each account’s weight is shared by its profiles. In this draw the prompted account 15 counts 1.05 times, and the unprompted account 1 counts 0.76 times. The drawn population also has its own propensities:

Code 
rows$accounts |>
  mutate(xi = xi) |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(e_hat = mean(Z), e_draw = sum(xi * Z) / sum(xi))
# A tibble: 4 × 3
    day  e_hat e_draw
  <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1     1 0.0512 0.0530
2     2 0.106  0.104 
3     3 0.247  0.248 
4     4 0.499  0.497

e_hat is the share prompted in our sample, and e_draw is the share in the drawn population. They differ by a fraction of a percentage point, and the inverse propensity weights follow e_draw. The draw’s effects are

Code 
draw_rows(rows, xi)
   tau_LATE       tau_R       rho_R 
 0.63926109 -0.03505879 -0.43253513

The posterior

We repeat this with draws.

Code 
set.seed(2)
B <- 1000
Xi <- matrix(rexp(nrow(rows$accounts) * B), ncol = B)
time_rows <- system.time({
  post <- map(seq_len(B), \(b) draw_rows(rows, Xi[, b])) |>
    do.call(what = rbind)
})[["elapsed"]]
head(post, 3)
      tau_LATE       tau_R      rho_R
[1,] 0.6683106 -0.02101254 -0.2865788
[2,] 0.6969682 -0.03455162 -0.4242041
[3,] 0.6891561 -0.01692444 -0.2301193

Each row is one draw of the population, and each column one effect. The three effects come from the same draws, so their posteriors are joint, and any function of them has a posterior too.

Code 
post_tab <- tibble(
  effect = colnames(post),
  `posterior mean` = colMeans(post),
  `posterior sd` = apply(post, 2, sd),
  `2.5%` = apply(post, 2, quantile, 0.025),
  `97.5%` = apply(post, 2, quantile, 0.975),
  `previous post: estimate` = c(css$estimate, NA),
  `previous post: se` = c(css$se, NA),
  truth = truth[colnames(post)])
post_tab |>
  kable(digits = 4)
Code 
as_tibble(post) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "effect") |>
  mutate(effect = factor(effect, levels = c("tau_LATE", "tau_R", "rho_R"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(effect = factor(names(truth), levels = c("tau_LATE", "tau_R", "rho_R")), value = truth),
             aes(xintercept = value), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~effect, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "draws") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)

Figure 1 shows the three posteriors. The product manager’s answer is the share of draws in which rebuffers per play fall by at least 10%. We also ask for larger cuts:

Code 
c(`P(rho_R < -10%)` = mean(post[, "rho_R"] < -0.10),
  `P(rho_R < -20%)` = mean(post[, "rho_R"] < -0.20),
  `P(rho_R < -30%)` = mean(post[, "rho_R"] < -0.30),
  `P(tau_LATE > 0)` = mean(post[, "tau_LATE"] > 0))
P(rho_R < -10%) P(rho_R < -20%) P(rho_R < -30%) P(tau_LATE > 0) 
          1.000           0.995           0.798           1.000

Every draw has rebuffers per play falling by at least 10%, so the posterior probability is 1.000 up to the resolution of 1,000 draws. A cut of at least 20% has probability 0.995, and a cut of at least 30% has probability 0.80. None of these numbers needed a delta method or a joint covariance: was computed on each draw, like the other effects.

Does the posterior agree with the sandwich?

The posterior standard deviations in Table 1 are close to the previous post’s standard errors: 0.0583 against 0.0572 for the LATE, and 0.00424 against 0.00410 for the ratio. With 1,000 draws, a posterior standard deviation carries Monte Carlo noise of about . Why should they agree?

The bootstrap post linearized a weighted least squares draw around the estimate and found the sandwich. The same argument works here. A draw is a smooth function of the weighted sums over accounts, and each weighted sum moves from its value at by (the account’s contribution). To first order, an effect’s draw is

where is account ’s influence on the effect, the change in per unit change in the account’s weight. The bootstrap weights are independent with variance 1, so the posterior variance is approximately , a sum of squared influences over accounts. The previous post’s cluster robust variance is also a sum of squared influences over accounts, with one difference: it held and fixed, so its only describes how the account moves . The bootstrap also moves the propensities and the compliers’ mean. Taddy et al. (2016) show the same first order equivalence for least squares in digital experiments.

How much do the extra terms matter? We rerun the same draws with the compliers’ mean held at its estimate.

Code 
draw_fixed_x_C <- function(rows, xi, x_C_c) {
  acc <- rows$accounts
  e_day <- rowsum(xi * acc$Z, acc$day)[, 1] / rowsum(xi, acc$day)[, 1]
  w_ap <- (xi * if_else(acc$Z == 1, 1 / e_day[acc$day], 1 / (1 - e_day[acc$day])))[rows$account]
  beta <- solve(crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$M_2), crossprod(rows$M_1 * w_ap, rows$Y))
  colnames(beta) <- y_cols
  effect_values(beta, x_C_c)
}
post_fixed <- map(seq_len(B), \(b) draw_fixed_x_C(rows, Xi[, b], x_C - x_ref)) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)
rbind(`previous post: se` = c(css$se, NA),
      `posterior sd, x_C held fixed` = apply(post_fixed, 2, sd),
      `posterior sd` = apply(post, 2, sd))
                               tau_LATE       tau_R      rho_R
previous post: se            0.05716055 0.004104151         NA
posterior sd, x_C held fixed 0.05662123 0.004216914 0.04443268
posterior sd                 0.05830711 0.004242300 0.04483163

Holding the compliers’ mean fixed brings the posterior standard deviation of the LATE to 0.0566, close to the sandwich. So the uncertainty in , which the delta method of the previous post left out, accounts for the difference in this experiment. The appendix shows over 1,000 simulated experiments that the difference is small on average, and that both are calibrated. The bootstrap includes it without any extra derivation.

Checking every design

The previous post showed that turning off the encouragement, the clusters or the ramp gives the textbook analysis of a simpler design. The posterior should follow along: with the encouragement off, the compliers are everyone and is the weighted mean of ; with the clusters off, each account has one profile, so the bootstrap weights are per profile; with the ramp off, the inverse propensity weights are 1. Table 2 compares, for each of the 8 combinations, the posterior mean and standard deviation of the LATE with the estimate and standard error of the textbook model from estimatr, and the ratio’s posterior standard deviation with the universal model’s sandwich. Each posterior has 500 draws, to keep this check fast, so each posterior standard deviation carries Monte Carlo noise of about 3%.

Code 
textbook <- function(df, x_C, clustered, encouraged, outcome, covs = x_cols) {
  df_c <- df |>
    mutate(across(all_of(covs), \(v) v - x_C[cur_column()]))     # coefficient on T is the line at x_C
  rhs <- paste0("(", paste(covs, collapse = " + "), ")")
  f <- as.formula(if (encouraged) paste(outcome, "~", rhs, "* T |", rhs, "* Z") else paste(outcome, "~", rhs, "* T"))
  estimator <- if (encouraged) iv_robust else lm_robust
  fit <- if (clustered) estimator(f, data = df_c, weights = w, clusters = account, se_type = "CR0")
         else estimator(f, data = df_c, weights = w, se_type = "HC0")
  c(estimate = fit$coefficients[["T"]], se = fit$std.error[["T"]])
}

check_design <- function(encouraged, clustered, ramp) {
  set.seed(7)
  df <- simulate_accounts(propensity = if (ramp) propensity else rep(0.3, 4), full_compliance = !encouraged,
                          one_profile = !clustered) |>
    prepare(ramp = ramp)
  x_C <- complier_mean(df)
  tb <- textbook(df, x_C, clustered, encouraged, "y")
  css <- effects(fit_rows(df), x_C, x_ref)
  rows <- rows_data(df)
  post <- map(1:500, \(b) draw_rows(rows, rexp(nrow(rows$accounts)), ramp, encouraged)) |>
    do.call(what = rbind)
  tibble(encouraged, clustered, ramp,
         textbook = tb[["estimate"]], posterior_mean = mean(post[, "tau_LATE"]),
         textbook_se = tb[["se"]], posterior_sd = sd(post[, "tau_LATE"]),
         ratio_se = css$se[2], ratio_posterior_sd = sd(post[, "tau_R"]))
}

In every design the posterior is centered at the textbook estimate, up to the Monte Carlo noise of 500 draws, and its standard deviation is close to the textbook standard error. The first row is a purely randomized AB test with one row per user and a mean metric, where the Bayesian bootstrap of Lin’s regression gives the heteroskedasticity robust standard error, as in the bootstrap post. The last row is our experiment.

The weight must go on the account

What if we ignore the clusters, and draw a bootstrap weight for each profile instead of each account? draw_rows can do that if we pretend that every profile is its own account.

Code 
rows_profile <- df |>
  mutate(account = row_number()) |>
  rows_data()
set.seed(3)
post_profile <- map(seq_len(B), \(b) draw_rows(rows_profile, rexp(nrow(df)))) |>
  do.call(what = rbind)
rbind(`weights per account` = apply(post, 2, sd), `weights per profile` = apply(post_profile, 2, sd))
                      tau_LATE       tau_R      rho_R
weights per account 0.05830711 0.004242300 0.04483163
weights per profile 0.05348719 0.003958555 0.04141338

Weights per profile make the posterior of the LATE 8% narrower. Profiles of the same account share network quality and engagement, so they are not independent, and a population that mixes profiles freely is more certain than the data justify. This is the posterior counterpart of using a heteroskedasticity robust standard error where a cluster robust one is needed. The appendix confirms over 1,000 simulated experiments that weights per profile under-cover the LATE, while weights per account are calibrated.

The Bayesian bootstrap of the universal model is the universal model fit with one more weight per account. It gives a posterior for every effect of every design that the model covers, and for any function of those effects.

Efficient Computation

The posterior took 12.7 seconds: 1,000 fits on 43,989 profile rows. Each draw reads every profile row, so an experiment with hundreds of millions of profile rows would need 1,000 passes over the data. The previous post reduced a single fit to one pass and a compressed dataset of 8 rows. Can we do the same for the posterior?

The compressed rows cannot be reweighted

The tempting shortcut is to apply the Bayesian bootstrap to the compressed dataset: draw one bootstrap weight per compressed row and refit. That would treat the 8 strata as the units of independence. A population would then be a mix of 8 kinds of strata, and the posterior would describe uncertainty about the strata’s shares, not about the accounts within them. Within a stratum, every account would always count the same, so the posterior would not see how much the accounts vary. By (A1) the unit is the account, and a compressed row has already added the accounts together.

What one draw needs

Look again at what a draw computes. Each step of draw_rows adds up profile rows with the combined weight , and is the same for all accounts of a stratum. Grouping the profiles by account and the accounts by stratum, the sums of a draw are sums over strata of the stratum’s inverse propensity weight times

The first entry, , is the stratum’s total bootstrap weight, which gives the propensities. The rest is the bootstrap-weighted sum of the account summaries, which gives and , exactly as gave them in the previous post. We write for the account summary with a 1 in front. One draw needs one weighted sum per stratum. fit_sums computes the three effects from these 8 sums.

Code 
fit_sums <- function(keys, sums, ramp = TRUE, encouraged = TRUE) {
  # keys: Z and day of each stratum; sums: one row per stratum, sum of xi_a v_a
  total <- sums[, 1]                                            # total bootstrap weight of the stratum
  e_day <- (tapply(total * keys$Z, keys$day, sum) / tapply(total, keys$day, sum))[as.character(keys$day)]
  w <- if (ramp) ifelse(keys$Z == 1, 1 / e_day, 1 / (1 - e_day)) else rep(1, nrow(keys))
  s <- colSums(sums[, -1] * w)                                  # all strata
  s_Z <- colSums(sums[, -1] * (w * keys$Z))                     # prompted strata
  i_Y <- 1:(d * o)
  i_S <- d * o + 1:(d * d)
  i_T <- d * o + d * d + 1:(d * d)
  block <- \(v, i, ncol = d) matrix(v[i], ncol = ncol)
  M1_W_M2 <- rbind(cbind(block(s, i_S), block(s, i_T)), cbind(block(s_Z, i_S), block(s_Z, i_T)))
  M1_W_Y <- rbind(block(s, i_Y, o), block(s_Z, i_Y, o))
  beta <- solve(M1_W_M2, M1_W_Y)
  colnames(beta) <- y_cols
  x_C_c <- if (encouraged) {
    s_0 <- s - s_Z                                              # unprompted strata
    diff <- block(s_Z, i_T)[, 1] / s_Z[i_S][1] - block(s_0, i_T)[, 1] / s_0[i_S][1]
    diff[-1] / diff[1]
  } else block(s, i_S)[-1, 1] / s[i_S][1]
  effect_values(beta, x_C_c)
}

The sums change with every draw, and the compressed dataset of the previous post kept only and , which are the same for every draw. There are two ways forward. We can compute the weighted sums of all draws in one pass over the profile rows. Or we can ask what the compressed dataset already tells us about them.

Exact: draw the weights during the compression pass

The previous post built each account summary in one pass over the profile rows, added it into its stratum’s sums, and discarded it. We change one line: instead of adding once, we add for every draw . The pass then produces, for every stratum, a matrix whose row is the weighted sum of draw .

The weights must be the same wherever the account is processed, and drawing them must not require knowing the other accounts. We compute from a hash of the account id and the draw number, turned into a uniform number and then into an Exponential(1) weight, . Any machine that holds account draws the same weights, as with the Poisson bootstrap. The kernel is written in C++ with Rcpp, like the compression kernel of the previous post. It also contains compress_moments, which builds the compressed dataset of the previous post in the same layout, which we use in the next section.

Code 
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include <vector>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdint>
using namespace Rcpp;

// The bootstrap weight of account a in draw b: a hash of (seed, a, b) turned into an Exponential(1) number.
// Every machine that holds account a computes the same weight, without knowing the other accounts.
inline double xi_weight(uint64_t seed, uint64_t a, uint64_t b) {
  uint64_t z = seed + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15ULL * (a * 1000003ULL + b + 1);
  z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9ULL;
  z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EBULL;
  z = z ^ (z >> 31);
  double U = ((z >> 11) + 0.5) / 9007199254740992.0;          // uniform on (0, 1)
  return -std::log(U);
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericMatrix bootstrap_weights(IntegerVector account, int B, double seed) {
  NumericMatrix xi(account.size(), B);
  for (int a = 0; a < account.size(); a++)
    for (int b = 0; b < B; b++) xi(a, b) = xi_weight((uint64_t) seed, account[a], b);
  return xi;
}

// Add profile row i into the account summary u = (vec S^Y, vec S, vec S^T), with R = (1, x) and Y the outcome columns.
inline void add_row(std::vector<double>& u, const NumericMatrix& R, const NumericVector& T, const NumericMatrix& Y, int i) {
  int d = R.ncol(), o = Y.ncol();
  for (int l = 0; l < o; l++) for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) u[l * d + j] += R(i, j) * Y(i, l);
  for (int m = 0; m < d; m++) for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) {
    double rr = R(i, j) * R(i, m);
    u[d * o + m * d + j] += rr;
    u[d * o + d * d + m * d + j] += T[i] * rr;
  }
}

// One pass over the profile rows, which must be grouped by account. For every stratum, row b of the output
// is the weighted sum of v_a = (1, u_a) over its accounts, with the bootstrap weights of draw b.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
List compress_bootstrap(IntegerVector account, IntegerVector stratum, NumericMatrix R, NumericVector T,
                        NumericMatrix Y, int n_strata, int B, double seed) {
  int n = R.nrow(), d = R.ncol(), o = Y.ncol(), q = d * o + 2 * d * d;
  std::vector<double> u(q, 0.0), xi(B);
  std::vector<int> nz;
  std::vector<NumericMatrix> sums;
  for (int h = 0; h < n_strata; h++) sums.push_back(NumericMatrix(B, q + 1));
  auto add_account = [&](int a, int h) {
    for (int b = 0; b < B; b++) xi[b] = xi_weight((uint64_t) seed, a, b);   // the account's B weights
    nz.clear();
    for (int k = 0; k < q; k++) if (u[k] != 0) nz.push_back(k);
    double* S = sums[h].begin();                                            // column k + 1 holds entry k of u
    for (int b = 0; b < B; b++) S[b] += xi[b];
    for (int k : nz) {
      double* col = S + (size_t) (k + 1) * B;
      for (int b = 0; b < B; b++) col[b] += xi[b] * u[k];
    }
    for (int k : nz) u[k] = 0;
  };
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i > 0 && account[i] != account[i - 1]) add_account(account[i - 1], stratum[i - 1] - 1);
    add_row(u, R, T, Y, i);
  }
  add_account(account[n - 1], stratum[n - 1] - 1);
  List out(n_strata);
  for (int h = 0; h < n_strata; h++) out[h] = sums[h];
  return out;
}

// One pass over the profile rows to the compressed dataset: per stratum, sum v_a and sum v_a v_a^T.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
List compress_moments(IntegerVector account, IntegerVector stratum, NumericMatrix R, NumericVector T,
                      NumericMatrix Y, int n_strata) {
  int n = R.nrow(), d = R.ncol(), o = Y.ncol(), q = d * o + 2 * d * d;
  std::vector<double> v(q + 1, 0.0);
  std::vector<int> nz;
  std::vector<NumericVector> first;
  std::vector<NumericMatrix> second;
  for (int h = 0; h < n_strata; h++) { first.push_back(NumericVector(q + 1)); second.push_back(NumericMatrix(q + 1, q + 1)); }
  auto add_account = [&](int h) {
    v[0] = 1;
    nz.clear();
    for (int k = 0; k <= q; k++) if (v[k] != 0) nz.push_back(k);
    NumericMatrix& S2 = second[h];
    for (size_t i = 0; i < nz.size(); i++) {
      first[h][nz[i]] += v[nz[i]];
      for (size_t j = i; j < nz.size(); j++) S2(nz[j], nz[i]) += v[nz[i]] * v[nz[j]];   // lower triangle
    }
    for (int k : nz) v[k] = 0;
  };
  std::vector<double> u(q, 0.0);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i > 0 && account[i] != account[i - 1]) {
      for (int k = 0; k < q; k++) { v[k + 1] = u[k]; u[k] = 0; }
      add_account(stratum[i - 1] - 1);
    }
    add_row(u, R, T, Y, i);
  }
  for (int k = 0; k < q; k++) v[k + 1] = u[k];
  add_account(stratum[n - 1] - 1);
  List out(n_strata);
  for (int h = 0; h < n_strata; h++) {
    NumericMatrix& S2 = second[h];
    for (int i = 0; i <= q; i++) for (int j = i + 1; j <= q; j++) S2(i, j) = S2(j, i);
    out[h] = List::create(_["first"] = first[h], _["second"] = S2);
  }
  return out;
}

strata numbers the strata, and posterior_one_pass runs the kernel and turns each draw’s 8 weighted sums into effects.

Code 
strata <- function(df) {
  accounts <- df |>
    distinct(account, Z, day) |>
    arrange(account)
  keys <- accounts |>
    distinct(Z, day) |>
    arrange(Z, day)
  list(keys = keys, h = match(paste(accounts$Z, accounts$day), paste(keys$Z, keys$day)))
}

posterior_one_pass <- function(df, B, seed) {
  st <- strata(df)
  sums <- compress_bootstrap(df$account, st$h[df$account], centered(df), df$T, as.matrix(df[y_cols]),
                             nrow(st$keys), B, seed)
  posterior_from_sums(st$keys, sums)
}

posterior_from_sums <- function(keys, sums) {      # sums: one B x (1 + q) matrix per stratum
  all_strata <- do.call(cbind, sums)                # row b holds draw b of every stratum, side by side
  map(seq_len(nrow(all_strata)), \(b) fit_sums(keys, matrix(all_strata[b, ], nrow = length(sums), byrow = TRUE))) |>
    do.call(what = rbind)
}

The two agree to floating point rounding. One pass over the profile rows gives the exact Bayesian bootstrap. The cost is that every account is multiplied into sums instead of one, and the output has rows per stratum instead of one.

From the compressed dataset: the compressed row is the posterior’s moments

Do we need a new pass at all? The compressed dataset of the previous post holds, for each stratum, and . Given the data, the account summaries are fixed and only the bootstrap weights are random. The weights are independent, with mean 1 and variance 1, so

where the covariance has no cross terms between accounts because their weights are independent. The mean and the covariance of the weighted sums that a draw needs are exactly the two fields of the compressed row. The count is there too, as the first entry of , since the first entry of is 1. The second moments are not centered, because the randomness comes from the weights varying around 1, not from the accounts varying around their mean. Weights of different strata are independent, so the weighted sums of different strata are independent.

The compressed row has the first two moments of the weighted sums, but not their whole distribution. Each weighted sum adds up hundreds or thousands of independent terms , one per account: the smallest stratum, the prompted accounts of day 1, has 412 accounts. By the central limit theorem, each sum is approximately normal. So we draw the sum of each stratum from the normal distribution with the compressed row’s mean and covariance, and push every draw through fit_sums. Only the weighted sums are approximated as normal. The fit, the propensities, the compliers’ mean and the ratios are computed exactly from each draw, so the posterior can still be skewed when the effects are nonlinear functions of the sums.

Code 
posterior_compressed <- function(moments, keys, B) {
  # One normal draw of the weighted sums per stratum and draw: mean sum v_a, covariance sum v_a v_a^T
  draws <- map(moments, \(m) {
    root <- eigen(m$second, symmetric = TRUE)
    A <- root$vectors %*% diag(sqrt(pmax(root$values, 0)))
    sweep(matrix(rnorm(B * ncol(A)), B) %*% t(A), 2, m$first, `+`)          # B x (1 + q)
  })
  posterior_from_sums(keys, draws)
}

The eigen call computes a square root of each stratum’s covariance. A Cholesky factorization would also work, except that repeats the off-diagonal entries of the symmetric blocks and , which makes the covariance singular.

The two posteriors come from different random numbers, so we compare them with draws each, to keep the Monte Carlo noise of each standard deviation below 1%.

Table 3 and Figure 2 show that the two posteriors agree. For the LATE, the posterior standard deviations are 0.0581 and 0.0587, and the quantiles fall on the line, including the tails. What the normal approximation drops is the third moment of the weighted sums. The Exponential(1) weights are skewed, with a third central moment of 2, so the exact sums lean slightly to the right, and the compressed dataset does not keep the third moments that would describe it. In our experiment this is visible only in the skewness column. The exact posterior of has a skewness of 0.29 and the compressed one 0.18: most of the skew comes from being a ratio, which the exact fit of every draw keeps, and the rest from the weights, which the normal approximation drops. With very heavy-tailed accounts, such as a few whales that dominate a stratum, the weighted sums are less normal, and Taddy et al. (2016) found skewed posteriors in an experiment with 13 million users. There the exact pass is the safer choice.

There is another way to read the compressed posterior. Drawing the weighted sums from a normal with mean and covariance gives exactly the same distribution as weighting each account by an independent N(1, 1) number instead of an Exponential(1) number, because a weighted sum of fixed vectors with normal weights is normal. That is a multiplier bootstrap with normal weights. Its weights have the same mean and variance as the Bayesian bootstrap’s, which is why the two agree, but a normal weight can be negative, so a draw is no longer a population. We use the Gaussian draws as an approximation of the Bayesian bootstrap posterior, not as a posterior of their own.

Compute and storage

To compare the costs, we run the same simulation with a million accounts, and time the three ways to get 1,000 draws: refitting on the profile rows, the exact one pass, and the compressed dataset. Refitting on the profile rows takes too long to run in full, so we time 20 draws and multiply by 50.

  walk(1:20, \(b) draw_rows(rows_big, rexp(nrow(rows_big$accounts))))
})[["elapsed"]]
rm(rows_big)

                                  as.matrix(big[y_cols]), nrow(st_big$keys))

})[["elapsed"]]

Table 4 shows the times on the machine that rendered this post, for 2,189,477 profile rows. Refitting on the profile rows reads all of them for every draw. The exact one pass reads them once, but multiplies every account into 1,000 sums. The compressed dataset reads them once and multiplies every account into its outer product, which here is cheaper, and its 1,000 draws then never touch the profile rows.

The two efficient methods also keep different amounts of data. Write for the number of distinct entries of , as in the previous post, where symmetric blocks count once. The exact one pass keeps numbers per stratum. The compressed dataset keeps the distinct entries of , which is numbers per stratum, and it already contains and as its first row. The first grows like , the second like .

Table 5 shows the trade-off. With our 5 covariates, the compressed dataset keeps 21,608 numbers, while the exact one pass keeps 584,000, about as many as the 527,868 numbers in the profile rows of this experiment of 20,000 accounts. Neither grows with the number of accounts, so for an experiment with a million accounts both are much smaller than the data. The two cross near : with 50 covariates the compressed dataset keeps more than the exact one pass. With prognostic scores, the previous post’s recommendation for many covariates, stays at one score per raw outcome, and the compressed dataset stays small.

The choice between the two:

  1. The compressed dataset is the default. It is the same compressed dataset that the previous post stores for standard errors, so a platform that already keeps it gets the posterior for free, for any number of draws and any function of the effects, without reading the profile rows again. Its only approximation is the normality of each stratum’s weighted sum.
  2. The exact one pass is for strata with few accounts or very heavy-tailed accounts, where the weighted sums are not normal, or when an exact posterior is required. It needs the number of draws, and the seed, before the pass.

Summary

The universal model of the previous post gets a posterior with one more weight. Under the assumptions of the design and of the Bayesian bootstrap, a draw of the population gives each account an Exponential(1) bootstrap weight, shared by its profiles, and the universal model is refit with the combined weight. The propensities and the compliers’ mean are recomputed in every draw, and every effect, including ratios and relative changes, is computed on the draw. The result is a posterior for the LATE, the ratio and any function of them, in every design the universal model covers, and the posterior agrees with the sandwich standard errors and with textbook fits of the simpler designs. The weight must go on the account: weights on profiles give a posterior that is too narrow.

The posterior does not need the profile rows once per draw. Each draw needs only one bootstrap-weighted sum of account summaries per stratum. One pass over the profile rows, with weights drawn from a hash of the account id, computes these sums for every draw exactly. And the compressed dataset of the previous post already holds the mean and covariance of these sums, so a posterior can be drawn from it directly, with a normal approximation for each stratum’s sum and the exact nonlinear fit for every draw.

Appendix

Monte Carlo

We repeat the experiment 1,000 times. In each one we compute the previous post’s estimates and standard errors, and three posteriors with 500 draws each: the exact posterior with weights per account, from the one pass; the posterior with weights per profile, from the same pass with every profile treated as its own account; and the posterior from the compressed dataset. A 95% credible interval is the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the draws. A posterior is not required to cover the truth in 95% of experiments, but when the posterior’s spread matches the sampling variability of the estimate, as the linearization argument says it should, it does. The SE/SD column divides the average standard error, or the average posterior standard deviation, by the standard deviation of the estimates across experiments.

Code 
analyze <- function(seed, B = 500) {
  set.seed(seed)
  df <- simulate_accounts() |>
    prepare()
  css <- effects(fit_rows(df), complier_mean(df), x_ref)
  st <- strata(df)
  moments <- compress_moments(df$account, st$h[df$account], centered(df), df$T, as.matrix(df[y_cols]), nrow(st$keys))
  posteriors <- list(
    "weights per account, exact" = posterior_one_pass(df, B, seed),
    "weights per profile" = posterior_one_pass(mutate(df, account = row_number()), B, seed),
    "weights per account, compressed dataset" = posterior_compressed(moments, st$keys, B))
  bind_rows(
    tibble(effect = css$effect, method = "previous post: estimate and SE", estimate = css$estimate, spread = css$se,
           lo = css$estimate - qnorm(0.975) * css$se, hi = css$estimate + qnorm(0.975) * css$se),
    imap_dfr(posteriors, \(p, name) tibble(effect = colnames(p), method = name, estimate = colMeans(p),
                                           spread = apply(p, 2, sd), lo = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.025),
                                           hi = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.975)))) |>
    mutate(rep = seed)
}
rm(Xi, post_fixed, post_profile, rows_profile)
invisible(gc())
mc <- mclapply(1:1000, analyze, mc.cores = cores) |>
  bind_rows()
mc_tab <- mc |>
  mutate(target = truth[effect]) |>
  group_by(effect, method) |>
  summarise(bias = mean(estimate - target), sd = sd(estimate), se_over_sd = mean(spread) / sd(estimate),
            coverage = mean(lo <= target & target <= hi), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(factor(effect, levels = names(truth)), method)
Code 
mc_tab |>
  kable(digits = 4, col.names = c("Effect", "Method", "Bias", "SD", "SE/SD", "Coverage"))

With 1,000 experiments, SE/SD is uncertain by about , and the coverage by about percentage points. Reading Table 6:

  1. With weights per account, the exact posterior and the posterior from the compressed dataset cover the LATE 94.0% and 93.7% of the time, within about one percentage point of the previous post’s standard errors, 94.5%, and of 95%. Their intervals are quantiles of only 500 draws, which adds a little noise to each interval’s endpoints. For the ratios, coverage is between 94.2% and 94.8%. The relative effect has no row for the previous post, which did not compute it.
  2. Weights per profile cover the LATE only 90.9% of the time, and their posterior standard deviation is 14% smaller than the spread of the estimates.
  3. The LATE and are unbiased, up to the Monte Carlo error of the bias, about 0.0020 for the LATE. The posterior mean of is off by 0.0020, 1.6 Monte Carlo standard errors and 5% of a standard deviation. A ratio of estimates has a bias that shrinks like , faster than its standard deviation, so it does not affect the coverage.

item.title: Every bootstrap is a reweighting
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
A team runs an AB test and reports a covariate-adjusted effect on hours streamed. A second team reports the difference in median hours. A third wants the probability that the effect is positive. The first has a textbook standard error, if we remember to make it robust. The second has no simple formula at all. The third needs a posterior, which in our previous post on posterior distributions required a prior, a likelihood, and some care when the likelihood was wrong.

The bootstrap answers all three with one recipe: refit the same estimator many times on perturbed versions of the data. In this post we describe three versions of it. The classical bootstrap of Efron (1979) resamples the data. The Poisson bootstrap reweights it, which makes it practical for big datasets. The Bayesian bootstrap of Rubin (1981) also reweights it, and produces a posterior. All three are the same computation with differently distributed weights. What changes is how the weights are drawn, and what the resulting distribution means.

The classical bootstrap: resample the data

The plug-in principle

Let be the population distribution that generates a user’s data. Each time generates a user, it produces one row of data : user ’s outcome, treatment indicator and covariates. determines how often each kind of row comes up, for example how common light viewers are relative to heavy viewers. This is also what makes a probability distribution: for any set of rows, it gives the probability that a generated user’s row falls in that set. Most things we want to estimate are summaries of : a mean, a median, a treatment effect, a regression coefficient. Call such an estimand . It is a fixed number, because is fixed.

We never see . We see the users it generated. From them we build a stand-in population, the empirical distribution . It is a population made only of our users, in equal shares: to generate a user from , pick one of our users at random, each with probability , and return that user’s row. We write it as

where is the population made only of copies of user : every user it generates has user ’s row . The sum here does not add up numbers. It is a recipe for mixing populations: with probability , generate the user from . A weighted sum of single-user populations is therefore itself a population, and so itself a distribution. The probability it gives to a set of rows is the total weight of the users whose rows are in that set, and averages under it are weighted averages over our users. For example, the mean outcome of is .

The plug-in estimate replaces by :

The sample mean is the mean of , the sample median is the median of , and so on.

is random, because a different sample of users gives a different . The distribution of over repeated samples of users generated by is its sampling distribution, and its standard deviation is the standard error. To see the sampling distribution directly we would need to generate new samples, which we cannot ask it to do.

Efron’s idea is to let generate the new samples instead. Generating users from means picking of our users uniformly at random, with replacement. The classical bootstrap is

  1. For , draw users from the sample with replacement, and compute the estimate on this resample.
  2. Use the spread of around as a stand-in for the spread of around .

The bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of the . The 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the give a percentile confidence interval, and estimates the bias of . None of these steps needs a formula for the variance of , which is what makes the bootstrap useful for medians, ratios, ranks and machine learning models.

Running example: an experiment on hours streamed

Consider an experiment on users. For user , is hours streamed during the experiment, is the treatment indicator, and is hours streamed in the pre-period. Treatment is randomized with probability 0.2, as in a test with a small treatment arm. We simulate from

where the noise has mean zero and standard deviation . Heavier viewers are noisier, and treatment doubles the noise. The noise variance is not constant, so the textbook standard error of least squares, which assumes it is, will be wrong.

Code 
tau <- 0.2

simulate_users <- function(n) {
  tibble(
    user = seq_len(n),
    X = rgamma(n, shape = 2, scale = 5),
    # Randomized treatment. Note that this masks R's shorthand T for TRUE
    T = rbinom(n, 1, 0.2)
  ) |>
    mutate(y = 2 + tau * T + 0.8 * X + rnorm(n, sd = 0.2 * X * (1 + T)))
}

set.seed(2026)
n <- 10000
users <- simulate_users(n)
head(users)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
   user      X     T     y
  <int>  <dbl> <int> <dbl>
1     1 11.0       0  8.40
2     2  2.35      0  3.05
3     3  0.302     0  2.27
4     4  3.97      0  4.28
5     5 10.9       0 13.0 
6     6 15.1       1 18.5

We estimate the coefficients with least squares. Stack the rows into the design matrix , with , and the outcomes into the -vector . Least squares minimizes , and the solution is

The second form writes both matrices as sums over users, because adds up the outer products and adds up the -vectors .

Code 
M <- cbind(1, users$T, users$X)
colnames(M) <- c("1", "T", "X")
y <- users$y
k <- ncol(M)

ols <- function(M, y) {
  solve(crossprod(M), crossprod(M, y))[, 1]
}

beta_hat <- ols(M, y)
beta_hat
        1         T         X 
1.8827625 0.3991198 0.8135292

The estimate of is 0.399, against a true .

The bootstrap standard error

We resample the users times and refit least squares on each resample.

Code 
set.seed(1)
B <- 1000

time_classical <- system.time({
  beta_classical <- do.call(rbind, map(seq_len(B), \(b) {
    rows <- sample(n, n, replace = TRUE)
    ols(M[rows, ], y[rows])
  }))
})["elapsed"]

head(beta_classical, 3)
            1         T         X
[1,] 1.853100 0.5247530 0.8125417
[2,] 1.977129 0.3472915 0.8000558
[3,] 1.830352 0.4649621 0.8198540

Each row is one replicate . The bootstrap standard error of each coefficient is the standard deviation of its column. We compare it with the textbook standard error, for coefficient , with and residuals . We call it the naive standard error, because it assumes every user has the same noise variance.

Code 
MtM_inv <- solve(crossprod(M))
eps_hat <- as.numeric(y - M %*% beta_hat)
se_naive <- sqrt(diag(sum(eps_hat^2) / (n - k) * MtM_inv))
se_classical <- apply(beta_classical, 2, sd)

rbind(naive = se_naive, classical = se_classical)
                   1          T           X
naive     0.05630463 0.07680789 0.004375192
classical 0.07294947 0.10969559 0.008279613

The two disagree on : 0.077 for the naive formula against 0.110 for the bootstrap. Which one is right? Because we simulated the data, we can check. We simulate 1,000 fresh experiments from the same population, fit least squares on each, and take the standard deviation of the 1,000 estimates of . Those 1,000 estimates are draws from the true sampling distribution, which the bootstrap is trying to imitate from a single experiment.

Code 
set.seed(2)
n_experiments <- 1000
beta_1_sampling <- map_dbl(seq_len(n_experiments), \(r) {
  fresh <- simulate_users(n)
  ols(cbind(1, fresh$T, fresh$X), fresh$y)[2]
})
sd(beta_1_sampling)
[1] 0.1095301

The true standard error is 0.110. The bootstrap recovers it from one experiment, without being told the noise variance changes across users, while the naive formula understates it by 30%. The bootstrap gets it right because resampling users keeps each user’s noise attached to that user’s and . In the post on the linear probability model we fixed the same problem with robust standard errors.

The bootstrap distribution is a sampling distribution

Figure 1 overlays the 1,000 bootstrap replicates of from our one experiment on the 1,000 estimates from fresh experiments.

Code 
bind_rows(
  tibble(source = "Bootstrap of one experiment", beta_1 = beta_classical[, "T"]),
  tibble(source = "Fresh experiments", beta_1 = beta_1_sampling)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = beta_1, fill = source)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tau, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = beta_hat["T"], color = "#D55E00") +
  annotate("text", x = tau, y = 0, label = "τ", vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1.5, size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = beta_hat["T"], y = 0, label = "estimate", vjust = -0.5, hjust = -0.1,
           size = 5, color = "#D55E00") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(beta)[1]), y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

The two curves have the same width but different centers. The fresh experiments scatter around the truth . The bootstrap replicates scatter around our estimate , because the bootstrap treats as if it were the population. What the bootstrap reproduces is the shape of the error: the distribution of approximates the distribution of .

Our experiment happens to be an unlucky one. Its estimate is 1.8 standard errors above , and 7% of the fresh experiments land at least that far from in either direction. From inside the experiment there is no way to tell.

So the bootstrap does create a distribution for the estimator, and that distribution is the sampling distribution. It answers the question “if we reran this experiment on new users, how much would our estimate move?”. The population, and with it , is held fixed while hypothetical datasets vary.

The classical bootstrap is not a posterior

In the posterior distribution post we separated two kinds of distributions. A confidence interval comes from the sampling distribution, where is a fixed constant and the randomness comes from the data. A posterior distribution treats as uncertain and holds the observed data fixed. Only the posterior supports a statement like “there is a 95% probability that is between these two numbers”.

The classical bootstrap sits firmly on the first side. Every replicate is a hypothetical dataset, and the histogram in Figure 1 describes how the estimate varies across datasets. The classical bootstrap is not a posterior distribution for , and reading its quantiles as probabilities about is the same mistake as reading a confidence interval that way.

Resampling is reweighting

A resample of users contains some users several times and others not at all. Let be the number of times user appears in a resample. To see this concretely, take the first 6 users and draw a resample of size 6.

Code 
set.seed(3)
users_6 <- users |>
  slice(1:6)
rows <- sample(6, 6, replace = TRUE)

# The resampled dataset
users_6 |>
  slice(rows) |>
  arrange(user)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
   user      X     T     y
  <int>  <dbl> <int> <dbl>
1     2  2.35      0  3.05
2     2  2.35      0  3.05
3     3  0.302     0  2.27
4     4  3.97      0  4.28
5     4  3.97      0  4.28
6     5 10.9       0 13.0
Code 
# The same information as a count for each original user
users_6 |>
  mutate(w = tabulate(rows, nbins = 6))
# A tibble: 6 × 5
   user      X     T     y     w
  <int>  <dbl> <int> <dbl> <int>
1     1 11.0       0  8.40     0
2     2  2.35      0  3.05     2
3     3  0.302     0  2.27     1
4     4  3.97      0  4.28     2
5     5 10.9       0 13.0      1
6     6 15.1       1 18.5      0

The resampled dataset and the original 6 users with a count column carry exactly the same information. Any estimator that adds up contributions from each row, as least squares adds up and , gives the same answer on the resample as on the original data with user counted times. A resample is therefore the original data with weights. In the classical bootstrap the weight vector is the vector of counts from draws with replacement, which is a multinomial distribution:

The rest of the post varies only the distribution of .

The Poisson bootstrap: reweight, don’t resample

The problem with multinomial weights at scale

Resampling is easy on one machine with 10,000 users. It is awkward on an experimentation platform with hundreds of millions of users whose rows are spread across many machines or arrive as a stream. The multinomial counts are coupled: they must add up to . To draw them we need to know before we start, and we cannot draw user ’s count without coordinating with every other user’s count. If we resample literally, we also build new datasets, or make passes over the data.

From multinomial to Poisson weights

Look at one user’s count on its own. Each of the draws picks user with probability , so the count is Binomial:

The limit is the Poisson(1) probability weight. The coupling between users is also weak: the covariance of two multinomial counts is , which vanishes as grows. The Poisson bootstrap drops the coupling and draws every weight independently,

This idea is due to Hanley and MacGibbon (2006), and Chamandy et al. (2012) describe its use at Google for massive data streams. Now each row draws its own weight in each replicate without knowing or anything about other rows. A machine holding a shard of users can draw their weights on the fly, for example by seeding a random number generator with the user id, and never needs to materialize a resampled dataset. The price is that the size of a replicate, , is no longer exactly . It is Poisson, which varies by about , or 1% of for our experiment.

We check the Poisson limit and the replicate sizes on our experiment by drawing one multinomial count vector and comparing the share of users with each count against a matrix of Poisson weights.

Code 
set.seed(4)
w_multinomial <- tabulate(sample(n, n, replace = TRUE), nbins = n)
w_poisson <- matrix(rpois(n * B, lambda = 1), nrow = n, ncol = B)

tibble(count = 0:4) |>
  mutate(
    multinomial = map_dbl(count, \(m) mean(w_multinomial == m)),
    poisson = map_dbl(count, \(m) mean(w_poisson[, 1] == m)),
    `Poisson(1) probability` = dpois(count, lambda = 1)
  )
# A tibble: 5 × 4
  count multinomial poisson `Poisson(1) probability`
  <int>       <dbl>   <dbl>                    <dbl>
1     0      0.365   0.371                    0.368 
2     1      0.374   0.370                    0.368 
3     2      0.180   0.184                    0.184 
4     3      0.0615  0.0587                   0.0613
5     4      0.0151  0.0134                   0.0153
Code 
# Replicate sizes: sums of each column of Poisson weights
summary(colSums(w_poisson))
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   9682    9934   10003   10004   10072   10373

The shares match the Poisson(1) probability weights in both columns. About 37% of users get weight zero and drop out of a replicate, and the replicate sizes range from 9,682 to 10,373 around . For the 6 users from before, the first three replicates are

Code 
users_6 |>
  mutate(
    `w (b = 1)` = w_poisson[1:6, 1],
    `w (b = 2)` = w_poisson[1:6, 2],
    `w (b = 3)` = w_poisson[1:6, 3]
  )
# A tibble: 6 × 7
   user      X     T     y `w (b = 1)` `w (b = 2)` `w (b = 3)`
  <int>  <dbl> <int> <dbl>       <int>       <int>       <int>
1     1 11.0       0  8.40           2           2           1
2     2  2.35      0  3.05           0           3           2
3     3  0.302     0  2.27           1           3           3
4     4  3.97      0  4.28           2           0           2
5     5 10.9       0 13.0            0           1           1
6     6 15.1       1 18.5            2           5           0

Any estimator that accepts weights works

The Poisson bootstrap never creates a new dataset. Each replicate is the original data with a new column of weights. So any estimator that accepts weights can run inside the Poisson bootstrap: a weighted mean, weighted least squares, weighted logistic regression, gradient boosted trees with sample weights. A weight of 2 means “this user counts twice” and a weight of 0 means “this user is left out”, which are exactly the operations a resample performs.

Least squares with weights

Earlier we computed . Weighted least squares minimizes , where user ’s squared error counts times. Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations , and solving them gives replicate ’s estimate

where is the weight vector of replicate . Compared with the sums for , each user’s contribution is multiplied by , which is what counting a user times does. With all weights equal to 1 we get back.

Computing all replicates in one pass

The direct implementation calls a weighted regression times, rereading and every time. But and never change across replicates; only does. We can exploit that.

Entry of the matrix is

where is entry of user ’s row. This is a dot product between the weight vector and the elementwise product of columns and of . If we place the weight vectors side by side as the columns of an matrix , a single product of that matrix with the column gives entry for all replicates at once. The matrix is symmetric, so there are only distinct entries to compute. In the same way, entry of is , which is a product of the weight matrix with the column .

So the whole bootstrap takes three steps.

  1. Build the matrix of column products of , and the matrix whose row is .
  2. Multiply each by the weight matrix. This gives a and a matrix, and it is the only step that touches all users, in one pass.
  3. For each replicate, unpack its 6 entries into a matrix and solve the system.

The product matrices only contain sums over users, so in a distributed system each machine computes them for its own users and the results add up. These are the same kind of sufficient statistics we used to compress experiment data, with one set per bootstrap replicate, all computed in the same pass.

Code 
fit_weighted_ols <- function(M, y, w) {
  k <- ncol(M)
  pairs <- expand_grid(u = seq_len(k), v = seq_len(k)) |>
    filter(u <= v)
  # Step 1: n x k(k+1)/2 column products, and n x k rows M_i y_i
  M_pairs <- do.call(cbind, map2(pairs$u, pairs$v, \(u, v) M[, u] * M[, v]))
  colnames(M_pairs) <- paste(colnames(M)[pairs$u], colnames(M)[pairs$v], sep = "·")
  My <- M * y
  # Step 2: one pass over the n users for all B replicates
  MtwM <- crossprod(M_pairs, w)
  Mtwy <- crossprod(My, w)
  # Step 3: B small k x k solves
  beta <- do.call(rbind, map(seq_len(ncol(w)), \(b) {
    MtwM_b <- matrix(0, k, k)
    MtwM_b[cbind(pairs$u, pairs$v)] <- MtwM[, b]
    MtwM_b[cbind(pairs$v, pairs$u)] <- MtwM[, b]
    solve(MtwM_b, Mtwy[, b])
  }))
  colnames(beta) <- colnames(M)
  list(M_pairs = M_pairs, MtwM = MtwM, Mtwy = Mtwy, beta = beta)
}

time_poisson <- system.time({
  fit_poisson <- fit_weighted_ols(M, y, w_poisson)
})["elapsed"]

Here are the column products for our 6 users, followed by the 6 distinct entries of for the first three replicates.

Code 
head(fit_poisson$M_pairs)
     1·1 1·T        1·X T·T      T·X         X·X
[1,]   1   0 11.0267102   0  0.00000 121.5883382
[2,]   1   0  2.3454366   0  0.00000   5.5010726
[3,]   1   0  0.3022907   0  0.00000   0.0913797
[4,]   1   0  3.9731932   0  0.00000  15.7862644
[5,]   1   0 10.8828167   0  0.00000 118.4357000
[6,]   1   1 15.1349497   1 15.13495 229.0667026
Code 
fit_poisson$MtwM[, 1:3]
          [,1]       [,2]      [,3]
1·1    9836.00    9936.00   10050.0
1·T    1984.00    2076.00    2053.0
1·X   98842.39  100025.08  102099.6
T·T    1984.00    2076.00    2053.0
T·X   19561.61   20691.24   20627.8
X·X 1498162.76 1506312.63 1556526.0

Each column of products has a physical meaning. The column is always 1, so its weighted sum is the size of the replicate, 9836 users in replicate 1. The column equals , because is 0 or 1, so its weighted sum is the number of treated users in the replicate. The column adds up pre-period hours. As a check, we solve replicate 1 with R’s weighted lm.

Code 
fit_lm_1 <- lm(y ~ T + X, data = users, weights = w_poisson[, 1])
rbind(engine = fit_poisson$beta[1, ], lm = coef(fit_lm_1))
              1         T         X
engine 1.752896 0.4970831 0.8275943
lm     1.752896 0.4970831 0.8275943

The two agree. The one-pass computation of all 1000 replicates took 0.18 seconds, against 0.52 seconds for the literal resampling loop of the classical bootstrap. At 10,000 users on one machine both are fast. The difference that matters at scale is that the one-pass version reads the data once and never builds a resampled dataset.

The Poisson bootstrap distribution and standard errors

Code 
beta_poisson <- fit_poisson$beta

bind_rows(
  tibble(method = "Classical", beta_1 = beta_classical[, "T"]),
  tibble(method = "Poisson", beta_1 = beta_poisson[, "T"])
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = beta_1, fill = method)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, color = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = beta_hat["T"], color = "#D55E00") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#009E73")) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(beta)[1]^{(b)}), y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Figure 2 shows that the two bootstraps produce nearly the same distribution. Their standard errors are

Code 
se_poisson <- apply(beta_poisson, 2, sd)
rbind(naive = se_naive, classical = se_classical, poisson = se_poisson)
                   1          T           X
naive     0.05630463 0.07680789 0.004375192
classical 0.07294947 0.10969559 0.008279613
poisson   0.07723449 0.11318564 0.008820526

The Poisson bootstrap standard error of is 0.113, against 0.110 for the classical bootstrap and the true 0.110. With replicates, a bootstrap standard error has Monte Carlo noise of about , so these are equal within noise.

Why both bootstraps land on the robust standard error

Both bootstraps agree with each other and with the truth, and both disagree with the naive formula. We can see why from the algebra of a single replicate. Write and substitute into the weighted least squares formula:

This identity is exact. The full-sample normal equations say , so we can subtract that zero from the sum and write it as . That sum has mean zero, because , and its size grows like . The matrix is , which grows like , plus a mean-zero perturbation that grows like . Replacing it by changes , which is of order , by an amount of order . This gives the linearized replicate

For Poisson weights the are independent with , so the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances, and

This is the HC0 sandwich, the heteroskedasticity robust covariance of Eicker and White.

For multinomial weights the counts are coupled, with and . Writing for user ’s contribution to the normal equations,

where the second line adds and subtracts to complete the outer product of the sums, and the last line uses the normal equations again, . The coupling between counts cancels exactly, and the classical bootstrap lands on the same sandwich. Lancaster (2006) gives the formal statement: the bootstrap covariance of least squares matches the Eicker–White covariance to order .

The intuition is that the naive formula assumes one noise variance for everyone, while the sandwich weights each user’s residual by that user’s own . The bootstrap never assumes a common variance. It perturbs how much each user counts, and each user carries their own residual along. The linearized replicate is also the cheapest computation of all: a single product of the matrix with rows and the weight matrix, with no solves.

Code 
beta_linearized <- t(beta_hat + MtM_inv %*% crossprod(M * eps_hat, w_poisson - 1))
se_linearized <- apply(beta_linearized, 2, sd)
se_HC0 <- sqrt(diag(MtM_inv %*% crossprod(M * eps_hat) %*% MtM_inv))
se_HC0_estimatr <- lm_robust(y ~ T + X, data = users, se_type = "HC0")$std.error

rbind(
  naive = se_naive,
  HC0 = se_HC0,
  `HC0 (estimatr)` = se_HC0_estimatr,
  classical = se_classical,
  poisson = se_poisson,
  linearized = se_linearized,
  `fresh experiments` = c(NA, sd(beta_1_sampling), NA)
)
                           1          T           X
naive             0.05630463 0.07680789 0.004375192
HC0               0.07594796 0.10957207 0.008628506
HC0 (estimatr)    0.07594796 0.10957207 0.008628506
classical         0.07294947 0.10969559 0.008279613
poisson           0.07723449 0.11318564 0.008820526
linearized        0.07735109 0.11310415 0.008828739
fresh experiments         NA 0.10953006          NA

Our HC0 matches estimatr. Every bootstrap row sits within Monte Carlo noise of HC0 and of the true standard error of , and the naive row is the outlier. For least squares, then, the Poisson bootstrap is a scalable way to get a robust standard error. Its real value is for estimators that have no sandwich formula, where the same weights plug into any weighted fit.

The Bayesian bootstrap: a posterior over the population

The problem: a posterior without a likelihood for the model

The classical and Poisson bootstraps give sampling distributions. In the posterior distribution post we wanted a posterior for , and to get one with covariates we wrote a Normal-Inverse-Gamma model: a Gaussian likelihood for , a conjugate prior for the coefficients, and, for a 0/1 outcome, a quasi-Bayesian patch that replaced the posterior covariance with a sandwich because the Gaussian likelihood was known to be wrong. Every new estimand would need a new likelihood and prior. Can we get a posterior for an arbitrary estimand without writing either one?

The Bayesian bootstrap says yes. Its trick is to put the prior and the likelihood on the population rather than on the parameter.

Deriving the Bayesian bootstrap

We need three assumptions.

(A1) generates users independently. This is the same assumption the classical bootstrap makes.

(A2) The population only contains the kinds of users we observed. Recall that is the population made only of copies of user , and that the empirical distribution mixes our users in equal shares. (A2) keeps that form but makes the shares unknown:

is still a population that generates users, and so still a distribution. The sum is the same recipe as before: with probability , generate the user from , so the generated user has user ’s row. is the share of the population that looks like user , and the probability weights describe the population completely. The empirical distribution is the special case . The unknown is no longer ; it is .

Under (A1) and (A2), a generated user has user ’s row with probability , and users are generated independently, so the probability of our sample is the product of the probabilities of the observed rows. Each observed row appears once, so the likelihood is

(A3) The prior on is a Dirichlet distribution with zero pseudo-counts. A prior on the shares is a distribution over populations. To explain this choice we first describe the Dirichlet distribution, then show why it is the natural family for , and then how to set its parameters.

The Dirichlet distribution

The Dirichlet distribution is a distribution over probability weight vectors: every draw is a vector with and . Because , every draw is also a population. Its parameters are positive numbers , and its probability density is

where the omitted constant makes the density integrate to 1 over all probability weight vectors. The parameters are best read as pseudo-counts: the distribution behaves as if we had already seen user ’s kind of row times. Two standard properties make that reading concrete.

  1. The mean share is the pseudo-count’s share of the total, .
  2. When every pseudo-count equals the same , the mean share is and . The total pseudo-count sits in the denominator, so more pseudo-counts concentrate the draws around equal shares, as more data would.

With the Dirichlet distribution is the Beta distribution, which the posterior distribution post used for Beta-Binomial conjugacy. To draw from a Dirichlet, draw independent and normalize, . On our first three users, here are four draws of for each of three values of a common pseudo-count , together with the mean outcome of each drawn population.

Code 
set.seed(8)
y_3 <- users$y[1:3]
y_3
[1] 8.400991 3.052972 2.270614
Code 
expand_grid(c = c(0.1, 1, 10), draw = 1:4) |>
  mutate(pi = map(c, \(c) {
    w <- rgamma(3, shape = c, rate = 1)
    w / sum(w)
  })) |>
  mutate(
    pi_1 = map_dbl(pi, 1),
    pi_2 = map_dbl(pi, 2),
    pi_3 = map_dbl(pi, 3),
    mean_y = map_dbl(pi, \(pi) sum(pi * y_3))
  ) |>
  select(-pi)
# A tibble: 12 × 6
       c  draw     pi_1          pi_2     pi_3 mean_y
   <dbl> <int>    <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
 1   0.1     1 0.00452  0.995         0.000110   3.08
 2   0.1     2 0.00688  0.631         0.362      2.81
 3   0.1     3 0.000869 0.892         0.107      2.97
 4   0.1     4 0.822    0.00000000847 0.178      7.31
 5   1       1 0.0382   0.0275        0.934      2.53
 6   1       2 0.440    0.233         0.327      5.15
 7   1       3 0.856    0.114         0.0296     7.61
 8   1       4 0.443    0.360         0.196      5.27
 9  10       1 0.393    0.245         0.362      4.87
10  10       2 0.202    0.466         0.332      3.88
11  10       3 0.300    0.253         0.448      4.30
12  10       4 0.263    0.354         0.383      4.16

With , as if we had already seen each kind of user 10 times, the draws stay close to equal shares of and the population means stay close to the sample mean of the three outcomes. With the draws spread evenly over all possible shares. With the draws pile into the corners: most draws are populations made almost entirely of one kind of user.

Why the Dirichlet is the natural family: conjugacy

Our likelihood is , because each observed row appears once. A row observed twice would contribute , so in general each row contributes raised to the number of times it was observed. That is the same algebraic form as the Dirichlet density, so multiplying a Dirichlet prior by our likelihood gives

which is again a Dirichlet density, with parameters . Updating the prior adds each observed row to its pseudo-count. The posterior stays in the same family and in closed form, which is the same reason we chose the conjugate Normal-Inverse-Gamma prior for the Bayesian linear model.

Choosing the pseudo-counts

Two choices remain.

  1. Equal pseudo-counts, . Under (A1) users are interchangeable before we see their data, so the prior should not favor any one of them.
  2. How many pseudo-counts. The prior with pseudo-count adds pseudo-observations to our real ones. The posterior is Dirichlet, and by property 2 its shares have variance . Compared with at , the total count in the denominator grows from to : the posterior is as concentrated as if we had observations instead of . Any therefore makes the posterior more certain than the data justify. With the prior is as strong as the data. The only choice that adds nothing beyond the data is .

The limit gives the prior

It is improper, because it does not integrate to a finite number, but the posterior is proper:
