The posterior is constant over all probability weight vectors . That is the Dirichlet distribution. Its mean share is , so on average the posterior population is the empirical distribution , the same stand-in population the classical bootstrap generates from. The spread around comes only from the data.

Two cautions about the word “non-informative”.

  1. Zero pseudo-counts is not the same as a flat prior. The flat prior, constant density over all , is ; it would give a Dirichlet posterior, which is too narrow. In the Bayesian bootstrap the posterior is flat, not the prior.
  2. The prior is the limit of the rows of the Dirichlet table: it puts nearly all its weight on populations made of a single kind of user. That is a strange belief to hold before seeing data. Rubin (1981) raised this concern himself. It is harmless here because the data’s one count per row overwhelms zero pseudo-counts.

(A2) and (A3) can also be derived together. A Dirichlet process prior (Ferguson, 1973) puts a prior on all populations, not only those built from our users. It is specified by a guess for the population and a concentration, the number of pseudo-observations that guess is worth. Its posterior mixes the guess with our observed users. As the concentration goes to 0 the guess drops out, the posterior contains only the kinds of users we observed, and their shares are Dirichlet: Gasparini (1995) showed this limit is exactly the Bayesian bootstrap.

Sampling the posterior

Setting every in the Gamma recipe gives Gamma, which is the Exponential(1) distribution. So a draw from the posterior is

The are weights but not probability weights, because they do not add up to 1; the are probability weights. A draw of is a draw of a plausible population .

A tiny example: three users

The rows of the Dirichlet table are already posterior draws. To see what a posterior draw means as a population, we draw five more for our first three users, with the Exponential recipe. The mean outcome of a population is the weighted average , as with but with weights in place of .

Code 
set.seed(5)
pi_draws <- map(1:5, \(d) {
  w <- rexp(3)
  w / sum(w)
})

map(1:5, \(d) {
  pi <- pi_draws[[d]]
  tibble(draw = d, pi_1 = pi[1], pi_2 = pi[2], pi_3 = pi[3], mean_y = sum(pi * y_3))
}) |>
  list_rbind()
# A tibble: 5 × 5
   draw   pi_1   pi_2   pi_3 mean_y
  <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1     1 0.818  0.152  0.0298   7.40
2     2 0.374  0.0521 0.573    4.61
3     3 0.0259 0.296  0.678    2.66
4     4 0.701  0.217  0.0826   6.74
5     5 0.640  0.342  0.0178   6.46

Each row is a different population built from the same three users. In one draw user 1 represents most of the population, in another user 3 does. The mean of each population is a weighted average of the three observed outcomes, so it always lies between the smallest and largest observed . Across draws the means form the posterior of the population mean.

Each draw is a population that generates users. Here are 1,000 users generated by the population of draw 1: the first six, and then the share of the 1,000 that copies each of our three users.

Code 
generated <- users |>
  slice(sample(3, 1000, replace = TRUE, prob = pi_draws[[1]]))
head(generated)
# A tibble: 6 × 4
   user     X     T     y
  <int> <dbl> <int> <dbl>
1     1  11.0     0  8.40
2     1  11.0     0  8.40
3     1  11.0     0  8.40
4     1  11.0     0  8.40
5     1  11.0     0  8.40
6     1  11.0     0  8.40
Code 
generated |>
  count(user, name = "generated") |>
  mutate(
    share = generated / sum(generated),
    pi = pi_draws[[1]][user]
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 4
   user generated share     pi
  <int>     <int> <dbl>  <dbl>
1     1       799 0.799 0.818 
2     2       170 0.17  0.152 
3     3        31 0.031 0.0298

Every generated user is a copy of one of our three users, because contains only the kinds of users we observed. The share of copies of each user is close to , which is what it means for to be that user’s share of the population.

From a posterior over the population to a posterior over any estimand

Once we have posterior draws of , every estimand gets a posterior for free: compute on each draw. Nothing about entered the prior or the likelihood, so can be anything that is defined for a discrete population.

  • The mean of under is .
  • The least squares coefficient under is the best linear fit in the population, , where the expectation is over a user generated by . For , the expectation is the weighted average of the squared errors of our users, , which is weighted least squares with weights :

Multiplying every by the same constant cancels between the inverse and the second sum, so we can use the unnormalized directly. The Bayesian bootstrap of least squares is the weighted fit from the Poisson bootstrap section with Exponential(1) weights in place of Poisson(1) weights. - The median of among treated users under is the smallest observed among treated users at which the cumulative weight over treated users, ordered by , reaches half of their total weight.

This answers the surprise of getting a posterior for an arbitrary model with no prior and no likelihood for that model. There is a prior and a likelihood, on . The “model”, least squares in our case, is not used as a likelihood at all. It is only a definition of which summary of the population we care about. is the coefficient of the best linear fit in the population whether or not the population is linear or Gaussian, just as a mean is defined whether or not the population is normal. This is the pseudo-true parameter from the quasi-Bayesian section of the posterior distribution post, the minimizer of the expected squared error under the true population, which we reached there by arguing that a wrong Gaussian likelihood still targets it. The Bayesian bootstrap puts a posterior on it directly.

Sanity check: the posterior of a mean

For the population mean we can compute the posterior variance exactly. By property 2 with , a Dirichlet draw has . The shares add up to 1, so , which gives . Expanding the variance of a weighted sum,

where the second line substitutes the Dirichlet variance and covariance, and the third line adds and subtracts to complete . Repeating the same steps for the Dirichlet posterior of a prior with pseudo-count gives , so the flat prior would cut the posterior variance of the mean almost in half, as we argued when choosing the pseudo-counts. The squared standard error of a sample mean is . The two differ by the factor , which is 0.9998 for our experiment. On our 10,000 users, with the same number of draws as before,

Code 
set.seed(6)
w_bayes <- matrix(rexp(n * B), nrow = n, ncol = B)
mean_y_bayes <- colSums(w_bayes * y) / colSums(w_bayes)

c(
  `posterior sd (draws)` = sd(mean_y_bayes),
  `posterior sd (exact)` = sqrt(sum((y - mean(y))^2) / (n * (n + 1))),
  `posterior sd, flat prior c = 1 (exact)` = sqrt(sum((y - mean(y))^2) / (n * (2 * n + 1))),
  `standard error of the mean` = sd(y) / sqrt(n)
)
                  posterior sd (draws)                   posterior sd (exact) 
                            0.06410441                             0.06557242 
posterior sd, flat prior c = 1 (exact)             standard error of the mean 
                            0.04636786                             0.06557898

The draws agree with the exact posterior standard deviation within the Monte Carlo noise of about 2% that draws carry, and the exact posterior standard deviation matches the standard error of the mean to three significant digits. The flat prior would report a posterior standard deviation about times as large.

How the Bayesian bootstrap differs from the classical bootstrap

Mechanically, the two bootstraps differ only in the weights. Classical weights are integer counts, and about 37% of users get a count of zero in each replicate. Bayesian bootstrap weights are continuous and strictly positive: every user stays in every draw, with more or less influence. All three kinds of weights have mean 1 and nearly unit variance: has variance , the multinomial count has , and the Poisson weight has exactly 1. These shared first two moments are why their histograms nearly coincide, and the argument we made for the sandwich goes through, to first order, for as well. Lancaster shows the classical and Bayesian bootstrap covariances agree to order .

The meaning is different. The classical bootstrap holds the population fixed at and varies hypothetical datasets, so it gives a sampling distribution. The Bayesian bootstrap holds the data fixed and varies the population according to its posterior, so it gives . The numbers come out nearly the same, but only the second justifies probability statements about , and only because we wrote down (A1)–(A3). The difference between the two is the probability model, not the arithmetic.

A posterior for the treatment effect

In a randomized experiment, the coefficient on in the population’s best linear fit is the treatment effect, , even when the outcome is not linear in and the effect varies across users; the covariate only reduces the variance, as in CUPED. So the posterior distribution of , derived from weighted least squares with Exponential weights, is the posterior distribution of the treatment effect. We compute it with the same one-pass function as the Poisson bootstrap, feeding it the Exponential weights we just drew.

For comparison we also compute the posterior of the Normal-Inverse-Gamma model with a flat prior. Letting the prior become flat in that post’s posterior formulas, the marginal posterior of the coefficients is a distribution with degrees of freedom, centered at , with scale matrix . A distribution with degrees of freedom has variance times its squared scale, so the posterior standard deviations are , nearly the naive standard error.

Code 
beta_bayes <- fit_weighted_ols(M, y, w_bayes)$beta
tau_bayes <- beta_bayes[, "T"]
sd_NIG <- sqrt(diag(sum(eps_hat^2) / (n - 2) * MtM_inv))

tibble(
  `posterior mean` = mean(tau_bayes),
  `posterior sd` = sd(tau_bayes),
  `2.5%` = quantile(tau_bayes, 0.025),
  `97.5%` = quantile(tau_bayes, 0.975),
  `P(tau > 0)` = mean(tau_bayes > 0)
)
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  `posterior mean` `posterior sd` `2.5%` `97.5%` `P(tau > 0)`
             <dbl>          <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>
1            0.395          0.109  0.176   0.619            1
Code 
rbind(
  `NIG posterior sd (flat prior)` = sd_NIG,
  `Bayesian bootstrap posterior sd` = apply(beta_bayes, 2, sd),
  HC0 = se_HC0
)
                                         1          T           X
NIG posterior sd (flat prior)   0.05630181 0.07680405 0.004374973
Bayesian bootstrap posterior sd 0.07415540 0.10903538 0.008631767
HC0                             0.07594796 0.10957207 0.008628506

The Bayesian bootstrap posterior of has mean 0.395 and standard deviation 0.109, and 1000 of its 1000 draws are positive, so the posterior probability of a positive effect is essentially 1. Its standard deviation matches HC0, while the flat-prior Normal-Inverse-Gamma posterior is 30% narrower, because its Gaussian likelihood assumes every user has the same noise variance. Figure 3 shows the difference.

Code 
tau_grid <- seq(min(tau_bayes), max(tau_bayes), length.out = 300)

tibble(tau = tau_bayes) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tau)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, fill = "grey75", color = "white") +
  geom_line(
    data = bind_rows(
      tibble(curve = "NIG, flat prior", tau = tau_grid,
             density = dnorm(tau_grid, beta_hat["T"], sd_NIG["T"])),
      tibble(curve = "Normal with HC0 sd", tau = tau_grid,
             density = dnorm(tau_grid, beta_hat["T"], se_HC0["T"]))
    ),
    aes(y = density, color = curve),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = expression(tau), y = "posterior density", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

In the earlier post, getting a robust posterior took a quasi-Bayesian argument and a hand-built sandwich. The Bayesian bootstrap produces it from the weighted least squares fit alone.

A posterior for an estimand with no likelihood: the difference in medians

Least squares at least has a familiar Gaussian likelihood next to it. The difference in medians does not: the median of hours streamed among treated users minus the median among control users, which is a different estimand from . Under a population , the median among treated users is the weighted median of the treated users’ outcomes, with weights . Since a weighted median does not change when every weight is multiplied by the same constant, we can again use the directly. We reuse the same Exponential weights, so each draw of the population gives one draw of each estimand.

Code 
weighted_median <- function(y, w) {
  ord <- order(y)
  cum_w <- apply(w[ord, , drop = FALSE], 2, cumsum)
  # Count the users whose cumulative weight is below half the total; the median is the next one
  below_half <- sweep(cum_w, 2, cum_w[nrow(cum_w), ] / 2, `<`)
  y[ord][colSums(below_half) + 1]
}

treated <- users$T == 1
median_diff_bayes <- weighted_median(y[treated], w_bayes[treated, ]) -
  weighted_median(y[!treated], w_bayes[!treated, ])
median_diff_hat <- median(y[treated]) - median(y[!treated])

# The true difference in medians, from a very large draw of the same population
set.seed(7)
population <- simulate_users(1e6)
median_diff_true <- median(population$y[population$T == 1]) -
  median(population$y[population$T == 0])
# The same population with the mean effect removed: only the wider noise remains
y_no_effect <- population$y - tau * population$T
median_diff_no_effect <- median(y_no_effect[population$T == 1]) -
  median(y_no_effect[population$T == 0])
rm(population, y_no_effect)

tibble(
  `sample estimate` = median_diff_hat,
  `posterior mean` = mean(median_diff_bayes),
  `posterior sd` = sd(median_diff_bayes),
  `2.5%` = quantile(median_diff_bayes, 0.025),
  `97.5%` = quantile(median_diff_bayes, 0.975),
  truth = median_diff_true,
  `truth without the mean effect` = median_diff_no_effect
) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "difference in medians")
# A tibble: 7 × 2
  quantity                      `difference in medians`
  <chr>                                           <dbl>
1 sample estimate                               -0.335 
2 posterior mean                                -0.378 
3 posterior sd                                   0.172 
4 2.5%                                          -0.707 
5 97.5%                                         -0.0441
6 truth                                         -0.315 
7 truth without the mean effect                 -0.515

The posterior of the difference in medians has mean -0.378 and a 95% credible interval from -0.707 to -0.044. The true difference is -0.315, which the interval covers.

The difference in medians is negative although treatment raises mean hours by . The last row explains why: removing the mean effect from the same population leaves a difference in medians of -0.515, which comes entirely from treatment doubling the noise. A change in the noise leaves the mean alone but can move the median, and here it moves it down by more than the mean effect moves it up.

A team that reports median hours would conclude that treatment hurts, while a team that reports mean hours would conclude it helps. Neither is wrong; they are asking about different summaries of the population. We never wrote a likelihood for medians. The posterior came from the same draws of as the posterior of .

Assumptions, and when the Bayesian bootstrap breaks

The posterior is only as good as (A1)–(A3), and each has a practical consequence.

  1. (A1), independent users. The unit that receives a weight must be the unit of independence. If an experiment randomizes accounts and we analyze profiles, the weights must be drawn per account and shared by its profiles, exactly as with a cluster-robust standard error.
  2. (A2), support on the observed values. Every posterior draw is a reweighting of the users we saw. A population can never contain a user more extreme than our most extreme user. With heavy tails, such as a few “whales” who stream far more than everyone else, or with small samples, the posterior is too narrow, because it cannot imagine the whale we have not yet seen. The classical bootstrap has the same weakness.
  3. (A3), the prior. The prior is a specific improper prior on , not a statement about . It cannot encode what we already know, for example that most effects in past experiments were small. The Normal-Inverse-Gamma model can, with a prior mean and variance on the coefficients that shrink a noisy estimate. With the Bayesian bootstrap, informative priors and shrinkage across experiments are not available.
  4. The estimand is a population summary. is the effect in the population that generated the users, not the effect on the specific users in the experiment. The prior also does not know that was randomized, so some draws of have a small chance correlation between and ; least squares adjusts for it in each draw.

So can we skip the Bayesian linear model?

For the most common case, yes. If we want a posterior for the average treatment effect, adjusted for covariates, with a variance that does not assume a common noise level, the Bayesian bootstrap of least squares delivers it. It is the same weighted fit as the Poisson bootstrap and runs in the same single pass over the data, even with data spread across machines, because Exponential weights, like Poisson weights, are drawn independently per user. The same posterior draws also give posteriors for estimands that have no convenient likelihood, such as the difference in medians.

We still need the Bayesian linear model when we want an informative prior, for example to shrink effects toward what past experiments have shown, or when the sample is small or heavy-tailed enough that (A2) bites.

Putting it together

Weights Drawn independently per user? The distribution is Answers
Classical Multinomial counts No, they add up to The sampling distribution of How much the estimate moves across datasets
Poisson Poisson(1) Yes Approximately the same sampling distribution The same, at scale and in one pass
Bayesian Exponential(1), normalized to Dirichlet Yes The posterior of What we believe about the estimand, given the data

All three bootstraps refit the same weighted estimator; they differ in how the weights are drawn and in what the resulting distribution means. For least squares in an AB test, all three give the robust sandwich variance rather than the naive one. The classical and Poisson bootstraps give a confidence interval. The Bayesian bootstrap, with its assumptions written down, gives a posterior for without a likelihood for . For a team at scale, the practical recipe is one pass over the data with independently drawn weights per user: Poisson weights for a standard error, Exponential weights for a posterior.

The examples in this post are simulations for education, not production systems.

item.title: What are AI Benchmarks?
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
In September 2026 OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra with a table of benchmark results, including 96.0% on GPQA Diamond, 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2), and “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1”. Around the same time Anthropic released Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, each with its own table. Each launch reports higher scores than the one before. The scores keep climbing, and it all looks impressive. But what is actually being tested? Who wrote the test, who graded it, and what does 74.1% mean?

This post opens up the benchmarks behind those tables. We treat a benchmark the way we would treat any measurement in an experiment: a sample of tasks, a procedure, a grader and an average. Seen this way, a benchmark score is an average with a standard error, just like a metric in an AB test, and it has the same kinds of biases. We start by decoding one score, “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1”. Then we tour the benchmarks that recur in launch tables, who made them, and who grades them. Finally we look at when a high score should raise our confidence, and when we should still have doubts.

The numbers in this post are as reported by the model developers and benchmark maintainers as of October 13, 2026, unless noted otherwise.

A benchmark is an exam with three parts

Every benchmark has three parts.

  1. The tasks. A fixed set of questions or jobs, written by someone, with a known correct outcome.
  2. The harness. The program that hands each task to the model, gives the model its tools (a terminal, a browser, a code editor), and decides how long it may work and how many tries it gets.
  3. The grader. The rule that turns the model’s output into pass or fail, or into a partial score.

The headline number is the average grade over the tasks. One more question sits on top of these three parts: who ran the exam? It might be the model’s developer, the benchmark’s maintainer, or an independent evaluation organization.

A score changes when any of these parts changes. “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” only means something once we know all of them.

What does “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” mean?

DeepSWE was built by Datacurve, a company that supplies expert-written coding data, training environments and benchmarks to AI developers.

The tasks. DeepSWE has 113 tasks drawn from 91 open-source repositories, each with at least 500 GitHub stars. The repositories are written in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript and Rust. Software engineers wrote each task from scratch. They came up with the problem, built the environment, wrote and verified the tests, and reviewed each other’s work. A typical task reads like a feature request. One example is adding cancellation support to Boa, a JavaScript engine written in Rust. The reference solutions are large: on average 668 added lines across 7 files.

The harness. The model works as an agent: it gets a copy of the repository and a terminal, and it can read files, run commands and edit code over many steps. For the public leaderboard, Datacurve runs every model in the same simple harness, mini-swe-agent, so that differences come from the model and not from tooling. The model finishes by committing its changes.

The grader. In version 1.1, a fresh container that the agent never touched applies the model’s changes and runs a hidden test suite. The suite contains new tests that check the requested behavior through public interfaces, plus the repository’s existing tests, which check that nothing else broke. No human and no AI reads the code to grade it. The tests do the grading. This setup is what distinguishes version 1.1 from 1.0, which uses the same tasks. Datacurve designed it to make the grader harder to game: an agent cannot patch the test framework inside the grading container, and a test that is dropped or cut short by an early exit shows up as missing or failed rather than passing.

The score. Each task is attempted many times. Datacurve notes that 73 of Claude Fable 5’s 2,260 attempts did not finish, and 2,260 / 113 = 20, so each model gets 20 attempts per task. Datacurve reports pass@1, the probability that a single attempt passes. With 20 attempts per task, a natural estimate takes the share of each task’s attempts whose code passes the hidden tests, then averages that share over all 113 tasks.

So “74.1% on DeepSWE v1.1” means: if we give GPT-6 Astra one of these 113 feature requests, its code passes the hidden tests 74.1% of the time on average, the equivalent of about 84 of the 113 tasks.

Who ran it? The 74.1% is OpenAI’s own run. Datacurve also runs Astra on its public leaderboard, in mini-swe-agent at the “xhigh” effort setting, and gets 74% ± 3%. Here the two agree. But a developer’s own run and a run by the benchmark maintainer are different measurements, and they do not always agree.

A tour of the recurring benchmarks

Some benchmarks appear in launch after launch, in four broad families. Table 1 summarizes them, and the subsections explain each one.

Software engineering: can it do a ticket?

Coding benchmarks used to be short puzzles: write a function, pass a few unit tests. Today’s coding benchmarks are agentic. The model gets a whole environment and a vague goal, much like a ticket handed to an engineer.

  • DeepSWE is described above. On Datacurve’s leaderboard, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Opus 5 are tied at the top at 74%.
  • Terminal-Bench 4.0 has 66 tasks spanning software, machine learning, science, operations, security, hardware and media. Each task runs in a real terminal, and the grader checks the final state of the machine. The project was started by Stanford and the Laude Institute in 2025. The task set is revised as models catch up: version 4.0 removed 8 tasks from 3.0 and fixed 19 others. Small models still lag far behind here. Anthropic reports Haiku 5.5 at 39.2% against Sonnet 5.5 at 70.6%.

Science and math: does it know what an expert knows?

  • GPQA (“Graduate-level Google-Proof Q&A”) was written by Rein et al. (2023). Domain experts with or pursuing PhDs wrote multiple-choice questions in biology, physics and chemistry. Other experts answered them correctly 65% of the time. Skilled non-experts managed only 34%, despite spending over 30 minutes per question with unrestricted web access. The Diamond subset keeps 198 questions on which the expert validators agreed with the answer key and most non-experts did not. Random guessing among four choices scores 25%. In 2023, the strongest GPT-4-based baseline scored 39%. OpenAI now reports 96.0% for GPT-6 Astra.
  • Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE), released by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI in January 2025, has 2,500 questions crowdsourced from experts. About 41% are math, and the rest cover physics, biology, chemistry, computer science, the humanities and more. A question was accepted only if the frontier models of the time failed it, and only after two rounds of expert review. So by construction, the models of early 2025 scored low on it. About three quarters of the answers are short exact answers rather than multiple choice. Anthropic reports Fable 5.1 at 60.9% without tools and 65.0% with tools.
  • FrontierMath, built by Epoch AI, contains unpublished research-level math problems. Each answer is a number or a mathematical object that a program can check. Tier 4 is the hardest tier. OpenAI reports 97.6% for GPT-6 Astra on Tier 4 (v2).

Computer use and knowledge work: can it do the job?

  • OSWorld puts the model in front of a real Ubuntu desktop and asks it to do things like edit a spreadsheet in LibreOffice or change a setting in VS Code. The model sees screenshots and acts with the mouse and keyboard. The original release had 369 tasks, and the 2026 tables use the revised 2.x versions. A script then inspects the computer, for example the file contents or the config, to check that the job was done.
  • GDPval is a set of 1,320 tasks OpenAI developed in 2025 with industry professionals, spanning 44 occupations in 9 industries: write a memo, build a spreadsheet model, design a slide deck. GDPval-AA is the version run by Artificial Analysis, an independent evaluation company, on 220 of these tasks. The model works as an agent with a shell and web browsing and produces a real deliverable. Unlike everything else in the table, the score is an Elo rating, not a percentage. An AI judge sees two models’ deliverables for the same task, without names, and picks the better one. In version 2.1 the scale is anchored by fixing one reference model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, at 1600. Only differences in Elo carry meaning: a larger gap means a higher expected win rate when two models’ deliverables are compared. Anthropic’s report of Haiku 5.5 at 1620 against Haiku 4.5 at 735 on version 2.1 means the newer model would be expected to win most head-to-head comparisons, not that it gets 1620 of anything right.

Cybersecurity: can it defend or attack?

  • CWE-bench v1, from Collinear AI, has 120 audit-and-patch tasks covering 73 categories of software weakness (CWEs) in 8 languages. The vulnerabilities are undisclosed, and the agent must find and fix them without breaking existing functionality. This is defensive work.
  • ExploitBench, from Lee and Brumley at Carnegie Mellon, is offensive. It contains 41 real bugs in V8, the JavaScript engine inside Chrome. Instead of a single pass or fail, it scores a ladder of 16 capabilities: from triggering the bug, through gaining read and write access to memory, up to arbitrary code execution. A deterministic verifier checks each rung. The exploit must work against the buggy version and fail against the patched one.

Who grades the AI?

Across Table 1 there are three kinds of graders, and they deserve different levels of trust.

  1. Programs. Hidden tests (DeepSWE, CWE-bench), check scripts on the final state of a machine (Terminal-Bench, OSWorld), answer keys (GPQA, FrontierMath) and exploit verifiers (ExploitBench). These graders are mechanical and reproducible. Their weakness is that a test can only check what its author thought to check.
  2. AI judges. HLE uses an AI model (o3-mini in the original paper) to decide whether an answer like “0.5” matches a key that says “1/2”. GDPval-AA uses an AI judge to compare deliverables, because no test can check whether a memo is persuasive. Datacurve also used an AI model to audit DeepSWE’s own tests. When the grader is itself a model, the score inherits the grader’s blind spots and tastes.
  3. Humans. Humans rarely grade the model directly, because human grading is slow and expensive. They show up earlier: they write the tasks and answer keys (DeepSWE’s engineers, GDPval’s professionals), and they validate the questions (GPQA’s expert and non-expert validators, HLE’s expert reviewers).

Who runs the exam?

A benchmark is not a sealed exam administered by a testing agency. Most are published openly: the tasks, the grader and often a reference harness are available for anyone to download and run against any model they can access. DeepSWE’s repository contains all 113 tasks with their tests and grader configuration, plus a quickstart that runs the benchmark with Datacurve’s Pier tool. The mini-swe-agent harness that Datacurve uses for its leaderboard is also open source, as is Terminal-Bench. The questions for GPQA and HLE are on Hugging Face; GPQA is gated, so we must request access and accept its terms first. Evaluation frameworks package many benchmarks with a ready-made harness and grader. The UK AI Security Institute’s Inspect Evals includes GPQA, HLE and OSWorld, and EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness covers a wide range of question-and-answer benchmarks.

The model is the other half. Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 cannot be downloaded: we reach them through their developers’ APIs with an API key, and the harness sends each task to the API. Open-weight models can be downloaded from Hugging Face, for example OpenAI’s gpt-oss-20b, and run on our own hardware. Either way, the same benchmark can be run by several different groups, and a score is only as informative as our knowledge of who ran it and how. Three groups do most of the running.

  1. The model’s developer, in house. Most numbers in a launch table come from the developer’s own evaluation team, running the benchmark on its own infrastructure before release. OpenAI’s launch post says its GPT evaluations “were run in our research environment or via our API”, which “may provide slightly different output from production ChatGPT due to differences in the system prompts, tools available, etc.” The developer chooses the harness and the settings, and OpenAI reports the maximum score at any effort setting. For competitors’ columns, a developer either copies the competitor’s published number, which OpenAI’s charts label “reported score only”, or runs the competitor’s model itself through that competitor’s public API. OpenAI did the latter for HealthBench Professional: “we independently evaluated all Claude models following the intended HealthBench Professional procedure.”
  2. The benchmark’s maintainer. Some maintainers run models themselves and publish a leaderboard. Datacurve runs every model on DeepSWE in the same harness, mini-swe-agent, so that differences come from the models rather than the tooling. This is how we got Datacurve’s 74% ± 3% for Astra, next to OpenAI’s in-house 74.1%. Maintainers sometimes test a model before its launch: OpenAI’s post quotes the ARC Prize Foundation, which maintains ARC-AGI-3, on its own testing of Astra, calling it “the best model we’ve ever tested”.
  3. Independent evaluation organizations. Companies like Artificial Analysis run many benchmarks across many models in one shared setup, and publish the results. They run GDPval-AA, and combined indices such as the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which OpenAI’s own table reports. They usually test models through the same public API that customers use, and sometimes get access before launch: Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 page notes that Artificial Analysis tested a pre-release deployment.

A launch table usually mixes all three, and the footnotes often say which is which. The in-house runs are the most numerous and come with the developer’s choices of harness and settings. The maintainer and independent runs are fewer, but they apply one setup to every model. When an in-house number and an independent number for the same model agree, as Astra’s do on DeepSWE, we learn that the result does not hinge on who ran it.

When a high score should raise our confidence

A high score is real evidence when the measurement was designed well. These are the properties to look for.

  1. The tasks are new to the model. DeepSWE’s tasks were written from scratch rather than adapted from public commits, so they were not on the internet before the benchmark was released. HLE keeps a private set of questions that is never published. A benchmark built from material that appeared after the model’s knowledge cutoff is the strongest version of this.
  2. The grader checks the outcome, and the grader itself was audited. Datacurve used an AI reviewer to audit the tests of DeepSWE v1.0 on a sample of 30 tasks. They found a 0.3% false-positive rate (passing a bad patch) and a 1.1% false-negative rate (failing a good one). The same check on SWE-Bench Pro, an earlier and widely used coding benchmark, gave 8.5% and 24%. An audit applies to the version it checked.
  3. Someone else reproduced it. OpenAI’s 74.1% for Astra on DeepSWE agrees with Datacurve’s independent 74% ± 3%. When the developer’s number and the maintainer’s number agree, the result does not depend on who ran it.
  4. Many benchmarks agree. One benchmark can have a quirk. A model that leads in coding, science and computer use at once is unlikely to owe all of it to quirks.
  5. The tasks resemble the consumer’s task. By the consumer we mean the team that will use the model for its own work. A consumer writing Go services learns more from DeepSWE than from GPQA, and a consumer automating spreadsheets learns more from OSWorld.
  6. The gap is bigger than the noise. A score is an average over a sample of tasks, so it has a standard error. For a sense of its size, suppose each of tasks were attempted once, and the model passes each one independently with probability . Then the score is a sample proportion, with standard error . For DeepSWE, plugging in and gives , about 4 points. Datacurve’s leaderboard prints error bars of ±1 to ±6 points, the same range. As with the minimum detectable effect in an AB test, a lead of a few points on about a hundred tasks may just be noise, which we describe next.

How much noise is in a benchmark score?

Datacurve’s leaderboard puts GPT-6 Astra at 74% on DeepSWE and Claude Fable 5 at 70%, both run by Datacurve in the same harness. Is a 4-point lead a real difference in skill, or the luck of which 113 tasks happened to be on the exam? In point 6 of the previous section we sized the noise as if each task were attempted once, and got about 4 points. DeepSWE attempts each task 20 times, so we need a closer look.

We can think of DeepSWE’s 113 tasks as a sample from a much larger population of feature requests that could have been written. Each task has a probability , a scalar between 0 and 1, that the model solves it on a single attempt. The quantity we actually care about is the model’s skill on the whole population, , where the expectation averages over the population of tasks. This is the same as in point 6, now allowed to differ from task to task. Datacurve’s per-task results show that pass rates vary widely across tasks, and that a task one model solves every time can be one another model rarely solves.

The benchmark score is a sample estimate of . With tasks and attempts per task, let be the fraction of the attempts on task that pass. The score is

varies for two reasons. The attempts are random, so rerunning the same tasks gives slightly different . And the tasks are random: the benchmark’s 113 tasks are one draw from the population, and a different 113 feature requests would give a different average.

To see how large each source is, we simulate a world that looks like DeepSWE. We build a pool of 10,000 possible tasks, each with a difficulty, and two models A and B with exactly the same average skill on the pool. The models are not identical task by task. Each has its own strengths, so and are correlated but not equal. Real models share many of the same hard tasks, but not all of them.

Code 
set.seed(2026)

N_pool <- 10000  # possible tasks that could have been written
n <- 113         # tasks on the benchmark
K <- 20          # attempts per task

# Each task has a difficulty d_j. Each model's solve probability on task j
# depends on the difficulty plus a model-specific strength or weakness on that task.
pool <- tibble(j = 1:N_pool, d_j = rnorm(N_pool, 0, 1.5)) |>
  mutate(
    theta_A = plogis(1.6 - d_j + rnorm(N_pool, 0, 1)),
    theta_B = plogis(1.6 - d_j + rnorm(N_pool, 0, 1))
  )

pool |>
  summarise(
    p_A = mean(theta_A),
    p_B = mean(theta_B),
    cor_theta_A_B = cor(theta_A, theta_B),
    theta_A_10pct = quantile(theta_A, 0.1),
    theta_A_90pct = quantile(theta_A, 0.9)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 5
    p_A   p_B cor_theta_A_B theta_A_10pct theta_A_90pct
  <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
1 0.742 0.740         0.651         0.332         0.980

Both models have a true skill of about 74% on the pool, close to the top of today’s leaderboard. Per-task solve rates range from about a third on hard tasks to nearly 1 on easy ones. Now we run the benchmark 2,000 times in two ways. First we keep the same 113 tasks and only redraw the attempts. Then we draw a fresh set of 113 tasks each time.

Code 
run_benchmark <- function(tasks) {
  tasks |>
    mutate(
      s_A = rbinom(n(), K, theta_A) / K,
      s_B = rbinom(n(), K, theta_B) / K
    ) |>
    summarise(p_hat_A = mean(s_A), p_hat_B = mean(s_B))
}

fixed_tasks <- slice_sample(pool, n = n)

sims <- bind_rows(
  map(1:2000, \(r) run_benchmark(fixed_tasks)) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(source = "Same 113 tasks, new attempts"),
  map(1:2000, \(r) run_benchmark(slice_sample(pool, n = n))) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(source = "New 113 tasks each time")
) |>
  mutate(gap = p_hat_A - p_hat_B)

sim_summary <- sims |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(
    sd_p_hat_A = sd(p_hat_A),
    mean_gap = mean(gap),
    sd_gap = sd(gap),
    share_gap_at_least_4 = mean(abs(gap) >= 0.04)
  )
sim_summary
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  source                       sd_p_hat_A mean_gap sd_gap share_gap_at_least_4
  <chr>                             <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>                <dbl>
1 New 113 tasks each time         0.0247   0.00156 0.0227               0.0755
2 Same 113 tasks, new attempts    0.00757  0.0185  0.0107               0.024
Code 
fixed_row <- filter(sim_summary, source == "Same 113 tasks, new attempts")
fresh_row <- filter(sim_summary, source == "New 113 tasks each time")
Code 
ggplot(sims, aes(x = 100 * gap, fill = source)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-4, 4), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e")) +
  labs(x = "Score of A minus score of B (points)", y = "Simulated runs", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Some patterns worth noting:

  1. Rerunning the attempts barely moves the score. With the tasks held fixed, the standard deviation of a model’s score is 0.8 points. Twenty attempts per task average away most of the run-to-run randomness.
  2. With fixed tasks, the gap is centered on A’s advantage on those tasks, not on zero. On this particular set of 113 tasks, model A’s average is 1.9 points above B’s, even though the two are equally skilled on the pool. Rerunning the attempts scatters the gap around that value with a standard deviation of 1.1 points, and the gap reaches 4 points in 2% of reruns. This is not a null distribution for “A and B are equally skilled”. It is the distribution of the gap when A really is ahead on these fixed tasks, so the 2% is not a p-value. Rerunning the same exam many times would not reveal that A’s advantage comes from the choice of tasks.
  3. The choice of tasks is the main source of noise. With a fresh draw of tasks, a single model’s score has a standard deviation of 2.5 points. That is the uncertainty in the claim “this model solves 74% of feature requests like these”. It is smaller than the single-attempt figure of about 4 points from point 6, because the 20 attempts average away the coin flips within each task. It is also in the range of the ±1 to ±4 points that Datacurve prints for its top three models.
  4. The fresh-task runs are the null distribution. Here the two models are equally skilled on the population, each run draws a new set of tasks, and both models are graded on the same tasks, as on a real benchmark. So this is the null distribution for the question we care about: is A better than B on feature requests like these in general? The gap is centered near zero, with a standard deviation of 2.3 points, and it is 4 or more points in either direction in 7.5% of runs. In this world, a 4-point lead, like Astra’s over Fable 5, has a two-sided p-value of about 0.075. It is not significant at the 5% level.

The two simulations answer different questions. If we asked instead whether A is better on these exact 113 tasks, the null would be centered at zero with the fixed-task spread of 1.1 points. A 4-point gap would then be 3.7 standard deviations out, which is highly significant. But that question is narrow: with 20 attempts per task, almost any real difference on a fixed task set is detectable. A benchmark is useful because we want to generalize beyond its tasks, and that is the question with the wider null.

These numbers depend on the assumptions in our simulated world, in particular how much the models’ strengths differ task by task. They are not a statement about Astra or Fable 5. The general lesson holds: a benchmark of about a hundred tasks cannot reliably separate models a few points apart. This is the same arithmetic as the minimum detectable effect in an AB test. A small sample of tasks has a large MDE.

Testing a gap with a paired comparison

With real data we cannot simulate the null, but we can estimate its spread from a single benchmark run. For each task , let be the difference in the two models’ pass rates. The gap in scores is the average difference,

If the tasks are a random sample from the population, the are independent draws, so is a sample mean with standard error , and . Each includes both sources of noise, the task’s difficulty for each model and the randomness of the attempts, so this standard error accounts for both. Pairing matters. A hard task lowers both and , and taking the difference cancels the shared part. This is the same logic as a within-user comparison in an AB test, with tasks in the role of users.

We can test this on one simulated benchmark run, and compare the paired standard error with the spread of the gap across the 2,000 fresh benchmarks. We also compute the unpaired standard error, which treats the two scores as if they came from independent task sets.

Code 
set.seed(7)

one_run <- slice_sample(pool, n = n) |>
  mutate(
    s_A = rbinom(n(), K, theta_A) / K,
    s_B = rbinom(n(), K, theta_B) / K,
    d_j = s_A - s_B
  )

paired_test <- one_run |>
  summarise(
    d_bar = mean(d_j),
    se_paired = sd(d_j) / sqrt(n()),
    se_unpaired = sqrt(var(s_A) + var(s_B)) / sqrt(n()),
    z = d_bar / se_paired
  )
paired_test
# A tibble: 1 × 4
     d_bar se_paired se_unpaired      z
     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>  <dbl>
1 -0.00619    0.0224      0.0346 -0.276

The paired standard error from this one run is 2.2 points, close to the 2.3-point spread of the gap across the fresh benchmarks. The unpaired standard error is 3.5 points. It overstates the noise, because it ignores that both models faced the same tasks. With per-task results for two real models, the same calculation would give a p-value for their gap without any simulation.

Being rigorous about what we read

Noise shrinks as a benchmark adds tasks. The problems below are different. They are biases: each one shifts the score systematically, up or down depending on the problem, and adding more tasks does not fix them.

The model may have seen the exam

Models are trained on large amounts of internet text. If benchmark questions, or their solutions, are on the internet, a model can score well by remembering rather than reasoning. This is called contamination, and it pushes scores up.

ExploitBench shows how contamination can be measured. Its 41 bugs are real V8 vulnerabilities disclosed in 2024 or later. Their descriptions, patches and bug-tracker discussions are public, although working exploits were published for only 2 of them. OpenAI reported that GPT-6 Astra reached arbitrary code execution on all 41, a score of 100%.

In the same launch post, OpenAI raised the question itself: “given concerns that exposure to historical software vulnerabilities may have affected benchmark results”, it also built an internal set of 20 high-severity V8 vulnerabilities disclosed between June and August 2026, after the model’s knowledge cutoff. Astra scored 39.0% on that set, against 5.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI notes that some of these vulnerabilities may not permit arbitrary code execution under the evaluation’s constraints, so 100% may not be achievable there. It also reports that Astra found two previously unknown vulnerabilities during the evaluation, which OpenAI is disclosing to their maintainers.

The two sets contain different bugs, so the scores are not directly comparable. Epoch AI’s review attributes part of the 100% to contamination, and notes that the size of the effect is hard to quantify. For newly disclosed vulnerabilities, the 39.0% is the more direct measurement, and running such a check is what makes the 100% interpretable.

Benchmark maintainers watch for this too. When Terminal-Bench moved to version 4.0, it removed 2 tasks because their solutions had become public.

Exposure can also come from how a benchmark is funded and shared. OpenAI commissioned Epoch AI to produce 300 advanced math problems for FrontierMath, owns them, and has access to the problems and their solutions. Epoch AI also maintains a separate holdout set of 50 problems, for which OpenAI receives only the problem statements, so that every lab’s models can be tested on solutions no lab has seen. When reading a FrontierMath score, it helps to know whether it was measured on the holdout set.

The answer key can be wrong

Benchmarks are written by people, and people make mistakes. When the grader is wrong, the error can push scores in either direction.

DeepSWE. Epoch AI reviews popular benchmarks. On September 7, 2026 it rated DeepSWE v1.1 “Flawed”. It found false negatives, where correct work is marked as failing, in at least 23 of the 113 tasks (20.3%). It stopped inspecting once the errors passed its published 20% threshold, so there may be more. 78% of these errors were collisions. The verifier adds its hidden tests to the model’s changes, so when the model had written its own test with the same name as a hidden one, the test package failed to compile. The models had no way to know this and were not told to avoid it. These errors push DeepSWE scores down.

Errors in the other direction have been reported too. On October 2, 2026 an outside audit firm opened a public issue on DeepSWE’s repository showing false positives. A submitted patch can change test infrastructure that the verifier then loads. In one example, a patch that only edited a test configuration file, rewriting failed test reports as passes, received full credit without implementing the feature. As of this writing the issue is open, with no public response from Datacurve.

HLE. In July 2025, FutureHouse reported that 29% ± 3.7% (95% confidence interval) of the answers to HLE’s text-only chemistry and biology questions conflicted with the peer-reviewed literature. That estimate came from 321 questions, checked by FutureHouse’s literature-search agent and validated by expert reviewers on a sample. In September 2025, FutureHouse posted an update: the HLE team’s own review, in which three experts examined each question in a subset of the biology and chemistry questions, found about 18% of them problematic. At least one of the three experts disagreed with the answer in about 25% of cases. The two estimates differ, but both are far from zero. The HLE organizers responded by committing to a rolling revision process for the benchmark.

A wrong answer key puts a ceiling on the score. If a fraction of the answer key is wrong, a model that always gives the truly correct answer is marked wrong on those questions and scores at most . The HLE team found about 18% of the questions they reviewed problematic. If all of those had wrong answers, and the ceiling on those questions would be 82%. Near the ceiling, we cannot tell a better model from one that better matches the mistakes in the key.

The harness and settings are part of the score

The same model gets different scores under different harnesses and settings. The differences can be larger than the gaps between models:

  • On ExploitBench, GPT-5.5 running in OpenAI’s Codex harness reached arbitrary code execution 12 times when allowed 3,000 turns. With a 300-turn limit, it reached it 0 times in the Codex harness and once without it. OpenAI’s launch post makes the same point about its own models: GPT-5.6 Sol’s 5.5% on the June–August set is an artifact of that set’s 300-turn limit, and Sol scored 11.5% at similar settings with fewer limits.
  • Scores are usually reported at a high “effort” or reasoning budget, which costs more and takes longer than many production settings. OpenAI’s table states that its “evaluation scores are the maximum at any effort”. Anthropic’s footnote for Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 says the reported number is the model’s highest score, obtained at the “xhigh” effort setting.
  • More effort is not always better. On FrontierCode, a coding benchmark that penalizes changes outside the task’s scope, Sonnet 5.5 scored lower at its maximum effort setting than at xhigh. At maximum effort it ran additional code-review subagents, which occasionally caused timeouts or extra edits.
  • On OSWorld 2.0 tasks where Anthropic’s production safeguards intervened, Fable 5.1 scored zero. Here the deployment setup lowers the score.

The same name can mean different scores

Sonnet 5.5 appears with two different OSWorld 2.1 numbers on Anthropic’s own pages: 80.1% under a “partial” scoring rule on the Sonnet launch page, and 83.9% on an “offline subset” of the tasks on the Haiku launch page. Fable 5.1 is reported at 77.9% on OSWorld 2.0 under the “partial” rule and 41.7% under a “strict” one. Neither number is wrong, but they are different measurements.

Benchmarks also get revised. Terminal-Bench calls version 4.0 a breaking change that requires re-running trials, because it changed both the task set and the resources given to the agent. So a model’s score on 4.0 cannot be compared with an older model’s score on 3.0. Anthropic’s OSWorld 2.0 scores use the benchmark authors’ August 2026 task release, and Anthropic re-ran its older models under the same conditions. That is the right practice, and it is worth checking for whenever a table compares models across versions.

The benchmark does not represent the consumer’s task

Even a perfect benchmark measures the model on its own task distribution. It’s not necessarily what the consumer cares most about. DeepSWE’s tasks are in five languages, from open-source repositories with at least 500 GitHub stars, each with a written task description. The consumer’s codebase may be private, old, underspecified and in a language the benchmark does not cover. A benchmark tells the consumer which models are worth trying. Whether a model improves the consumer’s product is still a causal question about that product’s users, and the final judge is an AB test.

Putting it together

When we read the next launch table, these questions help us interpret each row.

Question Why it matters Example
What are the tasks, and who wrote them? Defines what the score measures DeepSWE: 113 feature requests written from scratch
Could the model have seen them? Contamination inflates scores ExploitBench: 100% on public bugs, 39.0% on a newer, different set
Who or what grades the output? Tests, scripts, AI judges and humans fail differently HLE and GDPval-AA both use AI judges
Has the answer key been audited? Grading errors can lower, inflate or cap the score Epoch found errors in at least 20% of DeepSWE tasks
Who ran it, and with what harness and settings? Settings can move scores by more than the gaps between models ExploitBench: 300 vs 3,000 turns
Which version and scoring rule? Same name, different measurement OSWorld 2.0 partial 77.9% vs strict 41.7%
Is the gap bigger than the noise? About 100 tasks give a standard error of a few points DeepSWE: about 4 points at 74% on 113 tasks; the top three models are tied at 74%
Do the tasks look like the consumer’s task? A benchmark measures its own task distribution The consumer still needs its own AB test

A benchmark score is a measurement, not a verdict. It’s an average over a sample of tasks, produced by a harness and a grader that someone chose, and often run by the model’s developer. High scores across fresh, audited, independently reproduced benchmarks are strong evidence that a model has improved. A lead of a few points on a single benchmark is weaker evidence, whoever ran it. The scores will keep going up. Each time, it’s worth asking what the exam was.

item.title: Conditionally Sufficient Statistics
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
Experimentation has many special designs, each warranting a specialized type of model. Managing all of these can be difficult. Keeping the implementation sane is harder. In this post, we show that four features of experimental design, in any combination, are covered by one model, which we can fit efficiently. Let’s start with the motivation.

A streaming service wants to know whether a new playback setting helps. Accounts are shared by a household, and each account has up to five profiles. The setting changes how the app behaves on the household’s devices, so the service randomizes at the account level: it shows the account a prompt that invites its profiles to turn the setting on. Each profile then decides for itself. The service is cautious, so it ramps the prompt over four days, from 5% of new accounts to 50%. It measures each profile’s hours watched and its rebuffers per play.

This is a cluster randomized, encouragement experiment, with propensities that change by cohort, and with a ratio metric. In previous posts we analyzed several of these features separately: ratio metrics with a bivariate regression and the delta method, local average treatment effects with an instrument, and CUPED from aggregated data. This post claims that one model covers every combination of these features, and that the model can be fit exactly from a compressed dataset whose size does not grow with the number of rows.

The data in this post is synthetic and the scenario is educational. It does not describe a production system.

The Running Example

Each account enters the experiment on , and the accounts that enter on the same day form a cohort. An account is prompted, , with probability , which ramps up from day to day. Each profile of the account has covariates measured before the experiment: hours per day , tenure in years , whether it is a kids profile, and its main device. A prompted profile turns the setting on, , more often if it watches a lot, and less often if it is a kids profile. Take-up also depends on an engagement level that we do not observe, which also raises the profile’s hours. Profiles of the same account share network quality, so their outcomes are correlated.

Code 
simulate_accounts <- function(n_accounts = 20000, propensity = c(0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50), force_Z = NULL,
                              full_compliance = FALSE, one_profile = FALSE) {
  accounts <- tibble(
    account = seq_len(n_accounts),
    day = sample.int(length(propensity), n_accounts, replace = TRUE, prob = rev(seq_along(propensity))),
    n_profiles = if (one_profile) 1L else pmin(1L + rpois(n_accounts, 1.2), 5L),
    quality = rnorm(n_accounts, 0, 0.5),                       # shared by the account's profiles
    engagement = rnorm(n_accounts, 0, 0.5)                     # account part of engagement
  ) |>
    mutate(Z = rbinom(n(), 1, propensity[day]), Z = if (is.null(force_Z)) Z else force_Z)
  accounts[rep(accounts$account, accounts$n_profiles), ] |>
    mutate(
      profile = sequence(accounts$n_profiles),
      kids = rbinom(n(), 1, if_else(profile == 1, 0.05, 0.3)),   # the first profile is rarely a kids profile
      device = sample(c("tv", "mobile", "web"), n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.35, 0.15)),
      engagement_p = engagement + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.8),          # the profile's engagement, not observed
      x1 = rlnorm(n(), 0.7 - 0.12 * day - 0.6 * kids + 0.3 * engagement_p, 0.6),
      x2 = rgamma(n(), 2, 1) * (1.2 - 0.15 * day),
      complier = rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-0.3 + 0.5 * log(x1) + 0.6 * engagement_p - 0.8 * kids)),
      T = if (full_compliance) Z else Z * complier,
      y = 0.5 + 0.8 * x1 + 0.1 * x2 + 0.5 * engagement_p + quality +                 # hours per day
        T * (0.3 + 0.15 * x1 - 0.2 * kids) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5 + 0.3 * x1),
      D = 1 + rpois(n(), exp(1 + 0.4 * log(x1) + 0.3 * engagement_p + 0.2 * (device == "tv")) * (1 + 0.15 * T)),      # plays
      N = rpois(n(), D * 0.08 * exp(-0.4 * T * (1 + 0.5 * (device == "mobile")) + 0.4 * quality - 0.2 * engagement_p))  # rebuffers
    )
}

propensity <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50)
set.seed(2026)
profiles <- simulate_accounts()

Each row of the data is one profile. Table 1 shows the rows of two accounts: a prompted account in which some profiles turned the setting on and some did not, and an account that was not prompted.

Code 
example_accounts <- c(
  profiles |>
    group_by(account) |>
    filter(first(Z) == 1, n() >= 3, any(T == 1), any(T == 0)) |>
    pull(account) |>
    first(),
  profiles |>
    group_by(account) |>
    filter(first(Z) == 0, n() >= 2) |>
    pull(account) |>
    first())
profiles |>
  filter(account %in% example_accounts) |>
  select(account, profile, day, Z, T, kids, device, x1, x2, y, D, N) |>
  kable(digits = 2)

Table 2 summarizes the experiment by cohort.

Code 
profiles |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(e_day = propensity[first(day)], accounts = n_distinct(account), profiles = n(),
            prompted = mean(Z), takeup = mean(T[Z == 1]), kids = mean(kids), mean_x1 = mean(x1)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Day", "$e_{\\text{day}}$", "Accounts", "Profiles", "Share prompted", "Take-up", "Share kids", "Mean $x_1$"))

Why not add up each account’s profiles first, and analyze one row per account? Because the treatment, the covariates and the question all live at the profile level. Within a prompted account, some profiles turned the setting on and some did not, so an account total mixes treated and untreated profiles. A kids profile and an adult profile watch differently and respond differently, and an account total mixes those too. And the business question is about profiles: how much does the setting change a profile’s hours, and its rebuffers per play, when the profile actually uses it? So we model each profile as a row, , and handle the correlation between profiles of the same account in the standard errors.

Because we wrote the simulation, we can compute the true effects. We simulate the same accounts twice, once with every account prompted and once with none, and look at the profiles that turn the setting on when prompted, the compliers. Our two targets are the effect of the setting on compliers’ hours, , and on compliers’ rebuffers per play,

where and are a profile’s rebuffers and plays with the setting on, , or off, , and denotes the compliers.

Code 
truth_pair <- function(seed, n_accounts = 1e6) {
  set.seed(seed); p1 <- simulate_accounts(n_accounts, force_Z = 1)
  set.seed(seed); p0 <- simulate_accounts(n_accounts, force_Z = 0)
  C <- p1$complier == 1                                      # the same profiles comply in both worlds
  c(tau_LATE = mean(p1$y[C] - p0$y[C]),
    tau_R = sum(p1$N[C]) / sum(p1$D[C]) - sum(p0$N[C]) / sum(p0$D[C]))
}
truth <- colMeans(do.call(rbind, map(1:2, truth_pair)))
truth
   tau_LATE       tau_R 
 0.61334648 -0.02724864

One Universal Model

The design

The experiment has four features, and each one changes the analysis. Keeping track of the complexity is hard, but we will collapse these into a single, universal model.

  1. Clusters. We randomize accounts, and profiles of the same account are correlated, so the standard errors must be cluster robust.
  2. Encouragement. We randomize the prompt , but the treatment received is chosen by the profile, so is an instrument for .
  3. A ramp. The probability of a prompt depends on the cohort, so each account gets the inverse propensity weight if prompted and if not, where is the share of the accounts entering on that day that were prompted.
  4. A ratio metric. Rebuffers per play needs a numerator and a denominator, modeled jointly.

We rely on three assumptions.

(A1) Accounts are independent of each other. Profiles of the same account may be correlated in any way.

(A2) Within a cohort, the prompt is randomized with probability , independently of everything else.

(A3) The prompt affects a profile’s outcomes only through (exclusion), and no profile turns the setting on only when it is not prompted (monotonicity). Monotonicity holds trivially here, because an unprompted profile cannot turn the setting on.

The model

Two stage least squares with weights and cluster robust standard errors handles all four features at once. It is the universal model, and is formulated as

Here is the vector of the profile’s covariates: hours per day, tenure, the kids indicator, and the device as two indicators, mobile and web, so that tv is the baseline. is its -th entry, and is a fixed reference point (see Centering the covariates).

The second stage describes a profile’s outcome with two lines in its covariates. The baseline line is the outcome without the setting, and the treatment line is the effect of the setting. is the main effect of the treatment, the effect at , and lets the effect change with each covariate. Every covariate interacts with the treatment, but the covariates do not interact with each other.

The first stage handles the encouragement. Profiles choose whether to turn the setting on, so profiles with differ from profiles with in ways other than the setting. The treatment and its interactions are therefore endogenous, and each gets its own first stage equation. Each equation has the same form as the second stage, with the randomized prompt in place of : it predicts the endogenous regressor from the covariates, the prompt, and the prompt’s interactions with the covariates. The second stage is then fit with these predictions in place of and its interactions.

Three more choices complete the model. Each account carries its inverse propensity weight , which handles the ramp. The standard errors add up the profiles of an account before squaring, which makes them cluster robust. And one fit can hold several outcome columns: hours , and for the ratio metric, rebuffers , plays , and two more columns, and (see What the model estimates).

What the model estimates

When applying our universal model to this cluster randomized encouragement experiment, the model will be estimating the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE). However, when modeling other experiments, this universal model can also model an average treatment effect, and an intent to treat effect.

The treatment line describes the compliers. The prompt changes the treatment only for compliers, the profiles that turn the setting on when prompted. Every other profile has the same with or without the prompt, so the first stage, and the treatment line it feeds, can only learn from compliers. The treatment line is a fit to the compliers’ average effect at each value of the covariates, , where each counts in proportion to how many compliers have it. The appendix derives this from the model’s equations.

The LATE is the treatment line at the compliers’ average covariates. Because the line is fit to the compliers, its average over the compliers is their average effect, the LATE. A line’s average is its value at the average input, so

where is the mean of the covariates among compliers. This holds even when is not a line. We never observe who is a complier, but we can estimate their mean covariates with a ratio of two intent to treat effects. The product is nonzero only for profiles that took the treatment, so under (A3)

In our experiment the compliers watch more than the average profile, so reading the line at the average profile would answer a different question than the LATE.

The ratio needs the compliers’ own levels. Write for the treatment line of the outcome read at , and similarly for other outcomes. is the compliers’ effect on rebuffers, but needs the compliers’ levels, and . The baseline line does not give them: it describes all profiles, and compliers differ from the rest in ways that does not capture. The column does. It equals for profiles that turned the setting on and 0 otherwise, so its treatment line is fit to the compliers’ rebuffers with the setting on, and . Subtracting the effect gives . The same holds for plays, so

These are the two effects of our running example. The same fitted model answers other questions too.

  1. The effect for a type of profile. Reading the treatment line at other covariates gives the effect for profiles like those, for example kids profiles that watch one hour a day.
  2. How the effect varies. The slopes are the heterogeneity in the effect, for example how much smaller it is for kids profiles.
  3. Simpler designs. Each feature of our experiment can be switched off, and switching it off gives the textbook analysis of a simpler design:
    • No encouragement: when every prompted profile takes the treatment, , the first stage predicts perfectly, and the model is weighted least squares.
    • No clusters: when each account has one profile, the cluster robust standard errors are the heteroskedasticity robust standard errors.
    • No ramp: when the propensity is the same every day, the weights are a constant and cancel.
    • No ratio: when every row has , the ratio reduces to the LATE on .
    • No covariates: the model is a difference in means, or a Wald ratio with encouragement.

The switches touch different parts of the model, the first stage, the standard errors, the weights and the outcome columns, so they combine freely. A purely randomized AB test with one row per user and a mean metric is the model with every switch off; our experiment is the model with every switch on. The appendix proves each reduction, and Table 3 in Checking every design tests all 16 combinations against textbook code.

How the model is fit

In this section we describe how to train the model from scratch using first principles. It is possible to use off the shelf software like iv_robust from estimatr, but we write out all the steps and linear algebra here in order to be prepared for how to derive the compression formulas.

Centering the covariates

We center each covariate at a fixed reference point . Centering works like demeaning the columns, except that is a constant we choose before the experiment rather than the sample mean. Any choice gives the same fitted model; it only changes which point the coefficients and describe. We use a constant because the compressed version of the model, later in the post, is built in one pass over the data, before the sample mean is known. Here is 2 hours per day, 2 years of tenure, an adult profile and a tv. From here on, denotes the centered covariates, , so the reference point is . With an intercept in front, the profile rows of the prompted account from Table 1 become

Code 
x_cols <- c("x1", "x2", "kids", "mobile", "web")
x_ref <- c(x1 = 2, x2 = 2, kids = 0, mobile = 0, web = 0)

prepare <- function(profiles, ramp = TRUE) {
  e_hat <- profiles |>
    distinct(account, day, Z) |>
    group_by(day) |>
    summarise(e_hat = mean(Z))
  profiles |>
    left_join(e_hat, by = "day") |>
    mutate(w = if (ramp) if_else(Z == 1, 1 / e_hat, 1 / (1 - e_hat)) else 1,     # inverse propensity weight
           mobile = as.numeric(device == "mobile"), web = as.numeric(device == "web"),
           TN = T * N, TD = T * D)
}

centered <- function(df) {
  r <- cbind(1, sweep(as.matrix(df[x_cols]), 2, x_ref))
  colnames(r) <- c("1", paste0(x_cols, "_c"))
  r
}

df <- prepare(profiles)
example <- df |>
  filter(account == example_accounts[1])
centered(example)
     1       x1_c       x2_c kids_c mobile_c web_c
[1,] 1 -0.3299705 -0.4370072      0        0     1
[2,] 1  0.2090540 -0.3439723      1        1     0
[3,] 1 -1.2956183  0.3744773      0        1     0
[4,] 1 -1.5190796 -0.7822066      1        0     0
[5,] 1  3.6062466  1.4780119      1        0     0

The two stages as matrices

With centered covariates, the second stage is , with regressors and coefficients , where is the baseline line and is the treatment line. The first stage predicts the endogenous regressors and from the instruments ,

which stacks the first stage equations of the model, one for and one for each of the entries of . has one column of first stage coefficients per equation, the and the , and stacks the first stage errors. Stacking the rows gives the matrices and . Here are their rows for the prompted account. They differ only in their second half, where multiplies by the prompt and by the treatment received .

Code 
design <- function(df) {
  r <- centered(df)
  list(M_1 = cbind(r, `colnames<-`(df$Z * r, paste0("Z*", colnames(r)))),     # first stage: instruments
       M_2 = cbind(r, `colnames<-`(df$T * r, paste0("T*", colnames(r)))))     # second stage: regressors
}
round(design(example)$M_1, 2)
     1  x1_c  x2_c kids_c mobile_c web_c Z*1 Z*x1_c Z*x2_c Z*kids_c Z*mobile_c
[1,] 1 -0.33 -0.44      0        0     1   1  -0.33  -0.44        0          0
[2,] 1  0.21 -0.34      1        1     0   1   0.21  -0.34        1          1
[3,] 1 -1.30  0.37      0        1     0   1  -1.30   0.37        0          1
[4,] 1 -1.52 -0.78      1        0     0   1  -1.52  -0.78        1          0
[5,] 1  3.61  1.48      1        0     0   1   3.61   1.48        1          0
     Z*web_c
[1,]       1
[2,]       0
[3,]       0
[4,]       0
[5,]       0
Code 
round(design(example)$M_2, 2)
     1  x1_c  x2_c kids_c mobile_c web_c T*1 T*x1_c T*x2_c T*kids_c T*mobile_c
[1,] 1 -0.33 -0.44      0        0     1   1  -0.33  -0.44        0          0
[2,] 1  0.21 -0.34      1        1     0   0   0.00   0.00        0          0
[3,] 1 -1.30  0.37      0        1     0   0   0.00   0.00        0          0
[4,] 1 -1.52 -0.78      1        0     0   0   0.00   0.00        0          0
[5,] 1  3.61  1.48      1        0     0   0   0.00   0.00        0          0
     T*web_c
[1,]       1
[2,]       0
[3,]       0
[4,]       0
[5,]       0

With the weights in , two stage least squares replaces with its first stage prediction and regresses on it with weights . and have the same number of columns, one instrument for each regressor, so the estimate simplifies to

The matrix is the weighted cross product of the instruments with the regressors, and it plays the role that plays in least squares.

The residuals use the treatment actually received, . The cluster robust covariance of is the sandwich

The inner sum adds up the residuals of an account’s profiles, each multiplied by its instruments. Profiles are added within an account before the outer product is taken, so their correlation enters the covariance. That is what makes it robust to clustering.

The outcome can be a matrix with one column per metric. All columns share , and , so the coefficients form a matrix with rows and one column per metric. Stacking the inner sums of all the metrics into one vector per account gives the covariance between the coefficients of different metrics, which the ratio needs.

From coefficients to effects

Each effect is a function of . Reading a treatment line at is a dot product with the delta vector , which has zeros for the baseline line. Here is the compliers’ mean of the original covariates, so is that mean in centered units. Then for the column of that belongs to , and the LATE is . The variance of each effect follows from the delta method, with the gradient of the effect with respect to and the joint covariance of all the coefficients. We never pick coefficients by hand: we only write the effect as a function of .

fit_rows fits the model on the profile rows. The outcome matrix holds hours and the four columns for rebuffers per play.

Code 
y_cols <- c("y", "N", "D", "TN", "TD")
d <- length(x_cols) + 1                              # intercept and k covariates
o <- length(y_cols)                                  # number of outcome columns

fit_rows <- function(df) {
  m <- design(df); Y <- as.matrix(df[y_cols])
  M1_W_M2 <- crossprod(m$M_1 * df$w, m$M_2)                                   # M_1' W M_2
  B <- solve(M1_W_M2, crossprod(m$M_1 * df$w, Y))
  eps <- Y - m$M_2 %*% B                                                # second stage residuals
  inner <- do.call(cbind, map(seq_len(o), \(l) rowsum(m$M_1 * (df$w * eps[, l]), df$account)))   # one row per account
  M1_W_M2_inv <- kronecker(diag(o), solve(M1_W_M2))
  list(B = B, V = M1_W_M2_inv %*% crossprod(inner) %*% t(M1_W_M2_inv))
}

complier_mean <- function(df) {
  if (all(df$T == df$Z)) return(colSums(df$w * df[x_cols]) / sum(df$w))
  arm <- df |>
    group_by(Z) |>
    summarise(across(all_of(x_cols), \(v) sum(w * T * v) / sum(w)), T = sum(w * T) / sum(w))
  unlist(arm[arm$Z == 1, x_cols] - arm[arm$Z == 0, x_cols]) / (arm$T[arm$Z == 1] - arm$T[arm$Z == 0])
}

effects builds , writes each effect as a function of , and computes the gradient with complex step differentiation: adding an imaginary step to one coefficient and reading the imaginary part of the effect gives the derivative to machine precision, because nothing is subtracted.

Code 
gradient <- function(f, theta, kappa = 1e-20) {
  map_dbl(seq_along(theta), \(i) Im(f(theta + 1i * kappa * (seq_along(theta) == i))) / kappa)
}

effect_functions <- function(x_C, x_ref, cols) {
  delta <- c(rep(0, length(x_ref) + 1), 1, x_C - x_ref)               # reads a treatment line at x_C
  line <- \(B, col) sum(delta * B[, col])
  effect_list <- list(tau_LATE = \(B) line(B, "y"))
  if ("TN" %in% cols) effect_list$tau_R <- \(B) line(B, "TN") / line(B, "TD") - (line(B, "TN") - line(B, "N")) / (line(B, "TD") - line(B, "D"))
  effect_list
}

effects <- function(fit, x_C, x_ref) {
  effect_list <- effect_functions(x_C, x_ref, colnames(fit$B))
  theta <- as.vector(fit$B)
  map_dfr(names(effect_list), \(nm) {
    f <- \(th) effect_list[[nm]](matrix(th, nrow(fit$B), dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(fit$B))))
    grad <- gradient(f, theta)
    tibble(effect = nm, estimate = Re(f(theta)), se = sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% fit$V %*% grad)))
  })
}

fit <- fit_rows(df)
x_C <- complier_mean(df)
effects(fit, x_C, x_ref) |>
  mutate(truth = truth[effect])
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  effect   estimate      se   truth
  <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 tau_LATE   0.664  0.0572   0.613 
2 tau_R     -0.0255 0.00410 -0.0272

Both estimates are within 0.9 standard errors of the truth.

Checking every design

Table 3 checks the claim that the model covers every design. For each of the 16 combinations of the switches, with all covariates included, we simulate an experiment with those features and fit it twice: with fit_rows, and with the textbook model for that design from the estimatr package, either lm_robust or iv_robust, with or without weights and clusters. For a mean metric we use hours, and the textbook model reports the estimate and its standard error directly. For a ratio metric, estimatr fits one outcome at a time and does not report the covariance between outcomes, so we compare the estimates only. The appendix checks the ratio’s standard errors by simulation.

Code 
textbook <- function(df, x_C, clustered, encouraged, outcome, covs = x_cols) {
  df_c <- df |>
    mutate(across(all_of(covs), \(v) v - x_C[cur_column()]))     # coefficient on T is the line at x_C
  rhs <- paste0("(", paste(covs, collapse = " + "), ")")
  f <- as.formula(if (encouraged) paste(outcome, "~", rhs, "* T |", rhs, "* Z") else paste(outcome, "~", rhs, "* T"))
  estimator <- if (encouraged) iv_robust else lm_robust
  fit <- if (clustered) estimator(f, data = df_c, weights = w, clusters = account, se_type = "CR0")
         else estimator(f, data = df_c, weights = w, se_type = "HC0")
  c(estimate = fit$coefficients[["T"]], se = fit$std.error[["T"]])
}

check_design <- function(encouraged, clustered, ramp, metric) {
  set.seed(7)
  df <- simulate_accounts(propensity = if (ramp) propensity else rep(0.3, 4), full_compliance = !encouraged,
                          one_profile = !clustered) |>
    prepare(ramp = ramp)
  x_C <- complier_mean(df)
  fit_u <- effects(fit_rows(df), x_C, x_ref)
  if (metric == "mean") {
    tb <- textbook(df, x_C, clustered, encouraged, "y")
    tibble(universal = fit_u$estimate[1], textbook = tb[["estimate"]], universal_se = fit_u$se[1], textbook_se = tb[["se"]])
  } else {
    l <- map(set_names(c("N", "D", "TN", "TD")), \(col) textbook(df, x_C, clustered, encouraged, col)[["estimate"]])
    tibble(universal = fit_u$estimate[2], textbook = l$TN / l$TD - (l$TN - l$N) / (l$TD - l$D),
           universal_se = fit_u$se[2], textbook_se = NA_real_)
  }
}

designs <- expand_grid(encouraged = c(FALSE, TRUE), clustered = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                       ramp = c(FALSE, TRUE), metric = c("mean", "ratio"))
design_tab <- designs |>
  mutate(res = pmap(designs, check_design)) |>
  unnest(res)
Code 
design_tab |>
  mutate(across(c(encouraged, clustered, ramp), \(v) if_else(v, "yes", "no"))) |>
  kable(digits = 6, col.names = c("Encouragement", "Clusters", "Ramp", "Metric", "Estimate (universal)",
