                                  "Estimate (textbook)", "SE (universal)", "SE (textbook)"))

Every estimate agrees, and so does every standard error that the textbook model reports. The first row is a purely randomized AB test with one row per user and a mean metric, analyzed with Lin’s regression and heteroskedasticity robust errors. The last row is our experiment.

Compressing the Universal Model

The model is universal, but fitting it on the profile rows is expensive when there are hundreds of millions of them and dozens of metrics. We now derive, from first principles, a compressed dataset that still gives the exact estimate and the exact covariance. We start with the math, then build the compressed dataset by hand for two simple cases, and then for the full model.

What the model needs

The estimate needs and , which are sums over profile rows. Within an account, the instruments are , and and are the same for every profile, so these sums only need three blocks per account:

holds the account’s number of profiles, the sums of its covariates, and the sums of the products of every pair of covariates. holds the same sums over the profiles that took the treatment. holds the sums of the outcomes, and of the outcomes times each covariate; here is the row of , all outcome columns of the profile. Because and are constant within an account, each block of is a weighted sum of these blocks over accounts. For example, the block that pairs the instruments with the regressors is .

To see what these blocks hold, take the two accounts of Table 1, with one covariate, the pre-period hours , and the outcome hours . Account 15 was prompted, and only its first profile turned the setting on. Account 1 was not prompted.

Accounts with the same assignment and cohort share and , so the whole model needs only three sums per stratum :

  1. The number of accounts in stratum , .
  2. The first moments , which give the estimate.
  3. The second moments , which give the covariance.

These are conditionally sufficient statistics: given the stratum, they carry everything the model can learn from the data.

From here on we use three names for the data at each step.

  1. A profile row is a row of the original, uncompressed data: one profile of one account, with its day, prompt, treatment, covariates and outcomes, as in Table 1. Our experiment has 43,989 profile rows.
  2. An account summary is the vector of sums over the profile rows of one account. It is an intermediate: we build one per account in a single pass over the profile rows, add it into its stratum’s sums, and discard it.
  3. A compressed row holds the sums of one stratum. It has three fields: the count , the first moments , which is a vector, and the second moments , which is a matrix. The compressed dataset has one compressed row per stratum, 8 in our experiment, whatever the number of profile rows.

The functions below turn account summaries into the compressed dataset, and the compressed dataset into the fit. They work for any number of covariates , with for the intercept and the covariates, and any number of outcome columns .

Code 
compress_summaries <- function(accounts, u) {          # accounts: one row per account with Z, day, w; u: one row of u_a per account
  strata <- group_by(accounts, Z, day, w)
  h <- group_indices(strata)
  group_keys(strata) |>
    mutate(G = tabulate(h),
           first_moments = map(seq_len(n()), \(k) colSums(u[h == k, , drop = FALSE])),       # sum of u_a
           second_moments = map(seq_len(n()), \(k) crossprod(u[h == k, , drop = FALSE])))    # sum of u_a u_a^T
}

blocks <- function(s, d, o) {                        # split u (or a sum of u) into S^Y, S and S^T
  list(S_Y = matrix(s[1:(d * o)], d), S = matrix(s[d * o + 1:(d * d)], d), S_T = matrix(s[d * o + d * d + 1:(d * d)], d))
}

fit_first_moments <- function(compressed, d, outcomes) {            # the estimate needs only sum u_a
  o <- length(outcomes)
  b <- map(compressed$first_moments, blocks, d = d, o = o)
  M1_W_M2 <- reduce(map(seq_along(b), \(k) compressed$w[k] * rbind(cbind(b[[k]]$S, b[[k]]$S_T), compressed$Z[k] * cbind(b[[k]]$S, b[[k]]$S_T))), `+`)
  M1_W_Y <- reduce(map(seq_along(b), \(k) compressed$w[k] * rbind(b[[k]]$S_Y, compressed$Z[k] * b[[k]]$S_Y)), `+`)
  B <- solve(M1_W_M2, M1_W_Y); colnames(B) <- outcomes
  list(M1_W_M2 = M1_W_M2, B = B)
}

L_matrix <- function(B, d) {                         # vec(E_a) = L u_a
  o <- ncol(B)
  cbind(diag(d * o), -kronecker(t(B[1:d, , drop = FALSE]), diag(d)), -kronecker(t(B[d + 1:d, , drop = FALSE]), diag(d)))
}
stack_instruments <- function(Z, d, o) kronecker(diag(o), rbind(diag(d), Z * diag(d)))   # vec(E_a) -> vec(inner sum) / w_a

fit_compressed <- function(compressed, d, outcomes) {                   # the covariance also needs sum u_a u_a^T
  o <- length(outcomes)
  fit <- fit_first_moments(compressed, d, outcomes)
  L <- L_matrix(fit$B, d)
  meat <- reduce(map(seq_len(nrow(compressed)), \(k) {
    P <- stack_instruments(compressed$Z[k], d, o)
    compressed$w[k]^2 * P %*% L %*% compressed$second_moments[[k]] %*% t(L) %*% t(P)
  }), `+`)
  M1_W_M2_inv <- kronecker(diag(o), solve(fit$M1_W_M2))
  c(fit, list(V = M1_W_M2_inv %*% meat %*% t(M1_W_M2_inv)))
}

complier_mean_compressed <- function(compressed, d, o, x_ref) {        # Wald ratio of T (x - x_ref) over T, from sum u_a
  arm <- \(z_value) reduce(map(which(compressed$Z == z_value), \(k) {
    b <- blocks(compressed$first_moments[[k]], d, o)
    compressed$w[k] * c(b$S_T[, 1], b$S[1, 1])            # weighted sums of T, T (x - x_ref), and of 1
  }), `+`)
  share <- \(v) v[1:d] / v[d + 1]
  diff <- share(arm(1)) - share(arm(0))
  set_names(diff[-1] / diff[1] + x_ref, names(x_ref))
}

All covariates

The full model has five covariates and five outcome columns, so has 102 entries. Writing one dplyr column per entry would work, but it is tedious, so we write the loop in C++ using Rcpp. compress_profiles visits the profile rows once, in account order. It adds each row’s products into a buffer that holds its account’s summary . When the account’s rows end, it adds into its stratum’s first moments and into its stratum’s second moments, and clears the buffer, so the account summaries are never stored. The buffer keeps each distinct entry of once, since and are symmetric, and the outer product skips the entries of that are zero, such as all of for an account that was not prompted, or the indicators of devices the account does not use. This is the only step that visits every row. account_summaries builds the same but returns them, one row per account; delta vectors early need them for their second pass.

Code 
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include <vector>
using namespace Rcpp;

// Profile rows to account summaries u_a = (vec S^Y, vec S, vec S^T) in one pass, with R = (1, x) and Y the outcome columns.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericMatrix account_summaries(IntegerVector account, NumericMatrix R, NumericVector T, NumericMatrix Y, int n_accounts) {
  int n = R.nrow(), d = R.ncol(), o = Y.ncol();
  NumericMatrix u(n_accounts, d * o + 2 * d * d);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int a = account[i] - 1;
    for (int l = 0; l < o; l++) for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) u(a, l * d + j) += R(i, j) * Y(i, l);     // S^Y
    for (int m = 0; m < d; m++) for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) {
      double rr = R(i, j) * R(i, m);
      u(a, d * o + m * d + j) += rr;                                                                // S
      u(a, d * o + d * d + m * d + j) += T[i] * rr;                                                 // S^T
    }
  }
  return u;
}

// Profile rows to the compressed dataset in one pass; the rows of each account must be together.
// The buffer holds the distinct entries of u_a: S^Y, then the upper triangles of S and S^T.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
List compress_profiles(IntegerVector account, IntegerVector stratum, NumericMatrix R, NumericVector T,
                       NumericMatrix Y, int n_strata) {
  int n = R.nrow(), d = R.ncol(), o = Y.ncol();
  int nt = d * (d + 1) / 2, q = d * o + 2 * nt;
  std::vector<double> u(q, 0.0);
  std::vector<int> nz;
  IntegerVector G(n_strata);
  NumericMatrix first(n_strata, q);
  std::vector<NumericMatrix> second;
  for (int h = 0; h < n_strata; h++) second.push_back(NumericMatrix(q, q));
  auto add_account = [&](int h) {                                         // add u_a and u_a u_a^T into stratum h
    nz.clear();
    for (int k = 0; k < q; k++) if (u[k] != 0) nz.push_back(k);
    G[h] += 1;
    NumericMatrix& M = second[h];
    for (size_t a = 0; a < nz.size(); a++) {
      first(h, nz[a]) += u[nz[a]];
      for (size_t b = a; b < nz.size(); b++) M(nz[b], nz[a]) += u[nz[a]] * u[nz[b]];   // lower triangle
    }
    for (int k : nz) u[k] = 0;
  };
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i > 0 && account[i] != account[i - 1]) add_account(stratum[i - 1] - 1);
    for (int l = 0; l < o; l++) for (int j = 0; j < d; j++) u[l * d + j] += R(i, j) * Y(i, l);   // S^Y
    for (int m = 0; m < d; m++) for (int j = 0; j <= m; j++) {
      double rr = R(i, j) * R(i, m);
      int t = m * (m + 1) / 2 + j;
      u[d * o + t] += rr;                                                                  // S
      u[d * o + nt + t] += T[i] * rr;                                                      // S^T
    }
  }
  add_account(stratum[n - 1] - 1);
  List second_moments(n_strata);
  for (int h = 0; h < n_strata; h++) {
    NumericMatrix& M = second[h];
    for (int a = 0; a < q; a++) for (int b = a + 1; b < q; b++) M(a, b) = M(b, a);         // fill the upper triangle
    second_moments[h] = M;
  }
  return List::create(_["G"] = G, _["first"] = first, _["second"] = second_moments);
}

distinct_index <- function(d, o) {                     # where each entry of u_a sits among its distinct entries
  tri <- outer(0:(d - 1), 0:(d - 1), \(j, m) pmax(j, m) * (pmax(j, m) + 1) / 2 + pmin(j, m))
  nt <- d * (d + 1) / 2
  c(seq_len(d * o), d * o + 1 + as.vector(tri), d * o + nt + 1 + as.vector(tri))
}

compress_rows <- function(df, R, Y = as.matrix(df[y_cols])) {        # profile rows to the compressed dataset
  stopifnot(!is.unsorted(df$account))                                 # each account's rows are together
  accounts <- df |>
    distinct(account, Z, day, w) |>
    arrange(account)
  strata <- group_by(accounts, Z, day, w)
  h <- group_indices(strata)
  k <- compress_profiles(df$account, h[match(df$account, accounts$account)], R, df$T, Y, max(h))
  i <- distinct_index(ncol(R), ncol(Y))
  group_keys(strata) |>
    mutate(G = k$G, first_moments = map(seq_len(n()), \(s) k$first[s, i]), second_moments = map(k$second, \(m) m[i, i]))
}

Delta Vectors Optimization

Delta vectors are a convenient construct that compute treatment effects by combining the right coefficients and covariances for you. This works for an average effect, as well as conditional average effects. We saw its flexibility in the earlier section Section 2.4.3. Earlier, we used it after estimating the coefficients and their covariances.

Compression changes our way of thinking. We need to be conscious of data storage. We can compress the data to estimate coefficients and covariances, then combine those outputs with delta vectors to get effects. A step stands out though. To compute the covariances from compressed data, the compressed rows had to hold the second moments . These can be expensive. If we know in advance which effects we want, say the LATE, we can use the delta vectors earlier and never build , with exactly the same standard errors. The price is flexibility and a second pass over the data. We describe the two strategies, one using it flexibly after getting and covariances, and one earlier, and compare their costs in Benchmark.

Delta vectors at the end (most flexible)

The coefficient matrix has $2d = $ 12 rows and $o = $ 5 columns, so the covariance of its 60 entries is a 60 by 60 matrix. To get it, the compressed rows must hold , which has 10,404 entries per stratum. An effect only needs one number from it. For the LATE, the gradient with respect to is the delta vector in the block of the hours column and zeros elsewhere:

Delta vectors earlier (most efficient)

The variance of an effect with gradient is . Writing out the sandwich, it is a sum of squares over accounts,

where is the influence of account on the effect. The inner sums are , where the matrix maps to the stacked inner sums of and . Everything in front of is the same for all accounts in a stratum, so

This changes the order of the work. We fit from the first moments alone. Once and the effects we want are known, we compute for each stratum, and a second pass over the account summaries gives each account’s influence with one dot product. We never form .

Code 
compressed_first <- compressed |>
  select(Z, day, w, first_moments)                     # pass 1 only keeps sum u_a
fit_1 <- fit_first_moments(compressed_first, d, y_cols)
x_C_1 <- complier_mean_compressed(compressed_first, d, o, x_ref)
effect_list_1 <- effect_functions(x_C_1, x_ref, y_cols)
grads <- map(effect_list_1, \(effect) gradient(\(th) effect(matrix(th, nrow(fit_1$B), dimnames = list(NULL, y_cols))), as.vector(fit_1$B)))

projection <- function(fit, compressed_first, grad, d, o) {               # c_h for every stratum, one row each
  L <- L_matrix(fit$B, d)
  v <- kronecker(diag(o), t(solve(fit$M1_W_M2))) %*% grad
  do.call(rbind, map(seq_len(nrow(compressed_first)), \(k)
    as.vector(compressed_first$w[k] * t(L) %*% t(stack_instruments(compressed_first$Z[k], d, o)) %*% v)))
}
C_late <- projection(fit_1, compressed_first, grads$tau_LATE, d, o)
dim(C_late)
[1]   8 102

h <- group_indices(group_by(accounts, Z, day, w))
psi_late <- rowSums(u * C_late[h, ])                                 # pass 2: one dot product per account

Each method has its place. Delta vectors at the end need the second moments, but once we have them, we can ask for any effect later: a new segment, a new point on the treatment line, a slope. Delta vectors early must know the effects before the second pass, but they are cheaper. Forming costs operations per account, while the projections cost per account and effect.

Benchmark

We now have three ways from the profile rows to the effects: the textbook fit on the profile rows, and the compressed dataset with delta vectors at the end or early. This section compares how long each takes and how many numbers each keeps.

Compute

To see what each method costs, we run the simulation of the running example with a million accounts instead of 20,000, and time the textbook fit, one iv_robust per outcome column, against the two compressed methods. Delta vectors at the end compress the profile rows in one pass. Delta vectors early build the account summaries, add them into first moments, and take the second pass over them.

Code 
set.seed(1)
big <- simulate_accounts(1e6) |>
  prepare()
big_c <- big |>
  mutate(across(all_of(x_cols), \(v) v - x_ref[cur_column()]))
t_textbook <- system.time(walk(y_cols, \(col) iv_robust(
  as.formula(paste(col, "~ (x1 + x2 + kids + mobile + web) * T | (x1 + x2 + kids + mobile + web) * Z")),
  data = big_c, weights = w, clusters = account, se_type = "CR0")))[["elapsed"]]
t_end <- system.time({
  big_compressed <- compress_rows(big, centered(big))
  big_fit <- fit_compressed(big_compressed, d, y_cols)
  se_end_big <- effects(big_fit, complier_mean_compressed(big_compressed, d, o, x_ref), x_ref)$se
})[["elapsed"]]
t_early <- system.time({
  big_accounts <- big |>
    distinct(account, Z, day, w) |>
    arrange(account)
  big_u <- account_summaries(big$account, centered(big), big$T, as.matrix(big[y_cols]), nrow(big_accounts))
  h_big <- group_indices(group_by(big_accounts, Z, day, w))
  big_first <- group_keys(group_by(big_accounts, Z, day, w)) |>
    mutate(first_moments = map(seq_len(n()), \(k) colSums(big_u[h_big == k, , drop = FALSE])))
  big_fit_1 <- fit_first_moments(big_first, d, y_cols)
  effect_list_big <- effect_functions(complier_mean_compressed(big_first, d, o, x_ref), x_ref, y_cols)
  se_early_big <- map_dbl(effect_list_big, \(effect) {
    grad <- gradient(\(th) effect(matrix(th, nrow(big_fit_1$B), dimnames = list(NULL, y_cols))), as.vector(big_fit_1$B))
    sqrt(sum(rowSums(big_u * projection(big_fit_1, big_first, grad, d, o)[h_big, ])^2))
  })
})[["elapsed"]]
n_big <- nrow(big)
n_big_accounts <- nrow(big_accounts)
rm(big, big_c, big_u, big_accounts, big_first, h_big)
invisible(gc())
Code 
tibble(step = c("textbook: iv_robust on profile rows, once per outcome column",
                "delta vectors at the end: one pass to the compressed dataset, covariance, effects",
                "delta vectors early: account summaries, first moments, projections"),
       seconds = c(t_textbook, t_end, t_early)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Step", "Seconds"))

Table 5 shows the times on the machine that rendered this post. The 2,189,477 profile rows reduce to 1,000,000 account summaries in one pass over the profile rows, and to 8 compressed rows. The two compressed methods agree on the standard errors to within 6e-16.

Storage

The two compressed methods also keep different numbers. Delta vectors at the end keep, for every stratum, the count of accounts, the first moments and the second moments , and any effect can be computed from them later. Delta vectors early keep only the first moments after the first pass. The second pass visits the accounts again, one at a time: it rebuilds , takes its dot product with , and adds to a running total, one total per effect. Nothing is kept per account, so after the second pass the stored numbers are the first moments and one sum of squares per effect. Our code for delta vectors early keeps the account summaries in memory for convenience; at scale, the second pass reads the profile rows again instead.

Both methods grow with the number of covariates. has distinct entries, with , because and hold the product of every pair of covariates. That is quadratic in , and so are the first moments that delta vectors early keep. The second moments keep the products of every pair of entries of , so delta vectors at the end grow like .

Table 6 compares the numbers in the profile rows of our experiment with the numbers each method keeps, for the three models of the running example, and for the full model with more continuous covariates on the same 43,989 profile rows. A profile row holds the account, , the day, , the covariates and the raw outcomes; the columns and are computed from them. The methods’ counts take each distinct number once: a symmetric matrix by its upper triangle, and the repeated or always zero entries of once or not at all. The two models with one covariate estimate one effect, the LATE on hours, and the others estimate two, the LATE and the ratio. The reduction is the number of numbers in the profile rows divided by the number the method keeps.

Code 
n_strata <- nrow(compressed)
storage <- function(case, k, raw_outcomes, distinct_u, n_effects) {
  tibble(case = case, k = k,
         rows = nrow(df) * (4 + k + raw_outcomes),                                        # account, Z, day, T, covariates, raw outcomes
         end = n_strata * (1 + distinct_u + distinct_u * (distinct_u + 1) / 2),           # count, first and second moments
         early = n_strata * distinct_u + n_effects,                                       # first moments, one sum of squares per effect
         distinct_u = distinct_u)
}
full_u <- \(k) (k + 1) * o + (k + 1) * (k + 2)
storage_tab <- bind_rows(
  storage("one continuous covariate, hours", 1, 1, ncol(cuped_summaries) - 4, 1),
  storage("one categorical covariate, hours", 2, 1, ncol(device_summaries) - 4, 1),
  storage("all covariates, hours and rebuffers per play", length(x_cols), 3, full_u(length(x_cols)), length(grads)),
  map_dfr(c(10, 20, 50), \(k) storage(paste(k, "continuous covariates, hours and rebuffers per play"), k, 3, full_u(k), 2))) |>
  mutate(reduction_end = rows / end, reduction_early = rows / early)
rows_big <- n_big * (4 + length(x_cols) + 3)                                  # the full model's profile rows in the compute benchmark
Code 
times <- \(v) paste0(ifelse(v >= 10, format(round(v), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), formatC(signif(v, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2)), "x")
storage_tab |>
  transmute(case, k, rows = format(rows, big.mark = ","),
            end = format(end, big.mark = ","), reduction_end = times(reduction_end),
            early = format(early, big.mark = ","), reduction_early = times(reduction_early)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Case", "Covariates $k$", "Numbers in the profile rows", "Kept, delta vectors at the end", "Reduction",
                      "Kept, delta vectors early", "Reduction"))

For the full model, the 43,989 profile rows hold 527,868 numbers. Delta vectors at the end keep 21,608, 24 times fewer, and delta vectors early keep 578, 913 times fewer. The account summaries, 72 numbers for each of the 20,000 accounts, would hold more numbers than the profile rows; this is why neither method stores them, and each one is added into its compressed row, or into its running totals, as soon as it is built.

The methods keep the same numbers however many profile rows there are, so the reduction grows in proportion to the size of the experiment. The 2,189,477 profile rows of the compute benchmark hold 26,273,724 numbers for the full model, a reduction of 1,216 times at the end and 45,456 times early. More covariates shrink the reduction. With 20 covariates, delta vectors at the end already keep more numbers than the profile rows of our experiment, and with 50 they keep 33,837,488, while delta vectors early keep 23,258. The price of the smaller storage is flexibility and a second read: the effects must be chosen before the second pass, and a new effect, such as a new segment or a slope, needs another pass over the profile rows. A categorical covariate with levels counts as indicators here, which overstates its size: products of indicators of the same covariate are zero or repeated, as the device case showed.

When There Are Many Covariates

Table 6 showed that delta vectors early keep storage quadratic in , but they fix the effects in advance. Delta vectors at the end can answer any effect later, but their storage grows like , and experimentation platforms often adjust for dozens of pre-experiment signals. To keep the flexibility of delta vectors at the end, we reduce the covariates. In this section we add covariates to the running example and summarize them with prognostic scores.

More covariates for the running example

We add covariates to every profile row. Each is a noisy measurement of the profile’s engagement, and half of them also carry the account’s network quality, like the activity signals a service records before an experiment. Each signal on its own is weak, but together they predict hours well. The signals are drawn after everything else in the simulation, so the earlier profile rows, and the true effects, do not change.

Code 
add_signals <- function(profiles, m = 20) {
  signals <- map(seq_len(m), \(j) 0.4 * profiles$engagement_p + 0.2 * profiles$quality * (j %% 2) + rnorm(nrow(profiles)))
  bind_cols(profiles, as_tibble(set_names(signals, paste0("g", seq_len(m)))))
}
set.seed(31)
df_many <- profiles |>
  add_signals() |>
  prepare()
signal_cols <- paste0("g", 1:20)
sizes <- function(k, categorical = FALSE) {
  first <- if (categorical) (k + 1) * o + 2 * (k + 1) else full_u(k)
  totals <- o + 2 * (k + 1)
  c(exact = n_strata * (1 + first + first * (first + 1) / 2), second_order = n_strata * (1 + first + totals * (totals + 1) / 2))
}
X_many <- cbind(centered(df_many)[, -1], as.matrix(df_many[signal_cols]))    # 5 base covariates and 20 signals, centered
dim(X_many)
[1] 43989    25

With covariates, the compressed dataset for delta vectors at the end would hold 2,778,888 numbers, counting each distinct number once, against 1,407,648 in the profile rows: the account, , the day, , 25 covariates and 3 raw outcomes per row. The compressed dataset would be larger than the data.

Summarizing the covariates with prognostic scores

A covariate only reduces variance through what it predicts about the outcome, so we can replace the 25 covariates with a prediction of each outcome, a prognostic score, from a model trained on data from before the experiment. A fixed function of pre-experiment covariates is itself a pre-experiment covariate, so the scores are as valid as any other covariate, and a better model only makes them more precise. DoorDash calls this CUPAC, control using predictions as covariates.

We simulate a pre-experiment sample of the same population with nobody prompted, and fit one linear model per raw outcome, hours, rebuffers and plays. Any model would do, including a gradient boosted tree.

Code 
set.seed(99)
history <- simulate_accounts(50000, force_Z = 0) |>
  add_signals() |>
  prepare()
X_history <- cbind(centered(history)[, -1], as.matrix(history[signal_cols]))
score_models <- lm(as.matrix(history[c("y", "N", "D")]) ~ X_history) |>    # one fit for the three outcomes
  coef() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as.list()
score <- function(X) {
  map_dfc(score_models, \(b) drop(cbind(1, X) %*% b) - mean(drop(cbind(1, X_history) %*% b))) |>
    as.matrix()
}

fit_exact <- function(df, X) {
  compressed <- compress_rows(df, cbind(1, X))

                     numbers = c(sizes(25)[["exact"]], sizes(3)[["exact"]]),

The scores are as precise as all 25 covariates, with a standard error of 0.0528 against 0.0526, and their compressed dataset holds 6,888 numbers instead of 2,778,888. Its size does not depend on the number of covariates the scores summarize, only on the number of outcomes. Two practical notes:

  1. The scores are predictions, but they do not add a term to the standard error. Once trained on data from before the experiment, the score is a fixed function of observed covariates, and the effect is consistent whatever that function is. The appendix explains why and checks it by retraining the scores in every simulated experiment.
  2. Effects along the scores are hard to interpret. When we want the effect along a particular covariate, such as the effect for kids profiles, we keep that covariate in the model next to the scores.

The appendix compares the scores with three other strategies, a second order approximation of the compressed dataset, binning and clustering, and confirms over 400 simulated experiments that the scores are as precise as all 25 covariates.

End to End

Here is the whole analysis of our experiment in a few lines, starting from the profile rows. Both versions use the same weights and clusters.

With estimatr, we center the covariates at the compliers’ means, so that the coefficient on is the effect, and fit one two stage least squares model per outcome column. The ratio’s estimate combines four fits, but estimatr cannot give its standard error.

Code

df_c <- df |>
  mutate(across(all_of(x_cols), \(v) v - x_C_rows[cur_column()]))

  as.formula(paste(col, "~ (x1 + x2 + kids + mobile + web) * T | (x1 + x2 + kids + mobile + web) * Z")),
  data = df_c, weights = w, clusters = account, se_type = "CR0"))

tibble(effect = c("tau_LATE", "tau_R"),
       estimate = c(l$y, l$TN / l$TD - (l$TN - l$N) / (l$TD - l$D)),
       se = c(fits$y$std.error[["T"]], NA))

Summary

One model covers every design in this post: weighted two stage least squares, with the treatment interacted with each covariate, cluster robust standard errors, and one outcome column per metric, plus the columns and for a ratio metric. Turning off the encouragement, the clusters, the ramp or the ratio gives back the textbook analysis of each simpler design, from Lin’s regression to the Wald estimator. Two details matter for getting the right effect: the delta vector reads the treatment line at the compliers’ covariates, and a ratio metric needs the compliers’ own levels.

The model needs only one compressed row per assignment and cohort: the count of accounts, the sum of the account summaries , and the sum of their outer products. With one continuous covariate the compressed rows hold the CUPED aggregates and their products, and with categorical covariates they hold counts and sums by cell. When we know the effects we want, we can skip the outer products: the first moments give the fit, and one dot product per account gives each effect’s exact standard error.

The two ways to get standard errors trade storage for flexibility. Delta vectors at the end keep the outer products and can answer any effect later, but their storage grows like with the number of covariates; delta vectors early grow like , but fix the effects in advance. With many covariates, prognostic scores trained before the experiment keep the compressed dataset independent of , and are as precise as the covariates they summarize.

These are the normal equations of a weighted least squares fit of the treatment line to the complier effects , with weight , where is the probability density of . The first entry of is 1, so the first equation says that the weighted average of the line equals the weighted average of . Dividing the weight by its total, the overall share of compliers , gives the probability density of among compliers, , which turns the weighted average of into the LATE and the weighted average of the line into its value at the compliers’ mean, in centered units.

For the outcome , the same steps apply with , because the prompt changes only for compliers, from 0 to their rebuffers with the setting on. So the treatment line of is fit to , and at it equals .

Proofs of the reductions

Write , and write for the inner sums of account , so that .

No encouragement. If , then , so and , which is weighted least squares. The sandwich becomes with , the robust covariance of weighted least squares. Every profile is a complier, so is the mean of , and is the difference between the two arms’ lines at the mean, which is the coefficient on in Lin’s regression with covariates centered at their mean.

No clusters. If each account has one profile, then and , the meat of the heteroskedasticity robust covariance (HC0). The usual small sample corrections also agree: with clusters, rows and coefficients, the cluster correction equals the HC1 correction when .

No ramp. If every weight equals a constant , then . The inner sums are times their unweighted versions , so the covariance is , and the cancels.

No ratio. If for every row, the outcome is fit exactly by the intercept: has a 1 in the intercept and zeros elsewhere, and its residuals are zero. The outcome is fit exactly by the column, so has a 1 there and zeros elsewhere. Then and , so

the LATE on the metric . The columns and have zero residuals, so they add nothing to the covariance.

No covariates. With no covariates, is just , so and , and is the weighted Wald ratio , or the difference in means when .

Each reduction changes a different part of the model: the instruments, the grouping of the inner sums, the weights, or the outcome columns. So any combination of them is also a special case.

Monte Carlo

We repeat the experiment 500 times and compute both effects from the compressed dataset, with delta vectors at the end, each time. We also compute the ratio with the baseline line, read at , in place of the compliers’ levels, to show why the columns and are needed, and the kids slope, the coefficient on times the kids indicator, whose true value is .

Code 
analyze <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  df <- simulate_accounts() |>
    prepare()
  comp <- compress_rows(df, centered(df))
  fit <- fit_compressed(comp, d, y_cols)
  x_C <- complier_mean_compressed(comp, d, o, x_ref)
  base <- c(1, x_C - x_ref, rep(0, d)); delta <- c(rep(0, d), 1, x_C - x_ref)
  baseline_ratio <- \(B) { m0N <- sum(base * B[, "N"]); m0D <- sum(base * B[, "D"])
                           (m0N + sum(delta * B[, "N"])) / (m0D + sum(delta * B[, "D"])) - m0N / m0D }
  f <- \(th) baseline_ratio(matrix(th, nrow(fit$B), dimnames = list(NULL, y_cols)))
  theta <- as.vector(fit$B); grad <- gradient(f, theta)
  kids <- c(rep(0, d), 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0); i <- (match("y", y_cols) - 1) * 2 * d + seq_len(2 * d)
  bind_rows(effects(fit, x_C, x_ref),
            tibble(effect = "tau_R with the baseline line", estimate = Re(f(theta)),
                   se = sqrt(drop(t(grad) %*% fit$V %*% grad))),
            tibble(effect = "kids slope", estimate = sum(kids * fit$B[, "y"]),
                   se = sqrt(drop(t(kids) %*% fit$V[i, i] %*% kids)))) |>
    mutate(rep = seed)
}
invisible(gc())
mc <- mclapply(1:500, analyze, mc.cores = cores) |>
  bind_rows()
targets <- c(tau_LATE = truth[["tau_LATE"]], tau_R = truth[["tau_R"]],
             "tau_R with the baseline line" = truth[["tau_R"]], "kids slope" = -0.2)
mc_tab <- mc |>
  mutate(target = targets[effect]) |>
  group_by(effect) |>
  summarise(bias = mean(estimate - target), mc_se = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n()), sd = sd(estimate),
            se_over_sd = mean(se) / sd(estimate), coverage = mean(abs(estimate - target) <= qnorm(0.975) * se))
Code 
mc_tab |>
  kable(digits = 4, col.names = c("Quantity", "Bias", "MC SE of bias", "SD", "SE/SD", "Coverage"))

Reading Table 8:

  1. Both effects are unbiased, up to the Monte Carlo error of the bias, and their standard errors match the spread of the estimates, with coverage of 95.0% for the LATE and 93.4% for the ratio.
  2. Using the baseline line instead of the compliers’ levels biases the ratio by -0.0019, about 11 Monte Carlo standard errors and 47% of a standard deviation. It estimates a different quantity, the ratio with the baseline of all profiles, so its bias does not shrink as the experiment grows while its standard error does, and its coverage falls toward zero in larger experiments.
  3. The kids slope is also unbiased, so the same compressed dataset serves questions about heterogeneity as well as average effects. Its coverage, 92.0%, is a little below 95%, and its standard errors are 9% smaller than the spread of its estimates.

Other strategies for many covariates

The main text summarized 25 covariates with 3 prognostic scores. Here we compare that with three other ways to keep the compressed dataset small: approximating its second moments, binning the covariates, and clustering them.

A second order approximation: keep only the residual totals

The covariance needs, for every account, the sums of its residuals multiplied by its intercept and covariates. The second moments of the account summaries are what make computable for any coefficients, and they are the part that grows like . For the effects we care about, most of barely matters.

An effect reads the treatment line at some covariates . The first section of this appendix showed that the treatment line is a fit to the compliers, so in large samples its coefficients are driven by the moments of among compliers. For a line fit with an intercept, the influence of a data point with covariates on the line’s value at is proportional to

where and are the mean and covariance of the covariates among compliers. This is the same leverage that appears in any regression with an intercept. The LATE and the ratio read the line at , where the second term vanishes and every profile’s residual gets the same weight. So for these effects, an account’s influence depends approximately only on its residuals added up, , which is the first row of . Its second moments only need the account totals of , of and of : numbers per account instead of .

The estimate still needs the first moments, but those never needed the account summaries: they are sums over the profile rows of each stratum, so a crossprod per stratum computes them. The second moments only need each account’s totals, which rowsum computes in one pass. The full account summaries are never built.

Code 
compress_second_order <- function(df, X) {
  R <- cbind(1, X)
  Y <- as.matrix(df[y_cols])
  accounts <- df |>
    distinct(account, Z, day, w) |>
    arrange(account)
  strata <- group_by(accounts, Z, day, w)
  h_account <- group_indices(strata)
  h_row <- h_account[df$account]
  totals <- rowsum(cbind(Y, R, df$T * R), df$account)                       # account totals of y, (1, x), T (1, x)
  rows <- split(seq_len(nrow(df)), factor(h_row, seq_len(max(h_account))))
  group_keys(strata) |>
    mutate(G = tabulate(h_account),
           S = map(rows, \(i) crossprod(R[i, , drop = FALSE])),
           S_T = map(rows, \(i) crossprod(R[i, , drop = FALSE] * df$T[i], R[i, , drop = FALSE])),
           S_Y = map(rows, \(i) crossprod(R[i, , drop = FALSE], Y[i, , drop = FALSE])),
           second_moments = map(seq_len(n()), \(k) crossprod(totals[h_account == k, , drop = FALSE])))
}

fit_second_order <- function(compressed) {
  d <- nrow(compressed$S[[1]])
  o <- ncol(compressed$S_Y[[1]])
  M1_W_M2 <- reduce(map(seq_len(nrow(compressed)), \(k) with(compressed[k, ],
    w * rbind(cbind(S[[1]], S_T[[1]]), Z * cbind(S[[1]], S_T[[1]])))), `+`)
  M1_W_Y <- reduce(map(seq_len(nrow(compressed)), \(k) with(compressed[k, ], w * rbind(S_Y[[1]], Z * S_Y[[1]]))), `+`)
  B <- solve(M1_W_M2, M1_W_Y)
  colnames(B) <- y_cols
  L_totals <- cbind(diag(o), -t(B[1:d, , drop = FALSE]), -t(B[d + 1:d, , drop = FALSE]))   # residual totals from account totals
  first_row <- (0:(o - 1)) * d + 1
  meat <- reduce(map(seq_len(nrow(compressed)), \(k) {
    cov_E <- matrix(0, d * o, d * o)
    cov_E[first_row, first_row] <- L_totals %*% compressed$second_moments[[k]] %*% t(L_totals)
    compressed$w[k]^2 * stack_instruments(compressed$Z[k], d, o) %*% cov_E %*% t(stack_instruments(compressed$Z[k], d, o))
  }), `+`)
  M1_W_M2_inv <- kronecker(diag(o), solve(M1_W_M2))
  arm <- \(z_value) reduce(map(which(compressed$Z == z_value), \(k)
    compressed$w[k] * c(compressed$S_T[[k]][, 1], compressed$S[[k]][1, 1])), `+`)
  share <- \(v) v[1:d] / v[d + 1]
  diff <- share(arm(1)) - share(arm(0))
  list(B = B, V = M1_W_M2_inv %*% meat %*% t(M1_W_M2_inv), x_C = diff[-1] / diff[1])
}

compressed_many <- compress_second_order(df_many, X_many)
compressed_many |>
  transmute(Z, day, G, dim_S = map_chr(S, \(m) paste(dim(m), collapse = " x ")),
            dim_second_moments = map_chr(second_moments, \(m) paste(dim(m), collapse = " x ")))
# A tibble: 8 × 5
      Z   day     G dim_S   dim_second_moments
  <int> <int> <int> <chr>   <chr>             
1     0     1  7639 26 x 26 57 x 57           
2     0     2  5321 26 x 26 57 x 57           
3     0     3  2988 26 x 26 57 x 57           
4     0     4  1014 26 x 26 57 x 57           
5     1     1   412 26 x 26 57 x 57           
6     1     2   634 26 x 26 57 x 57           
7     1     3   981 26 x 26 57 x 57           
8     1     4  1011 26 x 26 57 x 57

The first moments hold two matrices, and , and one matrix, , per stratum, and the second moments are a matrix: the totals of 5 outcome columns, of the intercept and 25 covariates, and of the same 26 times .

Binning and clustering

Binning or clustering the covariates turns them into one categorical covariate. That helps a lot when each account has one profile row: a categorical covariate can then be a grouping key, and the compressed dataset becomes counts and sums per cell. With several profiles per account, it helps much less. A categorical covariate with levels still enters the model as indicators, so it costs about as much as continuous covariates, and binning each of 25 covariates into deciles would create 225 indicators. Binning only saves space when it bins a few directions that matter.

We try two versions with 10 and 20 levels. The first bins the hours score into deciles, which keeps the direction that predicts the outcome. The second runs k-means on the standardized covariates, which ignores the outcome. Both are fit on the pre-experiment sample.

Code 
bin_edges <- quantile(drop(cbind(1, X_history) %*% score_models$y), seq(0, 1, 0.1))
indicators <- function(level, n_levels) sapply(2:n_levels, \(j) as.numeric(level == j))
score_bins <- function(X) {
  level <- findInterval(drop(cbind(1, X) %*% score_models$y), bin_edges[2:10]) + 1
  indicators(level, 10)
}
scale_center <- colMeans(X_history)
scale_sd <- apply(X_history, 2, sd)
set.seed(1)
clusters <- kmeans(scale(X_history, scale_center, scale_sd), centers = 20, nstart = 3, iter.max = 50)
cluster_of <- function(X) {
  X_std <- scale(X, scale_center, scale_sd)
  distances <- -2 * X_std %*% t(clusters$centers) + rep(rowSums(clusters$centers^2), each = nrow(X_std))   # squared distance, less |x|^2
  max.col(-distances, ties.method = "first")
}
X_bins <- score_bins(X_many)
X_kmeans <- indicators(cluster_of(X_many), 20)
c(bins = ncol(X_bins), kmeans = ncol(X_kmeans))
  bins kmeans 
     9     19

Comparison

Table 9 compares the strategies on this experiment, with one row per strategy, next to two references: no covariates and the 5 base covariates. Every row uses the exact compressed dataset, except the second order approximation of all 25 covariates. For each one we report how many numbers its compressed dataset stores, counting each distinct number once, and the LATE with its standard error. The function sizes, from the section on many covariates, counts these numbers. A compressed dataset with continuous covariates stores, per stratum, the count, first moments, and either all their pairwise products (exact) or the products of the account totals (second order). Indicators of one categorical covariate have fewer distinct products, because two indicators of the same covariate are never both 1.

Code 
fit_second <- function(df, X) {
  fit <- fit_second_order(compress_second_order(df, X))
  effects(fit, fit$x_C, rep(0, ncol(X)))
}
strategies <- list(
  "no covariates" = list(X = matrix(numeric(0), nrow(df_many), 0), categorical = FALSE, second_order = FALSE),
  "5 base covariates" = list(X = centered(df_many)[, -1], categorical = FALSE, second_order = FALSE),
  "all 25 covariates" = list(X = X_many, categorical = FALSE, second_order = FALSE),
  "all 25 covariates, second order approximation" = list(X = X_many, categorical = FALSE, second_order = TRUE),
  "3 prognostic scores" = list(X = X_scores, categorical = FALSE, second_order = FALSE),
  "hours score in 10 bins" = list(X = X_bins, categorical = TRUE, second_order = FALSE),
  "k-means, 20 clusters" = list(X = X_kmeans, categorical = TRUE, second_order = FALSE))
many_tab <- imap_dfr(strategies, \(m, name) {
  fit <- if (m$second_order) fit_second(df_many, m$X) else exact_fits[[name]] %||% fit_exact(df_many, m$X)   # reuse the fits from the main text
  size <- sizes(ncol(m$X), m$categorical)
  tibble(strategy = name, k = ncol(m$X), numbers = size[[if (m$second_order) "second_order" else "exact"]],
         LATE = fit$estimate[1], se = fit$se[1])
})
Code 
many_tab |>
  mutate(numbers = format(numbers, big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable(digits = 4, col.names = c("Strategy", "Covariates $k$", "Numbers stored", "LATE", "SE"))

The second order approximation stores 19,888 numbers instead of 2,778,888, and its standard error, 0.0526, is within 0.1% of the exact one, 0.0526. The three prognostic scores give a standard error of 0.0528, as small as all 25 covariates, with fewer numbers still, 6,888, and their storage does not grow with the number of covariates. Binning the hours score into deciles keeps some of the gain over no covariates, but here it does worse than the 5 base covariates, and the k-means clusters do worse still: clusters that ignore the outcome mostly separate profiles along directions that do not predict it.

One experiment can be lucky, so we repeat it 400 times, refitting every strategy each time. The score models, the bins and the clusters stay fixed, as they would in practice, since they come from data before the experiment. Each replication also retrains the scores on its own pre-experiment sample, which we use in the next section.

An exact fit with all 25 covariates takes about 20 seconds per experiment, so every strategy here takes its standard errors from the second order approximation, which matched the exact standard error to within 0.1% in Table 9. The point estimates do not depend on the approximation, so the spread of the estimates holds for the exact compressed dataset too, while the SE/SD ratio and the coverage test the approximation itself.

Code 
analyze_many <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  df <- simulate_accounts() |>
    add_signals() |>
    prepare()
  X <- cbind(centered(df)[, -1], as.matrix(df[signal_cols]))
  history <- simulate_accounts(10000, force_Z = 0) |>                      # a fresh pre-experiment sample, for the next section
    add_signals() |>
    prepare()
  X_history <- cbind(centered(history)[, -1], as.matrix(history[signal_cols]))
  models <- lm(as.matrix(history[c("y", "N", "D")]) ~ X_history) |>
    coef() |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    as.list()
  X_retrained <- map_dfc(models, \(b) drop(cbind(1, X) %*% b) - mean(drop(cbind(1, X_history) %*% b))) |>
    as.matrix()
  list("no covariates" = matrix(numeric(0), nrow(df), 0), "5 base covariates" = centered(df)[, -1],
       "all 25 covariates" = X, "3 prognostic scores" = score(X), "hours score in 10 bins" = score_bins(X),
       "k-means, 20 clusters" = indicators(cluster_of(X), 20), "3 prognostic scores, retrained" = X_retrained) |>
    imap_dfr(\(Xm, name) fit_second(df, Xm) |>
               mutate(strategy = name, rep = seed))
}
invisible(gc())
many_mc <- mclapply(1:400, analyze_many, mc.cores = cores) |>
  bind_rows()
many_mc_tab <- many_mc |>
  filter(effect == "tau_LATE", strategy != "3 prognostic scores, retrained") |>
  group_by(strategy) |>
  summarise(bias = mean(estimate - truth[["tau_LATE"]]), sd = sd(estimate), se_over_sd = mean(se) / sd(estimate),
            coverage = mean(abs(estimate - truth[["tau_LATE"]]) <= qnorm(0.975) * se)) |>
  arrange(sd)
Code 
many_mc_tab |>
  kable(digits = 4, col.names = c("Strategy", "Bias", "SD", "SE/SD", "Coverage"))

Every strategy is unbiased, up to the Monte Carlo error of about 0.004 in the bias. The second order standard errors are between 95% and 98% of the spread of the estimates, and the coverage is between 94.0% and 96.0%, so the approximation is close to calibrated for the LATE. Across experiments, the prognostic scores are as precise as all 25 covariates, with a standard deviation of 0.0567 against 0.0566, and both beat the 5 base covariates (0.0626).

Table 11 shows how the compressed dataset grows with the number of covariates under each approach, with our 5 outcome columns and 8 strata.

Code 
tibble(k = c(5, 10, 25, 50, 100)) |>
  mutate(exact = map_dbl(k, \(k) sizes(k)[["exact"]]),
         second_order = map_dbl(k, \(k) sizes(k)[["second_order"]]),
         scores_exact = sizes(3)[["exact"]],
         scores_second_order = sizes(3)[["second_order"]]) |>
  mutate(across(-k, \(v) format(v, big.mark = ","))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Covariates $k$", "Exact", "Second order", "Scores, exact", "Scores, second order"))

The exact compressed dataset grows like , the second order one like , and with prognostic scores it does not grow at all. The recommendations follow:

  1. Reduce many covariates to a prognostic score per outcome, trained on data from before the experiment. This keeps the variance reduction and makes the compressed dataset independent of the number of covariates.
  2. Keep individual covariates in the model only when we want to read effects along them, such as the effect for kids profiles. Those questions read the treatment line away from the compliers’ covariates, so they need the exact second moments for the covariates involved.
  3. For the LATE and the ratio, use the second order compressed dataset, or delta vectors early when the profile rows can be read twice.
  4. Avoid clustering or binning covariates without regard to the outcome. With several profiles per account it saves little space, and it gives up precision.

Why the score’s modeling error does not enter the standard error

A prognostic score is a prediction, and a different pre-experiment sample would give a different . Should the standard error of the effect include that uncertainty? It does not need to, for two reasons.

First, conditional on the pre-experiment sample, is a fixed function. It is trained on data that is independent of the experiment, so for the experiment, is computed from observed covariates, exactly like or any other transformation we might choose. We condition on it the same way we condition on . The gap between and the true is real, but the model never assumes that the score is the true conditional mean, and its coefficient is estimated in the experiment, so the uncertainty of that coefficient is already in the cluster robust covariance.

Second, the effect does not depend on which we use. With a randomized prompt, two stage least squares with any pre-experiment covariate is consistent for the same LATE. A worse score leaves more noise and a wider interval, but not a bias. Averaging over pre-experiment samples as well as experiments, the law of total variance gives

The cluster robust standard error estimates the first term. The second term is close to zero, because is close to for every : different pre-experiment samples give different but equally valid adjustments of the same effect.

This argument needs the score to be trained without the experiment’s outcomes. A flexible model trained on the experiment itself could absorb part of the effect or fit its noise, which would bias the estimate and shrink the standard error. Training on pre-experiment data, as here, or cross-fitting, where the score of each profile comes from a model trained on other profiles, avoids that.

The Monte Carlo of the previous section kept the scores fixed. To check the second point, we use the scores it retrained on a fresh pre-experiment sample of 10,000 accounts in every simulated experiment, so the spread of the estimates includes the variation of . As in the previous section, the standard errors come from the second order approximation.

Code 
fresh_tab <- many_mc |>
  filter(strategy == "3 prognostic scores, retrained") |>
  group_by(effect) |>
  summarise(bias = mean(estimate - truth[effect]), sd = sd(estimate), se_over_sd = mean(se) / sd(estimate),
            coverage = mean(abs(estimate - truth[effect]) <= qnorm(0.975) * se))
Code 
fresh_tab |>
  kable(digits = 4, format.args = list(scientific = FALSE), col.names = c("Effect", "Bias", "SD", "SE/SD", "Coverage"))

Even with the scores retrained every time, the standard errors, which ignore the variation of , are within Monte Carlo error of the spread of the estimates, with coverage of 94.0% for the LATE and 94.8% for the ratio. With 400 replications, SE/SD is itself uncertain by about , and the coverage by about percentage points. The standard deviation of the LATE, 0.0568, is close to the 0.0567 we saw with fixed scores, so retraining the scores adds little variance. The bias of the LATE, -0.0023, is about -0.8 Monte Carlo standard errors from zero, and the same experiments with fixed scores gave -0.0023.

item.title: First Principles of Ranking
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
It is Friday night, and a member opens Netflix on their TV. Within a second, the home page fills with rows of titles: “Continue Watching”, “Trending Now”, “Because You Watched Titanic”, “Top Picks for You”. Behind every one of those rows is a ranker. A ranker receives a query, here the member and their context, picks a handful of titles out of a catalog of thousands, and decides what order to show them in.

The stakes are high and the time is short. Netflix reports that a typical member loses interest after perhaps 60 to 90 seconds of choosing, having reviewed 10 to 20 titles on one or two screens, and that recommendations influence about 80% of the hours streamed (Gomez-Uribe and Hunt, 2015). If the right title is not in the first few tiles of the first few rows, the member may never find it.

This post builds a ranker from first principles, using a single Netflix row, “Top Picks for You”, as the running example. We will start from the problem we would like to solve, see why it is intractable, and watch the standard three phase architecture fall out of the approximations we are forced to make:

  1. Candidate generation: cheaply narrow the whole catalog down to a few hundred titles.
  2. Utility prediction: use an expensive ML model to predict how much the member will value each candidate.
  3. Reranking: assemble the final row, accounting for the fact that titles in a row interact with one another.

Netflix has described parts of its system publicly, and we cite those descriptions where they exist. Elsewhere, the Netflix setting is our illustration of how a method would apply, not a claim about what Netflix runs in production.

The problem we would like to solve

Let the catalog contain items, indexed by . In our example, an item is a title, and is in the thousands. A query arrives. On the home page, is the member and their context: their viewing history, the device (a TV, not a phone), and the time (Friday night). When the member types into the search box, also includes the text. We must display a row of titles in order,

where is the title shown at position . Let be the utility generated by showing row to query : the probability that the member presses play, the expected minutes they stream, or whatever we value. The ideal ranker solves

There are ordered rows. With titles and tiles, that is roughly rows. We cannot evaluate them all, so we need structure.

The naive solution

The simplest structure comes from a model of how members scan a row. Say the member examines position with probability , where . On a TV, only the first few tiles of a row are visible before the member scrolls right, and the 60 to 90 second attention span means most never scroll far. If the member examines title , it generates expected utility , a scalar. Make two assumptions:

  • (A1) No interactions. The utility of title does not depend on which other titles are in the row.
  • (A2) Exhaustive scoring. We can evaluate for every one of the titles.

Under (A1), the row utility is a weighted sum over positions,

The optimal row sorts the titles by .

The three phases of a ranker exist because these assumptions fail in different ways.

  • (A2) fails because a good model of is expensive, and it must run for every row on every home page that every member opens. Candidate generation exists to cut down to a manageable .
  • is unknown. Utility prediction estimates it with an ML model, .
  • (A1) fails because titles in a row do interact: a row of ten romantic comedies is worth less than ten times one romantic comedy, because the member only needs one of them. Reranking exists to optimize the row as a whole.

Phase 1: Candidate generation

The job of candidate generation is to return a set of titles, where . For the “Top Picks” row, think of a few hundred candidates out of 10,000 titles. The scoring here must be cheap, much cheaper than the model in phase 2, so it will be less accurate. Netflix’s catalog is small compared with services that rank hundreds of millions of videos or products, so its funnel can be shallower, but the logic is the same.

Candidate generation is a ceiling on the entire system. If a title is not retrieved, no downstream model can ever show it. So candidate generation is judged by recall, not precision. Let be the set of the titles with the highest true utility. Then

The numerator counts how many titles of the ideal row survived retrieval, and dividing by turns that count into the fraction of the ideal row that is still within reach of phases 2 and 3. Equivalently, it is the probability that a title drawn at random from the ideal row made it into the candidate set. Even if the downstream phases were perfect, the best row they could build would contain only of the ideal titles. Note that the denominator is , not : retrieving extra titles that are not in the ideal row costs nothing in this metric, which is why candidate generators are free to return far more titles than the row can show.

How large does need to be? Suppose the cheap scorer produces a score that is correlated with the true utility (dropping for now) with correlation ,

For each of 200 members, we retrieve the top titles by out of , and ask what fraction of that member’s true top we caught.

Code 
set.seed(1)
N <- 1e4          # titles in the catalog
K <- 20           # tiles in the row
n_members <- 200
M_grid <- round(10^seq(log10(K), log10(N), length.out = 25))

# Recall@M at every candidate set size M, for one simulated member
recall_curve <- function(rho) {
  u <- rnorm(N)
  eps <- rnorm(N)
  s <- rho * u + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * eps
  top_K <- order(u, decreasing = TRUE)[1:K]
  ord <- order(s, decreasing = TRUE)
  tibble(M = M_grid, recall = map_dbl(M_grid, \(M) mean(top_K %in% ord[1:M])))
}

recall <- expand_grid(rho = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95), member = 1:n_members) %>%
  mutate(curve = map(rho, recall_curve)) %>%
  unnest(curve) %>%
  group_by(rho, M) %>%
  summarise(recall = mean(recall), .groups = "drop")

With a correlation of 0.8, a candidate set of about 200 titles, ten times the row, recovers only about three quarters of the true top 20, and it takes more than 400 titles to recover 90%. This is why candidate generation returns hundreds of titles rather than exactly , and why it pays to combine several cheap scorers that make different mistakes. Below are the most common ones.

Lexical retrieval

When the member types into the search box, the oldest method is to match words. Lexical retrieval needs no training data, and it handles exact matches on rare terms, such as an actor’s name, which embedding models can blur. An inverted index maps each term to the list of titles whose text (name, synopsis, cast) contains it. When the member searches for “heist”, we look up the entry for “heist” and get back only the titles whose text mentions a heist, rather than scanning all titles. Matched titles are scored with a formula such as BM25,

Here is the term frequency, the number of times term appears in title ’s text, is the length of that text, is the average length, and are tuning constants (usually written and ; we rename them to avoid a clash with position ). is the inverse document frequency, which grows as fewer titles contain , for example where is the number of titles containing . Each piece has a job:

  • says rare words are more informative than common ones. Nearly every synopsis contains “the”, but few contain “heist”.
  • The fraction saturates as grows: it is bounded by . A synopsis that says “heist” five times is not five times more relevant than one that says it once.
  • The term discounts long texts, such as a documentary series with a long episode guide, which contain many terms by chance.

On the BEIR benchmark, which evaluates retrievers on domains they were not trained on, BM25 proved to be a robust baseline that many neural retrievers failed to beat (Thakur et al., 2021).

The weakness of lexical retrieval is vocabulary mismatch. A member who types “bank robbery movies” does not match a synopsis that only says “a crew of thieves plans the perfect heist”.

Collaborative filtering

The “Top Picks” row has no search text at all, so we need to use behavior. Netflix made this problem famous with the Netflix Prize. In 2006, Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings and offered $1 million to anyone who could improve the root mean squared error of its in-house rating predictor, Cinematch, by 10%. The data contained no movie descriptions to speak of, only who rated what. Here, the query is simply the member, with no other context, and an item is a movie. The question is which movies a member will like, based only on the viewing history of that member and of everyone else.

The simplest approach is item-to-item collaborative filtering, which Amazon described in Linden, Smith and York (2003). If many members who watched movie also watched movie , then is a good candidate for anyone who just watched . To make this precise, arrange engagement into a matrix with one row per member and one column per movie, where records member ’s engagement with movie , for example if member watched movie and 0 otherwise. Column of , written , lists every member’s engagement with movie .

Consider a tiny Netflix with seven members and six movies: three romances (Notebook, Titanic, La La Land) and three action movies (Die Hard, The Matrix, Alien). We will come back to these movies throughout the post.

Code

  c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  c(1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0),
  c(0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0),
  c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0),
  c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1),
  c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1),
  c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)
)
dimnames(Y) <- list(paste0("member", 1:7),
                    c("Notebook", "Titanic", "LaLaLand", "DieHard", "Matrix", "Alien"))

The item-by-item co-occurrence matrix is , whose entries are inner products of columns,

With 0/1 engagement, counts the members who watched both and , and the diagonal entry counts the members who watched at all. Raw counts favor popular movies, since a blockbuster co-occurs with almost everything, so the counts are normalized. Dividing by the lengths of the two columns gives the cosine similarity between them,

Movie ’s neighbor list is the handful of movies with the largest , stored with their scores. The name comes from nearest neighbors: if we think of movies as points and similarity as closeness, the list holds movie ’s nearest neighbors. In our tiny Netflix, Notebook was watched by members 1, 2 and 7. Titanic was watched by members 1, 3 and 7, an overlap of two members, so . La La Land was watched by members 2, 3, 5 and 7, also an overlap of two, so . No one who watched Notebook watched an action movie. Notebook’s neighbor list is (Titanic 0.67, La La Land 0.58). We can compute every movie’s similarities at once.

Code

sim <- YtY / sqrt(diag(YtY) %o% diag(YtY))   # cosine similarity between columns of Y
round(sim, 2)

The neighbor lists are computed offline into a lookup table. At request time, we look up the lists of the member’s recent movies, take their union, and score each candidate by the sum of its similarities to the member’s movies. No model runs at request time, which is why this method is very cheap. This is exactly the shape of Netflix’s “Because You Watched” row, which Gomez-Uribe and Hunt describe as driven by an unpersonalized “sims” algorithm that computes a ranked list of similar videos for every video in the catalog.

Matrix factorization

The approach that dominated the Netflix Prize was matrix factorization. Early in the competition, Simon Funk described a simple version in a blog post, Try This at Home, that jumped near the top of the leaderboard. The winning teams built on it, as summarized by Koren, Bell and Volinsky (2009). Netflix later wrote that it put a matrix factorization model (SVD), together with a restricted Boltzmann machine, into production after the competition.

Return to the engagement matrix . Rather than comparing its columns pairwise, we approximate the whole matrix. Any real matrix has a singular value decomposition (SVD)

where is the rank of , has one row per member and orthonormal columns, has one row per movie ( rows) and orthonormal columns, and is an diagonal matrix of singular values sorted so that . Keep only the first columns of and and the first singular values, written , and . Then

is a rank matrix, and by the Eckart–Young theorem it is the closest rank matrix to in the sum of squared entries. To get two embedding matrices, split evenly between the two sides,

each with columns. Row of is member ’s embedding, and row of is movie ’s embedding. Write them as column vectors . Since , the two matrices multiply back to the rank approximation,

So the predicted affinity of member for movie is entry of , which is a dot product of the two embeddings,

Each of the dimensions acts like a latent taste. measures how much movie expresses taste , measures how much member has it, and measures how much of the variation in that taste explains. The recommendations come from what the approximation gets “wrong”. A rank matrix cannot reproduce every 0 in , so a movie the member has not watched, but that resembles the movies they did watch, gets a positive . Those are the candidates. The split of is a convention; and give the same .

Let’s factor the tiny Netflix matrix from above.

Code 
d <- 2
svd_Y <- svd(Y)
# The signs of singular vectors are arbitrary; flip them so that Notebook loads positively on each dimension
flip <- sign(svd_Y$v[1, 1:d])
W_d <- svd_Y$u[, 1:d] %*% diag(flip)
V_d <- svd_Y$v[, 1:d] %*% diag(flip)
Sigma_d <- diag(svd_Y$d[1:d])

Phi <- W_d %*% sqrt(Sigma_d)
Psi <- V_d %*% sqrt(Sigma_d)
dimnames(Phi) <- list(rownames(Y), c("taste1", "taste2"))
dimnames(Psi) <- list(colnames(Y), c("taste1", "taste2"))
round(Psi, 2)

The first dimension is positive for every movie. It measures how much a movie is watched overall. The second dimension separates Notebook and Titanic (positive) from the action movies (negative), which the SVD discovered without being told any genres. La La Land sits near zero because fans of both genres watched it. Multiplying the embeddings gives the predicted affinities.

Missing is not the same as zero

The SVD needs every entry of . For watch data, a 0 meaning “did not watch” is reasonable. For the star ratings in the Netflix Prize it is not: a missing rating does not mean the member would rate the movie 0 stars. It means we do not know.

To see this, give our tiny Netflix star ratings. Let be the matrix of ratings, with the same rows and columns as , where is member ’s rating of movie , and let be the set of pairs for which a rating exists. Each member has rated four of the six movies, including some movies they disliked, and the other two ratings are missing.

Members 1, 2, 3 and 7 like the romances and members 4, 5 and 6 like the action movies, but each member is missing two ratings. Filling the missing entries with 0 would tell the SVD that member 1 rated La La Land lower than Die Hard, which they gave 1 star.

Fitting only the observed ratings

Funk’s method, despite being called SVD, does not compute a decomposition at all. It never fills in the missing entries. Instead, it chooses the embeddings to fit only the observed ratings, with a ridge penalty to avoid overfitting,

Here is a scalar, the average of the observed ratings. Subtracting it means the embeddings only have to explain how a rating differs from a typical rating, and the ridge penalty shrinks predictions toward rather than toward 0 stars. and are now free parameters with the same shapes as before, one row per member and one row per movie, each with columns. We write the minimizers as and , with rows and , to keep them apart from the SVD embeddings. The predicted rating is

and it is defined for every pair , including the missing ones. Those predictions are what we use to rank candidates.

There is no closed form for the minimizer, because the loss involves the product of two unknowns. The loss is not convex in jointly. But it becomes a ridge regression as soon as we fix one of the two matrices.

Alternating least squares (ALS) algorithm

Fix and look at the terms of the loss that involve a single member’s embedding . Let be the movies that member rated. The other members’ terms do not involve , so minimizing over means minimizing

This is a ridge regression of member ’s centered ratings on the embeddings of the movies they rated, with playing the role of the coefficients. Setting the gradient with respect to to zero,

Stack the rows for into the matrix , and the ratings into the vector of length . Then , and the update is

The inverse always exists: is positive semidefinite, and adding with makes it positive definite. By the symmetry of the loss, fixing and letting be the members who rated movie gives

ALS alternates between updating every and updating every . Each half-step minimizes the loss exactly over one matrix while the other is held fixed, so the loss can never increase. Because the joint problem is not convex, ALS converges to a local minimum that can depend on the starting point. The members’ updates do not depend on each other, and neither do the movies’, so each half-step parallelizes across machines.

Let’s fit the tiny Netflix ratings with ALS, using and .

Code 
observed <- !is.na(Y_star)
mu <- mean(Y_star[observed])
eta <- 1

# Ridge regression of each row of Y on the fixed embeddings, using only that row's observed entries
ridge_rows <- function(Y, fixed, observed) {
  map(seq_len(nrow(Y)), \(row) {
    O_row <- observed[row, ]                      # O_q for a member, O^j for a movie
    fixed_O <- fixed[O_row, , drop = FALSE]
    as.vector(solve(t(fixed_O) %*% fixed_O + eta * diag(d),
                    t(fixed_O) %*% (Y[row, O_row] - mu)))
  }) %>%
    list_c() %>%
    matrix(ncol = d, byrow = TRUE)
}

# One ALS iteration: update every phi_q with Psi fixed, then every psi_j with Phi fixed
als_step <- function(embeddings, iter) {
  Phi_star <- ridge_rows(Y_star, embeddings$Psi_star, observed)
  Psi_star <- ridge_rows(t(Y_star), Phi_star, t(observed))
  list(Phi_star = Phi_star, Psi_star = Psi_star)
}

loss <- function(embeddings) {
  e <- (Y_star - mu - embeddings$Phi_star %*% t(embeddings$Psi_star))[observed]
  sum(e^2) + eta * (sum(embeddings$Phi_star^2) + sum(embeddings$Psi_star^2))
}

set.seed(5)
embeddings_0 <- list(Phi_star = matrix(rnorm(nrow(Y_star) * d, sd = 0.1), ncol = d),
                     Psi_star = matrix(rnorm(ncol(Y_star) * d, sd = 0.1), ncol = d))
iterates <- accumulate(1:20, als_step, .init = embeddings_0)
losses <- map_dbl(iterates[-1], loss)
round(losses[c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20)], 3)
[1] 56.926 23.560 23.137 23.048 23.041 23.041

The loss falls at every iteration and levels off within a few. The predicted ratings fill in the whole matrix.

Y_star_hat <- mu + als_fit$Phi_star %*% t(als_fit$Psi_star)
dimnames(Y_star_hat) <- dimnames(Y_star)
round(Y_star_hat, 1)
