Every missing rating is predicted in line with the member’s taste. Member 1, who rated Notebook 5 stars and Die Hard 1 star, is predicted to give La La Land 3.8 stars and The Matrix 2.5. Member 5, an action fan, is predicted to give Die Hard 3.9 stars and Notebook 2.3. Nothing in the model restricts predictions to the 1 to 5 star scale, and member 2’s predicted rating for Titanic is 5.1.

The penalty matters a great deal here. There are 28 observed ratings and embedding parameters, so without a penalty the model could almost memorize the observed ratings and say little about the missing ones. With instead of 1, the same code predicts that member 2 would give Titanic 6.2 stars and Alien 0.7, both off the scale, and that member 5, an action fan, would give Notebook 3.9. In practice, and are chosen by holding out some observed ratings and measuring the error on them, which is exactly how the Netflix Prize scored entries.

Koren, Bell and Volinsky also replace the single average with a per-member and a per-movie baseline, to capture generous raters and popular movies. Nonnegative matrix factorization (Lee and Seung, 1999) is another variant: it constrains every entry of and to be nonnegative, so each latent taste can only add to an affinity, which often makes the dimensions easier to interpret. In every variant, the predicted affinity is still built on the dot product .

Cold start

Matrix factorization only knows about members and movies that appear in . A member who signed up today, or a Netflix original that premiered this morning, has no row or column and so no embedding. There are a few simple fixes.

Fold in new members without retraining. Because has orthonormal columns, is the first columns of the identity, so

Multiplying both sides on the right by and using ,

Each member’s embedding is a function of only their own row of and the fixed movie embeddings. So when a new member with engagement row (a vector) arrives, we compute

which is the sum of the embeddings of the movies they watched, with each dimension divided by its singular value. By symmetry, a new movie that a few existing members have watched gets , where is its column of engagement, with one entry per member. We can check that the formula reproduces the existing members’ embeddings exactly, and then fold in a new member who has only watched Notebook.

Code 
max(abs(Y %*% Psi %*% solve(Sigma_d) - Phi))
[1] 2.220446e-16
Code 
y_new <- matrix(c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0), nrow = 1, dimnames = list("new member", colnames(Y)))
phi_new <- y_new %*% Psi %*% solve(Sigma_d)
round(phi_new %*% t(Psi), 2)
           Notebook Titanic LaLaLand DieHard Matrix Alien
new member      0.4    0.35     0.28   -0.11  -0.12 -0.12

After a single movie, the new member’s top candidates are the other romances.

Before any engagement, fall back on the crowd. A member with no history at all can be shown the titles that are popular overall or in their country. A common approach is also to ask new members to pick a few titles they like during sign up, which gives a nonzero to fold in right away.

Give new titles an embedding from their content. A Netflix original with no views can start from the average embedding of existing titles with the same genre, director or cast. More generally, fit a regression from content features to the learned embeddings across existing titles, , where is title ’s content feature vector and is a matrix of coefficients, and apply it to the new title. Once real views arrive, fold them in or retrain. To make sure those views do arrive, new titles are often guaranteed a minimum amount of exposure.

That regression from features to embeddings is the seed of the next idea: rather than learning an embedding per member and per title, learn a function that produces the embedding from features.

Two-tower embedding retrieval

The modern workhorse of candidate generation is the two-tower model, a direct descendant of matrix factorization. Matrix factorization is cheap at request time, and the reason is worth making explicit. The predicted affinity factorizes into a part that depends only on the member and a part that depends only on the movie. All the movie embeddings can be computed once, offline. When member opens the home page, we look up and score each candidate with a single dot product. The two-tower model keeps exactly this structure and changes only where the embeddings come from.

From lookup tables to neural networks. In matrix factorization, an embedding is a row of a table. If is a one-hot encoding of member ’s ID, a vector with a 1 in member ’s position and 0 elsewhere, then : a linear map applied to the member’s ID. Likewise , with the one-hot encoding of movie ’s ID. The two-tower model replaces each of these linear maps with a neural network, and replaces each one-hot ID with a richer description of the member or the title. The table lookups and become functions and , and the predicted affinity becomes a score,

As in the SVD, one side is about the member and the other is about the title. The query tower reads the member’s features: their recently watched titles, country, device and time of day. The title tower reads the title’s features: genre, cast, director, synopsis, maturity rating. Matrix factorization is the special case where the only feature is the ID and each tower is a single linear layer, and the content regression from the cold start section is a title tower with a single linear layer on content features.

The two towers have nothing in common but their output. Their inputs are different, not even of the same length, and the two networks typically share no parameters. The one requirement is that each tower ends in a layer with exactly outputs, so that the dot product

is defined. The member embedding and the title embedding are different objects that describe different things, exactly as row of describes a member and row of describes a movie in the SVD. What ties them together is that the dot product multiplies coordinate of one with coordinate of the other. For the score to be useful, coordinate must mean “how much the member likes latent taste ” on one side and “how much the title has latent taste ” on the other. In our tiny Netflix, Notebook’s movie embedding is and Die Hard’s is , so they sit on opposite sides of the romance versus action taste, and member 1’s affinity is 0.75 for Notebook and for Die Hard.

Nobody assigns these meanings in advance. They emerge because the two towers are trained jointly: the loss depends on the towers only through the dot products, so every gradient step updates both networks together, and each tower learns coordinates that line up with the other’s. The towers are separate networks, but they cannot be trained separately. What they can do is run separately once trained, which is where the savings come from:

  • The title embeddings do not depend on the member, so they are computed offline for all titles and refreshed as the catalog changes.
  • When the member opens the home page, we run once and search for the titles with the largest inner product.

The price of this separation is that cannot use cross features, features that describe the pair jointly, such as “this member finished season 1 of this show” or “this member has watched three other films by this director”. Such a feature belongs to neither tower alone. Cross features are left for phase 2.

The learned coordinates are also not unique. For any invertible matrix , replacing the embeddings with and leaves every score unchanged, since . The loss cannot tell the two sets of embeddings apart, so an individual coordinate has no fixed meaning unless something else pins it down. In the SVD, the orthonormal columns sorted by singular value pin the coordinates down up to sign, which is why our code had to flip signs to make the second taste read as romance. A two-tower network has no such constraint. This matters later: a cosine similarity between two title embeddings is unchanged when is orthogonal, but not for a general , so the similarity depends on choices made in training.

Advantages over matrix factorization. Replacing ID lookups with networks over features buys several things:

  • Cold start. Because reads content features, the Netflix original that premiered this morning gets an embedding on day one, with no views at all. Unlike the content regression we bolted onto matrix factorization, the title tower can be nonlinear and is trained jointly with the query tower, rather than fit afterward to embeddings learned without content.
  • Context. In matrix factorization, member has one embedding , whatever the context. The query tower can produce a different embedding for the same member on the living room TV on Friday night than on their phone during a weekday commute.
  • Freshness. Because reads the member’s recent viewing, their embedding changes the moment they finish a title, without refitting anything. This generalizes the fold-in formula , which is a fixed linear function of the viewing history, to a learned nonlinear one.
  • Sharing strength. Two titles with similar features get similar embeddings even if few members have watched both, so rarely watched titles borrow information from similar popular ones.

Training a two-tower model

To see what joint training means, make the parameters explicit. Write the query tower as , where collects all of its weights and biases, and the title tower as , where collects all of its weights and biases. The two sets are disjoint: no parameter belongs to both towers. The score is

In the matrix factorization special case, and : the parameters of each “tower” are just its embedding table.

The training data is a log of plays. Each element is a pair : the member’s state at the moment they pressed play, and the title they played. Following Covington, Adams and Sargin (2016), who introduced this framing for video recommendation, we treat retrieval as an extreme multiclass classification: given , which of the titles did the member play? A softmax over the catalog turns scores into probabilities,

and training minimizes the average negative log likelihood of the observed plays, jointly over both sets of parameters,

Substituting the softmax, the log of a ratio is the log of the numerator minus the log of the denominator, so each play contributes

Every term of involves both and , through the product of the two towers’ outputs.

Notice that contains only positives: it records the titles that were played, and has no records of titles that were not played. The negatives enter through the softmax denominator instead. The denominator sums over all titles in the catalog, not just the titles in , and after taking logs it becomes the log-sum-exp term above. So for every play , the numerator term rewards a high score for the played title , and the denominator term penalizes high scores for every title in the catalog. The net effect is to raise ’s score relative to all the others. Every title the member did not play acts as an implicit negative for that play. This carries the same caveat as missing ratings in matrix factorization: a title that was not played was not necessarily disliked. The member may simply never have seen it.

The gradients show why the towers cannot be trained separately. Take a single play and write its term of as . To shorten the notation, write for the member’s embedding, for title ’s embedding, and . The derivative of the log-sum-exp term with respect to is

so the gradients with respect to the two towers’ outputs are

The first is a vector built entirely from the title tower’s outputs. It pulls the member’s embedding toward the played title and away from the average title under the model’s current probabilities. The second is built entirely from the query tower’s output. It pulls the played title’s embedding toward the member, and pushes every other title away in proportion to its predicted probability. The chain rule carries these into the parameters,

where is the Jacobian of the query tower’s outputs with respect to its parameters, and is the Jacobian of the title tower for title . Backpropagation computes both. So the update to the query tower’s parameters requires the title tower’s current outputs, and the update to the title tower’s parameters requires the query tower’s current output. Each tower’s training signal comes from the other.

Let’s train a two-tower model on a small Netflix, with titles: 20 romances, 20 action movies and 20 family films, about half of them long. Title ’s features are , a genre indicator plus a runtime indicator. Each play comes from a member described by : the share of their history in each genre, and whether they are watching on the TV rather than a phone. We simulate 3,000 plays from a true model in which members play titles from their favorite genre, and prefer long titles on the TV and short ones on a phone.

Each tower has one hidden layer of 8 ReLU units and outputs,

so the query tower’s parameters are and the title tower’s are , with of size , , and of size .

In the code, X_q stacks the plays’ feature vectors as rows and F_titles stacks the titles’ , so the query tower’s output has row for each play and the title tower’s output has row for each title. The parameters are stored as a nested list omega, with one element per tower, omega$phi holding and omega$psi holding . With only 60 titles, we can afford the full sum over the catalog, and we run plain gradient descent on with learning rate alpha, which multiplies each gradient before it is subtracted from the parameters. Each step is a function gradient_step that takes the current parameters and returns updated ones, and accumulate applies it 1,000 times, keeping every intermediate set of parameters so that we can trace the loss. The matrix dS holds the derivative of with respect to each score, . Then dPhi and dPsi are exactly the two gradients above, averaged over plays, and the remaining lines carry them back through each tower’s layers.

Code 
set.seed(6)
genres <- c("romance", "action", "family")
N <- 60
title_genre <- rep(1:3, each = 20)
long <- rbinom(N, 1, 0.5)
F_titles <- cbind(diag(3)[title_genre, ], long)            # row j is f_j

n_plays <- 3000
favorite <- sample(1:3, n_plays, replace = TRUE)
share <- matrix(0.15, n_plays, 3)
share[cbind(1:n_plays, favorite)] <- 0.7                    # 70% of history in the favorite genre
on_tv <- rbinom(n_plays, 1, 0.5)
X_q <- cbind(share, on_tv)                                  # row q is x_q

# True model: favorite genre, long titles on the TV, short titles on a phone
true_score <- 4 * share[, title_genre] + 1.5 * outer(on_tv, long) + 1.5 * outer(1 - on_tv, 1 - long)
softmax_rows <- function(S) {
  row_max <- S[cbind(seq_len(nrow(S)), max.col(S, ties.method = "first"))]
  E <- exp(S - row_max)
  E / rowSums(E)
}
P_true <- softmax_rows(true_score)
j_played <- map_int(1:n_plays, \(q) sample(N, 1, prob = P_true[q, ]))
played <- cbind(1:n_plays, j_played)
J_true <- -mean(log(P_true[played]))                       # loss of the true model
Y_played <- matrix(0, n_plays, N)
Y_played[played] <- 1

# The two towers, each with one hidden layer of ReLU units
d <- 4
n_hidden <- 8
relu <- function(z) pmax(z, 0)
query_tower <- function(x, w) {
  Z <- sweep(x %*% w$G1, 2, w$g1, "+")
  list(Z = Z, A = relu(Z), out = relu(Z) %*% w$G2)
}
title_tower <- function(f, w) {
  Z <- sweep(f %*% w$H1, 2, w$h1, "+")
  list(Z = Z, A = relu(Z), out = relu(Z) %*% w$H2)
}

# Initialize the two towers' parameters separately
init <- function(r, c) matrix(rnorm(r * c, sd = 0.3), r, c)
omega_0 <- list(
  phi = list(G1 = init(ncol(X_q), n_hidden), g1 = rep(0, n_hidden), G2 = init(n_hidden, d)),
  psi = list(H1 = init(ncol(F_titles), n_hidden), h1 = rep(0, n_hidden), H2 = init(n_hidden, d))
)

two_tower_loss <- function(omega) {
  P <- softmax_rows(query_tower(X_q, omega$phi)$out %*% t(title_tower(F_titles, omega$psi)$out))
  -mean(log(P[played]))
}

alpha <- 0.5
gradient_step <- function(omega, iter) {
  # Forward pass through each tower, then the softmax over all N titles
  query_pass <- query_tower(X_q, omega$phi)
  title_pass <- title_tower(F_titles, omega$psi)
  P <- softmax_rows(query_pass$out %*% t(title_pass$out))

  # Gradients with respect to the scores and the two towers' outputs
  dS <- (P - Y_played) / n_plays
  dPhi <- dS %*% title_pass$out       # needs the title tower's outputs
  dPsi <- t(dS) %*% query_pass$out    # needs the query tower's outputs

  # Backpropagate through each tower to its own parameters
  dZ_q <- (dPhi %*% t(omega$phi$G2)) * (query_pass$Z > 0)
  dZ_t <- (dPsi %*% t(omega$psi$H2)) * (title_pass$Z > 0)
  gradient <- list(
    phi = list(G1 = t(X_q) %*% dZ_q, g1 = colSums(dZ_q), G2 = t(query_pass$A) %*% dPhi),
    psi = list(H1 = t(F_titles) %*% dZ_t, h1 = colSums(dZ_t), H2 = t(title_pass$A) %*% dPsi)
  )

  # Update both towers' parameters in the same step
  map2(omega, gradient, \(tower, d_tower) map2(tower, d_tower, \(w, dw) w - alpha * dw))
}

omega_trace <- accumulate(1:1000, gradient_step, .init = omega_0)
J_trace <- map_dbl(omega_trace, two_tower_loss)
omega_hat <- last(omega_trace)
round(c(start = J_trace[1], iter_100 = J_trace[100], iter_1000 = J_trace[1000], true_model = J_true), 3)
     start   iter_100  iter_1000 true_model 
     4.109      3.556      3.376      3.378

The loss starts near , the loss of a model that assigns every title the same probability, and falls to 3.376, essentially the 3.378 achieved by the true model that generated the data. It ends slightly below the true model because the towers are fit to these same 3,000 plays. Now we can use the trained towers the way they are used at serving time: run the title tower on title features and the query tower on member features, separately, and take dot products. The table scores the six kinds of titles for three members: a romance fan on the TV, the same romance fan on a phone, and an action fan on the TV.

Code 
phi <- function(x) query_tower(x, omega_hat$phi)$out   # trained query tower
psi <- function(f) title_tower(f, omega_hat$psi)$out   # trained title tower

title_types <- rbind(
  "romance-long" = c(1, 0, 0, 1), "romance-short" = c(1, 0, 0, 0),
  "action-long"  = c(0, 1, 0, 1), "action-short"  = c(0, 1, 0, 0),
  "family-long"  = c(0, 0, 1, 1), "family-short"  = c(0, 0, 1, 0)
)
members <- rbind(
  "romance fan, TV"    = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15, 1),
  "romance fan, phone" = c(0.7, 0.15, 0.15, 0),
  "action fan, TV"     = c(0.15, 0.7, 0.15, 1)
)
round(phi(members) %*% t(psi(title_types)), 2)
                   romance-long romance-short action-long action-short
romance fan, TV            3.23          1.66        0.68        -0.57
romance fan, phone        -1.30          0.11       -3.56        -2.06
action fan, TV             1.74          0.32        3.90         2.48
                   family-long family-short
romance fan, TV           1.04        -0.30
romance fan, phone       -3.39        -2.04
action fan, TV            1.66         0.40

Scores are only comparable within a row: adding the same constant to all of one member’s scores leaves the softmax unchanged, so only the order and the gaps within a row matter. Both advantages from the previous section show up. The romance fan’s highest score is for long romances on the TV and short romances on the phone: the same member gets a different embedding in a different context. And the table covers new titles too. A Netflix original that premiered this morning, a long romance, has features , so the title tower gives it exactly the embedding in the first row, and it is scored at the top for the romance fan on the TV before anyone has watched it. The same fact shows the limitation: the title tower only sees features, so it cannot tell two long romances apart. Real title towers add richer content features, and often an embedding of the title’s ID that is learned once the title has views.

In practice, nobody writes backpropagation by hand. Here is the same model written in the mlverse ecosystem: torch, the R interface to LibTorch, the C++ library behind PyTorch, and luz, which supplies the training loop. Each tower is an nn_sequential of a linear layer, a ReLU and another linear layer. The first nn_linear holds and (or and ), and the second holds (or ) along with a bias, which our hand-written version omits. The model’s forward pass returns the matrix of scores , one row per play and one column per title. nn_cross_entropy_loss applies the softmax to each row and averages over the plays, which is exactly . Autograd replaces our hand-written gradient lines, and the optimizer updates the parameters of both towers in every step, because the model’s parameter list contains both. Two choices differ from the version above: we use the Adam optimizer on mini-batches of 256 plays instead of gradient descent on all plays at once, and torch’s default initialization. The data are the same objects as before.

Code 
library(torch)
library(luz)

two_tower <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(f_titles, p_q, n_hidden, d) {
    self$query_tower <- nn_sequential(              # omega_phi
      nn_linear(p_q, n_hidden), nn_relu(), nn_linear(n_hidden, d)
    )
    self$title_tower <- nn_sequential(              # omega_psi
      nn_linear(ncol(f_titles), n_hidden), nn_relu(), nn_linear(n_hidden, d)
    )
    self$f_titles <- nn_buffer(torch_tensor(f_titles))   # all N titles' features, not trained
  },
  forward = function(x_q) {
    phi <- self$query_tower(x_q)                     # one row per play
    psi <- self$title_tower(self$f_titles)           # one row per title
    torch_matmul(phi, psi$t())                       # scores s(q, j)
  }
)

torch_manual_seed(6)
fitted <- two_tower %>%
  setup(loss = nn_cross_entropy_loss(), optimizer = optim_adam) %>%
  set_hparams(f_titles = F_titles, p_q = ncol(X_q), n_hidden = 8, d = 4) %>%
  set_opt_hparams(lr = 0.01) %>%
  fit(data = list(torch_tensor(X_q), torch_tensor(j_played, dtype = torch_long())),
      epochs = 50, dataloader_options = list(batch_size = 256, shuffle = TRUE),
      accelerator = accelerator(cpu = TRUE), verbose = FALSE)

model <- fitted$model
model$eval()
J_torch <- with_no_grad(
  nnf_cross_entropy(model(torch_tensor(X_q)), torch_tensor(j_played, dtype = torch_long()))$item()
)
round(c(torch = J_torch, true_model = J_true), 3)
     torch true_model 
     3.378      3.378

The torch model reaches the same loss. Its scores for the six kinds of titles are not the same numbers as the hand-written model’s, and they should not be: as noted above, the data only determine the gaps between scores within a row. Subtracting each row’s mean removes the arbitrary constant, and then the two models can be compared directly.

))
scores_base <- phi(members) %*% t(psi(title_types))   # the hand-written model from above
dimnames(scores_torch) <- dimnames(scores_base)
center <- function(S) S - rowMeans(S)

After centering, the two models agree to within 0.23 on every entry. They rank all six kinds of titles in the same order for the romance fan on the TV and on the phone. For the action fan, they agree on the top two, long and then short action movies, and only swap titles below that whose scores are nearly tied. The differences come from the different optimizer and initialization, fit to the same 3,000 plays.

Optimization using sampling

Although lists only plays, the loss and the gradients for each play contain a sum over all titles, which costs per play. That is wasteful when it is repeated over billions of plays. Instead, we estimate the sum by importance sampling. Draw negatives from a sampling distribution over titles, where is the probability of drawing title . Multiplying and dividing each term of the denominator by turns the sum into an expectation under , which the sample average estimates,

Each sampled term can be rewritten as

So sampled negatives enter the softmax with a corrected logit . The constant only shifts the loss, so it does not affect the gradient. The cheapest negatives are the titles that other members played in the same mini-batch (“in-batch negatives”). But those are drawn in proportion to how often titles are played, so is large for a hit like Stranger Things. Without the correction, Stranger Things appears as a negative in almost every batch, far more often than under uniform sampling, and the model learns to under-score it. Yi et al. (2019) apply this “logQ correction” to every logit in the batch softmax, estimate from streaming play counts, and serve with the uncorrected .

Phase 2: Predicting utility

Now we have a few hundred candidates instead of 10,000 titles, so we can afford a far more expensive model per title. The model receives a feature vector for each member and candidate pair. It includes member features (genre history, how much they watch on weeknights), title features (genre, runtime, popularity this week), context (TV or phone, Friday night), and the cross features that the two-tower model could not use (finished season 1 of this show). The model outputs , an estimate of .

What is utility?

Before choosing a model, we choose the outcome. Utility is the expected value of something we can measure for a displayed tile, . The choice of matters a lot:

  • Plays: indicates that the member pressed play, and is a play probability.
  • Minutes streamed: utility decomposes into whether the member plays the title and how long they watch once they do, each factor conditional on ,
  • Explicit feedback: whether the member gives the title a thumbs up.

What Netflix ultimately cares about is retention, whether the member keeps their subscription. Gomez-Uribe and Hunt report that viewing time is strongly correlated with retention, which is one reason engagement outcomes such as minutes streamed are useful proxies. Most systems care about several outcomes and combine them,

where is the -th outcome and the weights are a business choice, usually tuned with AB tests on retention and engagement.

Pointwise models

The simplest approach treats every displayed (member, title) tile as an independent row and fits a model to . For a play, that is logistic regression, , where , or a gradient boosted tree, or a neural network. A well-known design is Wide & Deep (Cheng et al., 2016). Its logit is the sum of a wide linear part on hand crafted cross features, which memorizes specific co-occurrences (“watched Breaking Bad” crossed with “candidate is Better Call Saul”), and a deep part, an MLP on learned embeddings, which generalizes to combinations it has never seen.

Predicting expected minutes streamed with a weighted logistic regression

Suppose the utility of a tile is the expected minutes streamed. The data still look like impressions that either were or were not played, and most were not. Covington et al. (2016) faced the same problem when ranking videos by expected watch time rather than click probability. They note that ranking by click-through rate tends to promote deceptive videos that viewers click but do not finish, a theme we return to at the end of this post. To predict expected watch time, they use a weighted logistic regression: played impressions are weighted by their minutes watched, and unplayed impressions get weight 1. Why does this estimate minutes streamed?

Take an intercept-only model for a single title, so we can solve it exactly, and drop the title subscript. The title has impressions, indexed by the query that saw it. Let if impression was played, and let be its minutes watched, with if it was not played. There are plays, a play rate of , and total minutes watched . With , the weighted log likelihood is

Setting the derivative to zero,

The odds are what the model outputs. An unplayed impression has zero minutes watched, so the expected minutes per impression is . Dividing the numerator and denominator by ,

When the play rate is small, is close to 1, and the gap shrinks at rate , so the odds are close to the expected minutes per impression. With features, the same argument applies within each cell of a saturated model, and approximately otherwise. We can check the identity numerically for a title that is played on 5% of its impressions and watched for 40 minutes on average when played.

Code 
set.seed(4)
n <- 1e5
play_rate <- 0.05
impressions <- tibble(y = rbinom(n, 1, play_rate)) %>%
  mutate(ell = if_else(y == 1, rexp(n, rate = 1 / 40), 0),   # minutes watched, 0 if not played
         weight = if_else(y == 1, ell, 1))                  # minutes if played, 1 if not
# quasibinomial gives the same point estimate as binomial, without the non-integer weight warning
fit <- glm(y ~ 1, family = quasibinomial, weights = weight, data = impressions)

impressions %>%
  summarise(n_1 = sum(y), y_bar = n_1 / n(), ell_bar = sum(ell) / n()) %>%
  mutate(odds = exp(coef(fit)[[1]]), ell_bar_over_1_minus_y_bar = ell_bar / (1 - y_bar)) %>%
  select(odds, ell_bar_over_1_minus_y_bar, ell_bar) %>%
  as.data.frame()
      odds ell_bar_over_1_minus_y_bar  ell_bar
1 2.130627                   2.130627 2.025182

Multi-task models

When combines plays, minutes streamed and thumbs up, it is wasteful to train a separate network per outcome. Multi-task models share a common trunk and attach one output head per outcome. Since the outcomes can conflict, for example a title that many members start but few enjoy, the trunk can be split into several shared expert subnetworks, with each outcome learning its own gate that decides how much of each expert to use. This is the Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) design that Zhao et al. (2019) use for video ranking.

Concretely, an MMoE has expert networks , indexed by , each mapping the features to a hidden vector of the same length, shared by every outcome. Each outcome has its own gate, a linear layer followed by a softmax,

whose entries are nonnegative and sum to 1, so they are probability weights over the experts. Outcome sees the weighted average of the experts,

and its own head network turns that into a prediction. Because the weights depend on , each outcome can lean on different experts, and differently for different members and titles.

Let’s build an MMoE for the minutes-streamed utility from earlier, , with one head for each factor. We simulate 20,000 impressions with features : how much of the member’s history is in the title’s genre, whether the title is long, whether the member is on the TV, and whether the title’s artwork is sensational. In the true model, sensational artwork is exactly the conflict described above: it raises the probability of a play, and cuts the minutes watched once the member discovers the title is not what the tile promised. The two heads are

Minutes are only observed for impressions that were played, so the two losses average over different sets of impressions. The play loss is the average binary cross entropy over all impressions. The minutes loss is the average squared error over played impressions only, which is what makes head 2 estimate minutes given a play. We minimize

where is a scalar weight, here 1 over the variance of the observed minutes, which puts the two losses on a comparable scale. Just as in the two-tower model, it helps to say which parameters each loss trains. The experts are shared, so they receive gradients from both losses. Each gate and each head belongs to one outcome, so it receives gradients only from that outcome’s loss.

Code 
library(torch)

# True model: sensational artwork raises plays but cuts minutes watched
p_play_true <- function(match, long, on_tv, sensational) {
  plogis(-2 + 3 * match + 1.5 * sensational + 0.5 * on_tv * long)
}
minutes_given_play_true <- function(match, long, on_tv, sensational) {
  5 + 50 * match + 30 * long * on_tv - 25 * sensational
}

set.seed(8)
n <- 20000
impressions <- tibble(
  match = runif(n),
  long = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  on_tv = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  sensational = rbinom(n, 1, 0.2)
) %>%
  mutate(
    y_play = rbinom(n, 1, p_play_true(match, long, on_tv, sensational)),
    y_minutes = if_else(y_play == 1,                                       # observed only if played
                        pmax(minutes_given_play_true(match, long, on_tv, sensational) + rnorm(n, sd = 8), 0),
                        NA_real_)
  )
X_qj <- impressions %>% select(match, long, on_tv, sensational) %>% as.matrix()

mmoe <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(p, n_experts, n_hidden, n_outcomes) {
    self$experts <- nn_module_list(map(1:n_experts, \(e)        # xi_e, shared
      nn_sequential(nn_linear(p, n_hidden), nn_relu())))
    self$gates <- nn_module_list(map(1:n_outcomes, \(m)         # gamma^(m), one per outcome
      nn_linear(p, n_experts)))
    self$heads <- nn_module_list(map(1:n_outcomes, \(m)         # head_m, one per outcome
      nn_sequential(nn_linear(n_hidden, n_hidden), nn_relu(), nn_linear(n_hidden, 1))))
  },
  gate_weights = function(x) {
    map(seq_along(self$gates), \(m) nnf_softmax(self$gates[[m]](x), dim = 2))
  },
  forward = function(x) {
    xi <- map(seq_along(self$experts), \(e) self$experts[[e]](x)) %>% torch_stack(dim = 3)
    gamma <- self$gate_weights(x)
    map(seq_along(self$heads), \(m) {
      xi_bar <- torch_sum(xi * gamma[[m]]$unsqueeze(2), dim = 3)   # weighted average of experts
      self$heads[[m]](xi_bar)$squeeze(2)
    })
  }
)

torch_manual_seed(8)
model <- mmoe(p = ncol(X_qj), n_experts = 3, n_hidden = 16, n_outcomes = 2)
x <- torch_tensor(X_qj)
y_play_t <- torch_tensor(impressions$y_play, dtype = torch_float())
played <- which(impressions$y_play == 1)
y_minutes_t <- torch_tensor(impressions$y_minutes[played])
nu <- 1 / var(impressions$y_minutes[played])

optimizer <- optim_adam(model$parameters, lr = 0.01)
walk(1:500, \(epoch) {
  optimizer$zero_grad()
  out <- model(x)
  J_play <- nnf_binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(out[[1]], y_play_t)    # all impressions
  J_minutes <- nnf_mse_loss(out[[2]][played], y_minutes_t)              # played impressions only
  J <- J_play + nu * J_minutes
  J$backward()
  optimizer$step()
})

Now compare four kinds of titles for a member on the TV whose history matches the title’s genre well (match = 0.8), with and without sensational artwork.

title_kinds %>%
  mutate(
    P_play_hat = plogis(as_array(out_new[[1]])),
    P_play_true = p_play_true(match, long, on_tv, sensational),

Both heads land close to the true values. The two outcomes disagree about sensational artwork. Among short titles, the play head prefers the sensational one, 0.84 to 0.62, but the minutes head expects it to be watched for 20 minutes instead of 45. Multiplying the two heads gives the expected minutes per impression , which ranks the honest title above the sensational one, 28.0 to 16.8 minutes. A ranker that sorted by the play head alone would put the sensational title first. We will return to this problem when we discuss click-bait.

The gates show how the two outcomes divide the experts. Averaged over all impressions, the weight each outcome puts on each expert is

  set_names(c("play", "minutes")) %>%

In this run, the play head relies mostly on one expert, while the minutes head spreads its weight over the other two. The experts are not labeled in advance and their numbering is arbitrary, so a different seed can permute them, but the pattern of each outcome leaning on different experts is the point of having separate gates.

Learning to rank

A pointwise model predicts for each title in isolation, but a ranker only needs the order within each row to be right. Learning to rank methods optimize the order directly. The pairwise RankNet model says that for two titles and shown to the same member, with scores and ,

and minimizes the cross entropy against the observed preference, for example the member played Titanic but skipped past Die Hard in the same row. Ranking quality is usually measured with normalized discounted cumulative gain,

where is a graded relevance label of the title at position , for example 0 if not played, 1 if played, and 2 if finished. The discount is a hand chosen version of the examination probabilities from our row utility. LambdaRank scales the gradient of each pair by how much NDCG would change if the two titles swapped places, and LambdaMART fits that with boosted trees (Burges, 2010).

There is a trade-off. As with the softmax in the two-tower model, a ranking loss is unchanged if we add the same constant to every score for a member, so its scores are not calibrated: they are not on the scale of plays or minutes. As we will see, phase 3 trades utility against penalties and combines several predictions, which only makes sense when is on a meaningful scale. This is one reason many industrial systems prefer calibrated pointwise models, even though they optimize the order only indirectly.

Position bias: the causal problem inside the training data

Every model above is trained on logs from the previous ranker, and those logs are not an experiment. Recall the examination model from the start of this post. A tile at position is examined with probability , so

where is the probability of a play given that the tile is examined, the quantity we actually want to learn. The observed play rate mixes the title’s appeal with the effect of its position. If last month’s ranker put Stranger Things in the first tile of the row, it collected plays partly because it was the first thing every member saw. Position is a treatment, and the previous ranker assigned it non-randomly: it put the titles it liked at the front. A model trained on raw plays learns that whatever the old ranker liked is good, and then it puts those titles at the front again. This is a feedback loop.

Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel (2017) correct this with inverse propensity weighting. Weight each impression by . Then for a title shown at position ,

The right side does not depend on , so averaging the weighted plays over all of a title’s impressions is unbiased for , no matter how the old ranker distributed the title across positions. Two conditions are required. First, must be known; in practice it is estimated with small randomized experiments that swap or shuffle the tiles in a row for a small fraction of members. Second, the title must have been shown at all. A title the old ranker never displayed has no data, and no reweighting can fix that.

An alternative that fits naturally into a neural model is to give the model the position as an input during training, so that the position effect is absorbed by its own parameters. At serving time, the position input is dropped or set to a constant. Zhao et al. (2019) do this with a small “shallow tower” whose output is added to the main logit.

Let’s simulate it. To keep it small, there is one kind of member, so we drop and write the true appeal of title as . There are 20 titles, and we track only the first 10 tiles of the row, with . On each home page visit, the old ranker fills those 10 tiles with the top titles according to a noisy version of .

Code 
set.seed(2)
J <- 20
K <- 10
n_visits <- 20000
r <- runif(J, 0.05, 0.5)
theta <- 1 / (1:K)

# One home page visit: the old ranker fills the 10 tiles using a noisy version of r
simulate_visit <- function(visit) {
  shown <- order(r + rnorm(J, sd = 0.15), decreasing = TRUE)[1:K]
  tibble(visit = visit, j = shown, k = 1:K, y = rbinom(K, 1, theta * r[shown]))
}

titles <- map(1:n_visits, simulate_visit) %>%
  list_rbind() %>%
  group_by(j) %>%
  summarise(r_naive = mean(y),                # raw play rate
            r_ipw = mean(y / theta[k])) %>%   # inverse propensity weighted
  mutate(r = r[j], .after = j)

The raw play rate is not just shrunk by a constant. The estimate divided by the true is largest for the best titles, because the old ranker gave them the front tiles, so the raw estimate overstates the differences between titles. The weighted estimate sits on the 45 degree line. Titles with low are rarely shown, so their weighted estimates are the noisiest, which is the positivity condition showing up as variance.

Phase 3: Reranking

After phase 2, every candidate has a predicted utility . If (A1) held, we would sort and be done. Reranking exists because it does not hold, and because predicts what we can measure, which is not always what we value. Reranking runs on the top scored candidates. It modifies the objective, enforces constraints, and removes titles that should not be shown. Netflix describes a version of this one level up: its page generation algorithm assembles the rows of the home page, taking into account both the relevance of each row to the member and the diversity of the page (Gomez-Uribe and Hunt, 2015). Here we stay within a single row.

Redundancy, and where diversity comes from

Why should a row of near duplicates be worse than the sum of its parts? Diversity is often presented as a heuristic, but it falls out of a model of row utility. Our member opens Netflix on the living room TV on Friday night. We do not know their mood: they might want a romance, an action movie, or, if the kids are on the couch too, a family film. Let the mood, or intent, be , with probability . Let be the probability that title satisfies a member whose intent is . Ignoring position for simplicity, take the row utility to be the probability that the row satisfies the member, and write it since the member is fixed,

where the product is the probability that no title in the row satisfies intent , assuming titles satisfy the intent independently. This is the objective of intent-aware diversification (Agrawal et al., 2009). Now ask: what is the marginal value of adding title to a partial row ?

When the row is empty, the product is 1 and the marginal value is . That is exactly the isolated utility that phase 2 predicts. So the isolated utility is the marginal value of a title only when it is placed first. After that, each intent’s contribution is discounted by the probability that the intent is still unsatisfied. Once the row has two strong romances, a third romance adds little, while the first good action movie keeps nearly all of its value. This is redundancy, derived rather than assumed.

The marginal value can only shrink as the row grows, because every factor is at most 1. This property is called submodularity. For a monotone submodular function and a fixed row length, the greedy algorithm, which repeatedly adds the title with the largest marginal value, is guaranteed to reach at least a fraction of the optimal row utility (Nemhauser, Wolsey and Fisher, 1978). That is why greedy row construction is so common in reranking.

Let’s compare sorting with greedy selection for the first 5 tiles of the row. The member’s intents are romance, action and family with , and there are 10 candidate titles of each kind. Each title satisfies only its own intent, .

Code 
set.seed(3)
intents <- c("romance", "action", "family")
P_z <- c(0.6, 0.3, 0.1)
z_j <- rep(1:3, each = 10)          # the intent served by each title
p <- runif(30, 0.3, 0.9)            # p_{j z_j}; p_{jz} = 0 for other intents
u <- P_z[z_j] * p                   # isolated utility u(q, j)

U <- function(row) {
  map_dbl(1:3, \(z) P_z[z] * (1 - prod(1 - p[row][z_j[row] == z]))) %>% sum()
}

# Greedy: repeatedly add the title with the largest marginal gain in U
add_best_title <- function(row, step) {
  candidates <- setdiff(seq_along(u), row)
  gain <- map_dbl(candidates, \(j) U(c(row, j)) - U(row))
  c(row, candidates[which.max(gain)])
}

K <- 5
list("sorted by u" = order(u, decreasing = TRUE)[1:K],
     "greedy on U" = reduce(1:K, add_best_title, .init = integer(0))) %>%
  imap(\(titles_in_row, name) tibble(
    row = name,
    intents_shown = paste(intents[z_j[titles_in_row]], collapse = ", "),
    sum_of_u = sum(u[titles_in_row]),
    row_utility_U = U(titles_in_row)
  )) %>%
  list_rbind()
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  row         intents_shown                               sum_of_u row_utility_U
  <chr>       <chr>                                          <dbl>         <dbl>
1 sorted by u romance, romance, romance, romance, romance     2.06         0.598
2 greedy on U romance, action, romance, family, action        1.46         0.934

Sorting by fills every tile with a romance. It maximizes the sum of isolated utilities, which is the additive objective, but the row only satisfies the member if they are in the mood for a romance. The greedy row has a lower sum of isolated utilities and a much higher probability of satisfying the member. The additive objective cannot see the difference.

Calibrating the row to the member’s interests

A related failure is that sorting by amplifies a member’s main interest and crowds out their lesser ones. If a member’s history is 70% romance and 30% action, a row sorted by predicted utility can easily be 100% romance. Steck (2018), writing from Netflix, proposes calibrated recommendations. Let be the distribution of genres in the member’s history, and the distribution of genres in the row. Choose the row to maximize

where the KL divergence measures miscalibration and again weights the penalty. is smoothed slightly toward so that a genre missing from the row does not make the divergence infinite. This objective is again optimized greedily.

Maximal marginal relevance

Return to redundancy. The intent model needs and , which in practice we rarely know. Maximal marginal relevance (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998) keeps the greedy structure and replaces the marginal gain with a heuristic: utility minus a penalty for similarity to what is already in the row,

where is the weight on the similarity penalty. The similarity can come straight from phase 1. Collaborative filtering used the cosine similarity of the columns of ; here we use the cosine similarity of the title embeddings, . Let’s compute it for the six movies of our tiny Netflix, using the embeddings from the matrix factorization.

Code 
Psi_unit <- Psi / sqrt(rowSums(Psi^2))   # rescale each movie embedding to unit length
S <- Psi_unit %*% t(Psi_unit)            # S[j, j'] = cos(psi_j, psi_j')
round(S, 2)
         Notebook Titanic LaLaLand DieHard Matrix Alien
Notebook     1.00    0.97     0.75   -0.13  -0.26 -0.26
Titanic      0.97    1.00     0.89    0.12  -0.01 -0.01
LaLaLand     0.75    0.89     1.00    0.55   0.44  0.44
DieHard     -0.13    0.12     0.55    1.00   0.99  0.99
Matrix      -0.26   -0.01     0.44    0.99   1.00  1.00
Alien       -0.26   -0.01     0.44    0.99   1.00  1.00

Notebook and Titanic have a similarity of 0.97, and the three action movies are nearly identical to one another. If Notebook is already in the row, MMR discounts Titanic heavily and barely discounts Die Hard, whose similarity to Notebook is negative. Setting recovers sorting by . Since and the similarity are added together, MMR is one place where the scale of matters.

The general reranking objective

Calibration and MMR are both variations on one template,

where is a row level penalty (redundancy, miscalibration) and sets the trade-off, playing the same role as in MMR and calibration. For our “Top Picks” row, typical constraints include: no titles the member has already finished, at most one season of the same show, only titles licensed in the member’s country, only titles within the maturity rating of the profile, and no duplicates of a title retrieved by two different candidate sources. Offline data cannot tell us the right , since the value of diversity shows up in long-term behavior, such as whether members keep their subscription. So is usually chosen with AB tests.

Going one step further, a model can score the row as a whole. The personalized re-ranking model of Pei et al. (2019) runs a Transformer over the initial list, so each title’s final score depends on the other titles via self attention. Another pattern is generate-and-evaluate: build several candidate rows (sorted, MMR at a few values of , a calibrated row), score each row with a row level model, and serve the best one.

Removing click-bait

The last job of reranking is to remove titles that score well for the wrong reasons. On Netflix, the click-bait risk lives in the artwork. Decompose utility the way we did for minutes streamed,

Sensational artwork that misrepresents a title raises the first factor and lowers the second: members press play, realize the show is not what the tile promised, and quit within a few minutes. A model trained on plays only sees the first factor, so it ranks such tiles highly. Worse, the ranker’s own feedback loop amplifies it, since the tile collects even more plays once it is placed at the front of the row. This is a surrogate outcome problem: the label we can measure cheaply is not the outcome we care about. Netflix faced exactly this when it began personalizing artwork: it wanted artwork that is “engaging, informative and representative of a title to avoid ‘clickbait’”, and chose its training labels by looking at the quality of engagement, so as not to learn images that entice a member to start playing but end in low-quality engagement (Chandrashekar et al., 2017). Remedies work at different levels:

  • Change the label. Predict an outcome measured after the play, such as minutes streamed, whether the member finished the title, a thumbs up, or whether they came back the next day.
  • Use post-play behavior as a signal. A title that members frequently abandon in the first few minutes is a warning sign, even if its play rate is high.
  • Train a dedicated classifier. Have people label tiles for whether the artwork misrepresents the title, train a classifier on those labels, and let it produce the probability that tile is click-bait. A reranker uses either as a hard filter (a tile with above a threshold is removed) or as a soft demotion, such as .

The same filter-or-demote pattern handles titles that are about to leave the catalog, low-quality titles, and content that violates policy.

Putting it together

Phase Input Output Typical models In our Netflix row Judged by
Candidate generation titles (thousands) candidates (hundreds) BM25, item-to-item CF, matrix factorization, two-tower “heist” matches, Because You Watched neighbors, SVD affinities, two-tower scores Recall@
Utility prediction candidates per title Logistic regression, GBDT, Wide & Deep, multi-task networks, learning to rank Play probability, expected minutes streamed, corrected for the position of past tiles Calibration, NDCG, log loss
Reranking Top scored candidates A row of Greedy submodular selection, calibration, MMR, row level models, filters A row that covers romance, action and family moods, without click-bait artwork Row utility, measured online

Each phase exists to repair an assumption that made the ideal problem easy. Exhaustive scoring is too expensive, so phase 1 trades accuracy for recall at low cost. Utility is unknown, so phase 2 estimates it, and in doing so must undo the causal effect of position that the previous ranker baked into its training data. Titles in a row interact, so phase 3 replaces the additive row utility with an objective that values coverage and penalizes redundancy and click-bait. And because offline logs only show the rows the old ranker chose to display, the final judge of any change to the ranker is an AB test.

item.title: What does it mean to be the average effect?
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Wong
item.description:
Oh what’s in a name?

The term “average treatment effect” embodies two concepts - the treatment effect, which has a distribution, and its average over users. It is very precise, and yet the term is used loosely in the industry. This post will drill down into the mathematical underpinnings of what it means to be an average treatment effect, and explore its many variations such as the conditional effect, the marginal and relative effects, the incremental effect, the intent to treat effect and the local effect.

Grounding the mathematical foundations

What is an Average?

Say that we have a random variable . It is able to take values in a set , and it has probability density . Then the mathematical definition of an average has two parts, the value , and its probability density. It is computed as

Transformations of the random variable, for example , have mean

As we go over different types of effects, we will consolidate them all into the form

again emphasizing the product of a value and a probability weight.

Averages that Vary with Covariates

So far the value of varied randomly. Now say that it can vary as a function of covariates , which have their own probability density , and the distribution of depends on through the conditional probability density . At this point there are three probability densities to remember, , , and . In experiment analyses we can assume that we are given a fixed value. The conditional mean for becomes

The quantity is still , but the probability weight is now . For each outputs a number. As varies, is a function of .

The unconditional average can be rebuilt from the conditional ones. The marginal probability density of is the conditional probability density averaged over , . We substitute this into the definition of , then swap the order of integration, which is allowed when :

This is the law of iterated expectations. In our notation, the quantity is now the conditional average and the probability weight is . Averaging happens in two stages: first within the users who share the same , then across values of , weighted by how common each is.

Most of the subtlety in this post is identifying the value and the probability weight. If we keep the quantity but replace the probability weight with a different probability density, for example , the probability density of covariates among treated users, we get a different average, one over the covariates of treated users rather than of all users.

The Difference in Expectations

Now we apply this to an AB test. Each user has two potential outcomes: , the outcome if treated, and , the outcome if not treated. When treated, user receives an individual effect that depends on their covariates,

Here is the baseline, a scalar function of , so the noise satisfies . We also write . Taking the conditional expectation of the second line gives .

We only ever observe one of the two potential outcomes. With indicating whether user was treated, the observed outcome is

This is the model from the post on controlled randomization, with a heterogeneous effect and a baseline that varies with covariates.

The difference in expectations compares the average outcome of treated users with the average outcome of untreated users. We apply the law of iterated expectations again within each arm, using that arm’s own covariate probability density, and then substitute the model for :

So the difference in expectations is a difference of two integrals. Randomization means is independent of both and , which has two consequences:

  1. , so both integrals use the same probability weight.
  2. , so the noise terms vanish.

With a shared probability weight, linearity of the integral gives the reduction

This is our grounding for the word “average” in “average treatment effect”. The quantity is the personalized effect , and the probability weight is , the probability density of covariates.

Note that without randomization, the two integrals use different probability weights, and the reduction breaks!

What does it mean to be a treatment effect?

Within the science of cause and effect, there are actually many different types of effects that we can report. Average effects, incremental effects, conditional effects, and relative effects. It can be daunting to manage the nuances of all of these different types of treatment effects, but actually we can consolidate them all under one roof. Mathematically, they are all different variations of an average.

Individual Effects and Conditional Average Treatment Effect

We start with the finest grained effect possible, then build our way up. The individual effect of user is , which we can never truly observe. The conditional average treatment effect (CATE) averages the individual effects among users who share the same covariates,

As an average, the quantity is the individual effect and the probability weight is the conditional probability density of individual effects among users with . Let denote a value of the individual effect , and let be its probability density among users with . Then

This is the same form as , with the individual effect in place of .

Average Treatment Effect

Just as the CATE is the average of individual effects, the average treatment effect (ATE) is an average of the CATE over the covariate probability density,

The ATE is an average with respect to , the covariate probability density of the population the experiment samples from. Here, it is very important to note who qualifies to be in the population. If an experiment only enrolls users who visit a certain page, then is the probability density among those visitors, and is the average effect for visitors, not for all users.

Marginal Effect and Relative Effects

Given two mean functions, and , there are two aggregation strategies that turn these functions into a single number for experimentation reporting.

The classic ATE computes at each , then averages. It starts from the granular level then aggregates. Uniquely, it’s fine to reverse the order of operations.

The other approach is to compute averages first, and then compare. We saw the importance of this in the post on ratio metrics.

and the marginal effect is a contrast of and . This prompts an interesting thought though, is the relative effect an outlier in this taxonomy on averages? We will explain below that it is not.

The Difference: Order Does Not Matter

For the difference contrast, both orders give the same number. Using the linearity of the integral and then the definition of ,

The Relative Effect: Order Matters

For a nonlinear contrast, the two orders can give different numbers. The clearest example is the relative effect. The post on relative effects described an experiment with a few power users and many casual users, where the metric goes down for power users but up for casual users. To make it concrete, say power users make up 10% of users and have a baseline of 100, while casual users make up 90% and have a baseline of 1. The treatment lowers the metric of power users by 1% and raises the metric of casual users by 10%.

Segment Share Baseline Relative effect
Power users 0.1 100
Casual users 0.9 1

Did the treatment move the metric up or down? There are two natural ways to answer.

  1. How did the typical user change? We compute the relative effect within each segment, then average across users: . Most users improved by 10%, so the answer is up.
  2. How did the total change? We average the metric within each arm first, then compute the relative change. The control mean is and the treatment mean is , so the relative change is . Power users carry most of the volume, so the answer is down.

Neither answer is wrong, and neither is better. They are different interpretations of the same experiment. The first counts users, and the second counts volume. A team that wants to help as many users as possible is asking the first question. A team that reports total revenue is asking the second.

To see how the two are related, we write them in general. Assume for all . The conditional relative effect is a function of ,

In the example, is the segment, and is the last column of the table. With a discrete covariate, an integral against becomes a sum over segments, weighted by their shares. The two answers generalize to

  1. Contrast first, then average. The average of the conditional relative effects is .
  2. Average first, then contrast. The marginal relative effect is .

is already an average of . At first glance is a ratio of two averages rather than an average of anything. But it shares the same root, . First we write and replace the numerator with . Then we multiply and divide the integrand by , which is allowed because :

The probability weight is a valid probability density. It is nonnegative because , and it integrates to by the definition of . Therefore the two approaches now have something in common

Both relative effects are averages of the same quantity, . They differ only in the probability weight. uses , which counts each user once. uses , which counts each user in proportion to their baseline volume. In the example, the probability weights for are for power users and for casual users, and recovers the second answer. So choosing how to express the relative effect is simply choosing a probability weight.

The choice only matters when the relative effect is related to the baseline. The gap between the two is

where the expectations and the covariance are over , and we used and . When the relative effect is unrelated to the baseline, the two probability weights give the same answer. In the example, the users with large baselines have the worst relative effects, so the covariance is negative and .

The Incremental Effect

So far we have discussed treatments and controls as binary. The incremental effect concerns treatments given in multiple doses. It measures the effect of providing an additional dose of the treatment.

A Curve of Potential Outcomes

Say each user enters the experiment having already received doses, which we call their prior dose, using for the starting point. Different users have different prior doses, so is a pre-treatment covariate, and we write for the joint probability density of and the other covariates . The experiment randomizes an increment , and user receives a total dose of . Users in the control arm, , continue with doses. Users in the top arm receive doses, and the arms in between receive , and so on.

In the binary case, each user had two potential outcomes, and . Now each user has a potential outcome for every dose , so is a curve. From here on, the argument of is a number of doses, so is the outcome with one dose. The conditional mean of that curve is

a scalar for each dose , prior dose and covariate value . It conditions on because two users with the same covariates but different prior doses can respond differently to the same dose.

The Incremental Effect is an Average

Today, the users in our sample have a distribution of prior doses. Say some users have 1 dose, some have 2, and some have 3. A natural question is: what happens if we give everyone one extra dose, which shifts them to 2, 3 and 4 doses? For user , the answer is the difference between their outcome with one extra dose and their outcome at their current dose, . With extra doses, the individual effect is .

Averaging these individual effects among users who share the same prior dose and covariates gives a conditional effect, which plays the role of the CATE,

The incremental effect of extra doses averages over the joint probability density of prior doses and covariates,

so the quantity is and the probability weight is , in the same form as the ATE. The incremental effect curve plots against the number of extra doses . It starts at , because zero extra doses changes nothing.

In the example, let be the share of users with prior doses. With a discrete prior dose, the integral over becomes a sum weighted by these shares, and the first point on the curve is

Figure 1 draws the curve for this example, with shares , and . For illustration we use a dose response with diminishing returns, with , which depends only on the total dose . The colored lines are the conditional curves , one for each prior dose, and the black line is the incremental effect curve , their average weighted by the shares.

Code 
library(ggplot2)

# Share of users at each prior dose, p_s
p_s <- c(`1` = 0.5, `2` = 0.3, `3` = 0.2)
s <- as.numeric(names(p_s))
k <- 0:5

# Dose response with diminishing returns, depending only on the total dose
g <- function(d) 10 * log(1 + d)

# Conditional curves C_k(s) = g(s + k) - g(s), one per prior dose
C_k_s <- expand.grid(k = k, s = s)
C_k_s$C <- g(C_k_s$s + C_k_s$k) - g(C_k_s$s)
C_k_s$series <- paste0("C[k](s)*\", s = ", C_k_s$s, "\"")

# Incremental effect curve C(k) = sum_s p_s C_k(s)
C_k <- data.frame(k = k, C = sapply(k, function(k) sum(p_s * (g(s + k) - g(s)))))
C_k$series <- "C(k)*\", average\""

curves <- rbind(C_k_s[, c("k", "C", "series")], C_k)
# Series names are plotmath expressions, so C_k(s) renders with a subscript
series <- c(unique(C_k_s$series), C_k$series[1])
series_colors <- setNames(c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#0b0b0b"), series)
series_widths <- setNames(c(0.6, 0.6, 0.6, 1.2), series)
labels <- curves[curves$k == max(k), ]

ggplot(curves, aes(x = k, y = C, color = series)) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = series)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(label = series), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.12,
            size = 4, color = "#52514e", parse = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = series_colors, breaks = series,
                     labels = parse(text = series), name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = series_widths, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.35))) +
  labs(x = "Number of extra doses, k", y = "Incremental effect") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

Two patterns are visible. First, every curve flattens as grows, because each extra dose adds less than the one before it. Second, users who start from more doses gain less from the same number of extra doses, so the conditional curves are ordered by prior dose. The average lies between them, and above the middle curve for at every , because the curve for carries half of the probability weight and pulls the average up.

Step Effects are the Slope of the Curve

is the total effect of extra doses. The step from to extra doses is the effect of the -th dose alone. Among users with prior dose and covariates , the step effect is

and averaging over gives .

So the step effect is the slope of the incremental effect curve between and . Conversely, the curve is the accumulation of its steps. Writing as a sum of differences, the intermediate terms cancel in pairs, and gives

AB Tests and Incremental Tests Measure Different Things

It is tempting to think of the classic AB test as an incremental test with a single step. It is not, and the two tests answer different questions.

The AB test compares zero doses with a nonzero number of doses. The control group receives zero doses. The treatment group receives a nonzero number of doses, but that number varies from user to user: one treated user might receive 2 doses, and another might receive 10. What we randomize is access to the treatment, , not the number of doses. Each user has a potential dose , the number of doses user would receive if treated, and . Unlike the increment in an incremental test, the experimenter does not choose . It is determined by the user’s behavior, or by how the treatment is delivered. A treated user’s outcome is and a control user’s outcome is , so by randomization the AB test measures

The AB test is also an average over doses, but of a self-selected curve. Let be the share of treated users who receive doses. Applying the law of total expectation over the potential dose, and noting that for users with ,

where we define the self-selected curve as the effect of doses among the users who would receive doses,

This looks similar to the incremental effect. is an average with quantity and probability weight , the distribution of doses in the treatment arm. But the identity holds by construction: both sides are computed from the same treated users, once all together and once grouped by dose. It tells us how is assembled, not how the outcome responds to the dose.

Note: The self-selected curve is only sometimes equal to the dose response. Compare with the incremental effect curve from earlier, at prior dose :

averages the effect of doses over every user, while averages it only over the users who choose doses. for every only when there is no selection on gains, meaning the number of doses a user receives is unrelated to how much they would gain from any given number of doses. That is usually unreasonable. The dose is often how many times a user opens a feature or clicks a notification, and users who find the treatment valuable use it more. It also cannot be tested, because for a user who receives doses we never observe their outcome at any other dose. Similarly, the differences are not the step effects . Each point of averages over a different group of users, so a difference between two points mixes the effect of the extra dose with the difference between the two groups.

AB test results depend on the dose distribution. Because , the word “average” in the ATE refers to the dose distribution as well as to the covariate probability density . Two launches of the same treatment can yield different results: if users of the first launch mostly receive 2 doses and users of the second mostly receive 10, the two AB tests average over different parts of the curve and report different values of , even when the treatment itself is unchanged.

AB test results cannot be reconstructed from incremental results. They are different. That’s OK. Even if an incremental test mapped perfectly, would equal only under no selection on gains, which is when . In the other direction, the AB test cannot map , because the dose is not randomized. Even cannot be estimated from it, because is never observed for control users. The two tests serve two different purposes.

  • The AB test measures . It answers: what happens if we launch the treatment and let users choose their own dose?
  • The incremental test measures . It answers: what happens if we change how many doses users receive? This is the question behind dosing decisions, such as sending every user three notifications instead of one.

Analyzing an Incremental Test in R

To measure the incremental effect curve, the experiment needs one row per user with four pieces of information:

Column Symbol Measured Description
X Before randomization Covariates, such as pre-period engagement
S Before randomization Prior dose, the number of doses the user already receives
K Randomized Number of extra doses, , with as the control arm
y After treatment Outcome

The randomization structure has two requirements. First, must be randomized independently of and , so that every arm has the same joint probability density . Second, every point on the curve needs its own arm. An experiment with only the arms and measures , but not the shape of the curve on the way there.

We simulate such an experiment with , so there are six arms, and users are split evenly across them. Prior doses follow the example from earlier, with shares , and , and users with more prior doses tend to be more engaged, so and are correlated. The outcome is

so the conditional mean of the potential outcome curve is . The baseline cancels in , and depends only on the total dose, so the true incremental effect curve is the black curve in Figure 1.

Code 
set.seed(3)
n <- 60000
k_bar <- 5

S <- sample(s, n, replace = TRUE, prob = p_s)  # prior dose, with shares p_s
X <- rnorm(n, mean = 0.5 * (S - 1.7))          # engagement, higher for larger S
K <- sample(0:k_bar, n, replace = TRUE)        # randomized number of extra doses
y <- 20 + 8 * X + g(S + K) + rnorm(n, sd = 5)

df <- data.frame(user_id = seq_len(n), X = X, S = S, K = K, y = y)
knitr::kable(head(df), digits = 2)
user_id X S K y
1 -0.86 1 2 22.84
2 2.35 3 0 55.76
3 -0.97 1 4 26.66
4 -0.63 1 2 35.88
5 -0.54 2 5 36.09
6 1.31 2 5 52.20

We estimate the curve in two ways. The first is the difference in means between each arm and the control arm, , with standard error , where , and are the mean, variance and size of arm . Each point on the curve is an ordinary AB comparison against the control arm.

The second is a regression of on indicators for each arm, adjusting for and ,

The coefficient estimates . Because is randomized independently of and , remains a consistent estimate of even though the model leaves out interactions between and . The covariates explain much of the variation in the baseline, which shrinks the standard errors, the same idea as CUPED.

The step effects are differences of adjacent points, with . We compute them with a contrast matrix , a matrix with 1 on the diagonal and just below it, so that and .

Code 
# Difference in means against the control arm, K = 0
y_bar <- tapply(df$y, df$K, mean)
s2 <- tapply(df$y, df$K, var)
n_k <- tapply(df$y, df$K, length)
C_hat_dm <- y_bar - y_bar["0"]
se_C_hat_dm <- sqrt(s2 / n_k + s2["0"] / n_k["0"])

# Regression with arm indicators, adjusting for X and S
fit <- lm(y ~ factor(K) + X + factor(S), data = df)
beta_hat <- coef(fit)[paste0("factor(K)", 1:k_bar)]
V_beta_hat <- vcov(fit)[names(beta_hat), names(beta_hat)]
C_hat_reg <- c(0, beta_hat)
se_C_hat_reg <- c(0, sqrt(diag(V_beta_hat)))

# Step effects tau_k = beta_k - beta_{k-1}
L <- diag(k_bar)
L[cbind(2:k_bar, 1:(k_bar - 1))] <- -1
tau_k_hat <- drop(L %*% beta_hat)
se_tau_k_hat <- sqrt(diag(L %*% V_beta_hat %*% t(L)))

# Ground truth from the dose response and the shares p_s
k_values <- 0:k_bar
C_true <- sapply(k_values, function(k) sum(p_s * (g(s + k) - g(s))))
tau_k_true <- diff(C_true)
Code 
est_se <- function(est, se) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", est, se)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    k = k_values,
    C_true = sprintf("%.2f", C_true),
    C_hat_dm = c("—", est_se(C_hat_dm[-1], se_C_hat_dm[-1])),
    C_hat_reg = c("—", est_se(C_hat_reg[-1], se_C_hat_reg[-1])),
    tau_k_true = c("—", sprintf("%.2f", tau_k_true)),
    tau_k_hat = c("—", est_se(tau_k_hat, se_tau_k_hat))
  ),
  col.names = c("$k$", "True $C(k)$", "$\\hat{C}(k)$, difference in means",
                "$\\hat{C}(k)$, regression", "True $\\tau_k$", "$\\hat{\\tau}_k$, regression"),
  align = "rrrrrr"
)
Code 
estimates <- data.frame(k = k_values, C_hat = C_hat_reg,
                        lower = C_hat_reg - 1.96 * se_C_hat_reg,
                        upper = C_hat_reg + 1.96 * se_C_hat_reg)
truth <- data.frame(k = k_values, C = C_true)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = truth, aes(x = k, y = C, color = "True C(k)"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_errorbar(data = estimates, aes(x = k, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, color = "Estimate"),
                width = 0.15, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = estimates, aes(x = k, y = C_hat, color = "Estimate"), size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("True C(k)" = "#0b0b0b", "Estimate" = "#2a78d6"),
                     breaks = c("True C(k)", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = k_values) +
  labs(x = "Number of extra doses, k", y = "Incremental effect") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

The regression estimates track the true closely at every .

What does it mean to be treated?

In many experiments we randomize an assignment , not the intervention itself. means we intend to treat the user. The treatment the user actually receives, , can differ from . This paper argues that there are multiple stages of delivering treatment, and describes mistakes when confusing with .

As a running example, say we launch a new feature and announce it by email. The assignment is whether a user is sent the email. When we are trying to treat the user, when we are trying to withhold from the user. The treatment is whether the user actually uses the feature, which is the user’s choice and not something we can control. The outcome is the user’s engagement. Figure 3 shows how these variables affect one another. collects everything about the user that influences both their choice and their outcome: the covariates , the compliance type defined below, and traits we do not measure.

The graph separates the three ways the outcome can change. The feature changes behavior for users who use it, along . Whether a user uses it is their own choice, which depends on who they are, along . And the email can change behavior on its own, along the dashed arrow , for example by reminding users that the product exists. Because points into both and , the users who choose the feature differ from those who do not, even before they use it. This is why we randomize rather than compare users by .

Each user has two potential treatments: , the treatment user would receive if assigned to the treatment, and , the treatment they would receive if assigned to the control. The observed treatment is . The pair sorts users into four compliance types, which we label :

Type Description
Always-taker, 1 1 Receives the intervention regardless of assignment
Never-taker, 0 0 Never receives the intervention, for example because delivery fails
Complier, 1 0 Receives the intervention if and only if assigned to it
Defier, 0 1 Does the opposite of the assignment

Let be the share of type among users with . The overall share is .

Connecting the ITT to the effect of the feature takes three assumptions: randomization, exclusion and monotonicity. Rather than state them all at once, we introduce them one at a time, each at the step where it is first needed. This makes clear which conclusions rest on which assumptions. Only the first is needed to define the ITT.

  1. Randomization. is independent of , the type , and the potential outcomes . In the figure there is no arrow , because a coin flip, not the user’s traits, decides who gets the email.

The intent to treat effect (ITT) is the difference in expectations between the assignment arms, and here we emphasize that it is not the effect from being treated, rather it is the effect from the business trying to treat the user. This quantity is rooted in randomness and is robust, whereas analysis on is much more complex and it is hard to be robust. The ITT looks just like the ATE, with a quantity and a probability weight, and has the following analogous formulas.

These formulas rely on randomization alone. Even if the email has its own effect, along the dashed arrow in Figure 3, is still exactly the effect of sending the email. The next two assumptions are needed only when we try to attribute the ITT to the feature itself.

Decomposing the ITT

To see what the ITT says about the intervention itself, we decompose . The first step needs the second assumption.

  1. Exclusion. The assignment affects the outcome only through the treatment received, so the potential outcomes and do not depend on . In Figure 3, this means the dashed arrow is absent, and the only path from to runs through . It fails if the email changes behavior even among users who never use the feature.

Under assignment , user receives . Without exclusion, their outcome would depend on both the assignment and the treatment received, . Exclusion removes the direct dependence on , so their outcome is . Randomization means that, among users with , the assignment does not change the distribution of types or potential outcomes, so

Next we apply the law of total expectation over the four types, , and evaluate for each type using the table above:

  • Always-takers have , so the difference is .
  • Never-takers have , so the difference is .
  • Compliers have and , so the difference is .
  • Defiers have and , so the difference is .

Let be the CATE within type . Then

The defiers enter with a negative sign. If they exist, their effect can cancel the compliers’ effect, and the ITT can be zero even when the intervention helps! So we add a third assumption.

  1. Monotonicity. There are no defiers, for every user, so . Assignment never makes a user less likely to receive the intervention. This often holds by design. For example, if control users have no way to access the intervention, there are neither always-takers nor defiers.

Under monotonicity, , and integrating over ,
